false_friends.divergence: 党派 (tōha, dǎngpài) names factional groupings or partisan alignments more broadly, often with the classical negative valence of 党 still active — 党派性 (tōhasei, partisanship) carries the specifically negative register of factional bias against the public interest. 政党 in its modern usage names the legitimate institutional form of the political party as a permanent organized association, while 党派 covers a broader range from legitimate parties to informal factional groupings to negatively-valenced cliques. Reading 政党 as if it were equivalent to 党派 imports the classical negative register that the modern compound is calibrated to overcome.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized in the 1880s constitutional drafting process under Itō Hirobumi (with German jurist Hermann Roesler as legal adviser); institutionalized through the Meiji Constitution of 1889 (大日本帝国憲法) and authoritatively glossed in Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries on the Constitution (憲法義解, 1889)

components.meaning: lord, master, that which is principal — here the structural-political register of supremacy, naming the bearer of the highest authority within the polity
right, power, authority — the calibrated weight on the steelyard, here in its authoritative-power register; paired with 主 to articulate 'the master power' that grounds the legal-political order

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in constitutional law and political theory; carries the modern Western register of supreme authority that is not subject to any superior power

literal-decompositional rendering — preserves the structural sense of 主 (master) + 権 (power) by foregrounding the supremacy register; useful for explaining the compound's articulation of sovereignty as the highest authority within the constitutional order

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the German constitutional-theoretical lineage from which the Meiji constitutional drafters most directly inherited; the German Staatsgewalt (state power) is doctrinally close to 主権 in its register of foundational political authority

conceptual_remainder: 主権 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango that uses native East Asian characters to render a distinctively modern Western legal-political concept — the Bodinian-Hobbesian-Rousseauian articulation of supreme authority as the structural ground of the political order — for which there is no precise classical-Chinese precedent. Classical Chinese political vocabulary articulated the structure of supreme authority through different categories: 天命 (the heavenly mandate), 帝権 (imperial prerogative), 王権 (royal authority), 国家 (the state-house), but none of these compounds carries the specifically modern register of sovereignty as a singular indivisible legal-political category that is the conceptual core of the Western constitutional-theoretical tradition. The Meiji compound 主権 was calibrated to render this modern register through a Sino-Japanese articulation that was structurally novel: 主 (the master/principal) combined with 権 (right/power) produces a compound that names not the person who holds authority (帝, 王, 皇) but the abstract structural-political category itself. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of supreme authority: 主 (master) + 権 (power). What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Bodinian register of sovereignty as indivisible, perpetual, and absolute — Bodin's articulation rests on a doctrinal foundation in Roman-law conceptions of imperium and in early-modern European theological-political reflection on the location of the highest authority in a Christian commonwealth that the Japanese characters themselves do not transmit. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asia has been doctrinally consequential. The Meiji Constitution of 1889 located 主権 in the Emperor (Article 1: 大日本帝国ハ万世一系ノ天皇之ヲ統治ス, 'the Empire of Japan shall be reigned over and governed by a line of Emperors unbroken for ages eternal'), reflecting the German Staatssouveränität / monarchical-sovereignty tradition rather than the Atlantic Volkssouveränität / popular-sovereignty tradition. The post-war 1947 Constitution inverted this relocation by grounding sovereignty in the people (主権の存する日本国民, 'the Japanese people, in whom resides sovereignty'), but the same compound 主権 carries both the imperial-sovereignty articulation of 1889 and the popular-sovereignty articulation of 1947, and the question of where sovereignty is properly located within the constitutional order has been one of the load-bearing questions of modern Japanese political life across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as part of the institutional cluster of liberal-democratic political vocabulary alongside 憲法 (constitution), 民主 (democracy), 共和 (republic), 革命 (revolution), 国会 (national assembly). 主権 is structurally pivotal within the cluster because it names the supreme authority that the other terms operationalize: 憲法 is the foundational instrument that articulates the structure of 主権 within the constitutional order; 民主 names the political form in which 主権 is located in the people; 共和 names the political form in which 主権 is exercised through representative institutions rather than vested in a hereditary monarch. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji Constitution's location of 主権 in the Emperor (1889) and the post-war Constitution's relocation of 主権 in the people (1947) frame the central political-constitutional transformation of modern Japanese political history. The compound's adoption into Chinese (zhǔquán) made it the operating term of late-Qing and Republican Chinese constitutional discourse, and it remains the operating term of the People's Republic's constitutional vocabulary, with Article 2 of the 1982 PRC Constitution articulating that 'all power in the People's Republic of China belongs to the people' (中华人民共和国的一切权力属于人民) — a popular-sovereignty articulation that uses the same Japanese-coined vocabulary the Meiji constitutional drafters had stabilized. The compound is also embedded in the broader vocabulary of modern international relations through 国家主権 (kokka shuken, state sovereignty), 主権国家 (shuken kokka, sovereign state), and 主権平等 (shuken byōdō, sovereign equality) — the operating vocabulary of the post-Westphalian international state-system as it has been articulated in modern East Asian discourse.

false_friends.divergence: 統治権 (tōchiken, tǒngzhìquán) names the right or power to govern — the active prerogative of governance exercised by the bearer of sovereignty rather than the abstract structural category of sovereignty itself. The Meiji Constitution's Article 1 deploys 統治 (to reign and govern) as the verb whose subject is the Emperor and whose object is the Empire, with 主権 as the abstract structural category that 統治権 actualizes in concrete governance. Reading 主権 as equivalent to 統治権 conflates the structural-political category with the operational-governmental prerogative; the distinction between them is doctrinally consequential in constitutional theory and in the legal-political analysis of where supreme authority is located versus how it is exercised.

coinage_notes: Classical Chinese compound (attested across the Confucian classical corpus including the Analects, Mencius, Xunzi, and the official histories) re-coined in Meiji Japan to render Western 'politics' as a systematic discipline; institutionalized through Meiji-period political and academic vocabulary

components.meaning: to govern, government, political affairs — the rectifying-administrative function of the polity; here the domain-naming first character of the compound, locating 政治 in the field of governance

to regulate, to order, to heal — the restoration of disordered conditions to proper measure; paired with 政 to articulate the systematic activity of governance as the regulated administration of the polity

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in political science and political theory contexts; carries the modern Western register of politics as both a practical activity and a systematic discipline

alternative rendering — foregrounds the classical-Chinese register of 政治 as the activity of governing rather than the modern register of politics as systematic discipline; useful in classical-Chinese contexts and in discussions of pre-modern political theory
rendering used when the compound names the domain of public affairs rather than the activity or discipline; standard in compounds like 内政 (domestic affairs) and 外政 (foreign policy)

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the German and French political-theoretical lineages from which Meiji translators drew; the German Politik carries both the activity-and-discipline register that 政治 articulates

conceptual_remainder: 政治 in its classical Chinese register named the activity of governance — the rectifying-administrative function of the ruler in ordering the polity. The compound is attested across the Confucian classical corpus, with the Analects's articulation 政者正也 ('to govern is to rectify') supplying the doctrinal frame within which classical 政治 was received: governance is the activity of restoring the polity to proper order through the moral cultivation of the ruler and the calibrated administration of the people. The Meiji repurposing extends this classical compound from the register of governance-as-activity to the modern register of politics-as-systematic-discipline, supplying the operating term for political science as an academic field and for the broader Western category of politics as a distinct domain of human practice and inquiry. The extension is doctrinally consequential. What the classical compound carried — governance as the moral-administrative activity of the ruler — is preserved in the modern usage but is now subordinated to a broader frame in which politics names a structural domain (alongside law 法律, economy 経済, society 社会) rather than the activity of a particular agent. The Meiji compound thereby articulates politics as an autonomous sphere of practice and inquiry, in line with the Western differentiation of social-scientific disciplines, while preserving the classical-Confucian register of 政治 as continuous with the moral-political tradition. What the Japanese characters cannot easily carry is the specifically agonistic register of Western political theory — the Schmittian articulation of politics as the friend-enemy distinction, the Machiavellian register of politics as the contestation of power for its own sake, the modern liberal-pluralist articulation of politics as the procedural management of irreducible conflict. The classical-Confucian register of governance-as-rectification continues to inflect the modern compound and tends to displace the agonistic-conflictual register that the Western tradition foregrounds. This unresolved tension — modern systematic discipline carrying classical moral-administrative valence — has been generative across modern East Asian political thought, with debates about the proper relationship between politics and morality, politics and ethics, and politics and rectification recurring across the post-Meiji period in vocabulary that the classical 政治 supplies.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as the structural-domain term that organizes the broader cluster of Meiji liberal-political vocabulary: 政治 names the field within which 主権 is located, 憲法 is articulated, 民主 is structured, 政党 compete, 選挙 are conducted, and 国会 deliberates. The compound is institutionally pivotal because it supplies the operating term for political science (政治学, seijigaku) as the academic discipline that emerged in the Meiji university system through the Faculties of Law and Letters at Tokyo Imperial University and other early Meiji higher educational institutions. The disciplinary establishment of 政治学 across the Meiji period made the compound the operating term of the East Asian academic study of politics, and the Japanese coinage was adopted into Chinese (zhèngzhì) and Korean (정치) as the standard term for both the activity of politics and the academic discipline of political science. The compound is also embedded in an extensive vocabulary of modern political life: 政治家 (seijika, politician), 政治哲学 (seiji tetsugaku, political philosophy), 政治経済 (seiji keizai, political economy), 国際政治 (kokusai seiji, international politics), 政治体制 (seiji taisei, political system), 政治改革 (seiji kaikaku, political reform), 政治運動 (seiji undō, political movement). The character 政 heads the entire institutional vocabulary of the modern political domain — 政治, 政府, 政党, 政策, 政権, 行政 — and 政治 in its modern Meiji-stabilized sense is the structural anchor around which this larger vocabulary organizes itself.

false_friends.divergence: 政事 (seiji, zhèngshì) is a distinct compound, homophonous with 政治 in modern Japanese but differently constituted: 政 (government) + 事 (affairs/matters). Classical Chinese usage frequently pairs the two compounds, with 政事 carrying the register of 'affairs of state, administrative matters' (the concrete particular business of governance) and 政治 carrying the register of 'governance, political order' (the activity and structure of governing). Modern Japanese usage has largely displaced 政事 in favor of 政治 across most contexts, but the classical distinction remains active in formal-register and historical-Chinese contexts. Reading 政治 as if it were equivalent to 政事 imports the concrete-administrative register at the expense of the structural-political register that the modern compound is calibrated to articulate.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized across the 1870s and 1880s as the productive Japanese suffix for Western -isms; deployed across Meiji translations of Western philosophical, political, and economic vocabulary and adopted into Chinese (zhǔyì) through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings

conceptual_remainder: 主義 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango that supplies the productive Japanese suffix for Western -ism doctrines while preserving the classical-Confucian register of 義 as guiding principle. The compound is structurally novel in East Asian intellectual vocabulary: pre-modern Sino-Japanese discourse had names for particular schools (儒, 佛, 道) and for particular doctrines (仁, 礼, 性), but no productive suffix that could attach to substantives and convert them into doctrine-names. The Meiji translators recognized that rendering Western -isms required exactly such a productive element, and 主義 was stabilized as that compound across the 1870s and 1880s through wide-scale deployment across Western political, philosophical, and economic vocabulary. What the Japanese characters carry is the literal sense of 'the principle one takes as master' — 主 (master) + 義 (principle/doctrine) — which gives 主義 a moral-doctrinal register that the purely affixal Western -ism does not always carry. To commit to a 主義 in the Sino-Japanese register is to take a guiding principle as one's master, with the Confucian-ethical resonance of 義 (rightness, fidelity to principle) lingering across the compound. What the Japanese characters cannot easily carry is the secular-procedural register of modern Western 'ism' as a neutral doctrine-name — the 主 (master) and 義 (rightness) registers tend to make every 主義 carry a moral-doctrinal weight that the Western suffix does not always intend. This has been doctrinally consequential: the Marxian distinction between 'ideology' as false consciousness and 'theory' as scientific articulation does not translate cleanly into the Sino-Japanese vocabulary, because both 'ideology' and 'doctrine' tend to be rendered through 主義 and the moral-doctrinal weight of the compound carries across both registers. The compound's structural feature — that it is itself a substantive that can stand alone as a noun ('-ism, doctrine, principle') as well as functioning as a suffix in compound formation — distinguishes it from the purely affixal Western -ism. One can say 主義者 (shugisha, 'a doctrine-person, an ideologue'), 主義主張 (shugi shuchō, 'doctrine and assertion'), and 主義に固執する (shugi ni koshitsu suru, 'to cling to one's doctrine') in ways that English -ism cannot directly support.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as the most productive suffix-element across modern East Asian political, philosophical, and economic vocabulary. The systematic deployment of 主義 in compound formation across the Meiji period generated an enormous vocabulary of doctrine-names that became operating in modern Japanese, Chinese, and Korean discourse: 民主主義 (democracy-ism), 共産主義 (communism), 社会主義 (socialism), 資本主義 (capitalism), 自由主義 (liberalism), 保守主義 (conservatism), 国家主義 (nationalism / statism), 帝国主義 (imperialism), 個人主義 (individualism), 集団主義 (collectivism), 理想主義 (idealism), 現実主義 (realism), 実用主義 / 実利主義 (pragmatism), 唯物論 / 唯物主義 (materialism), 民本主義 (people-as-foundation-ism), 軍国主義 (militarism), 平和主義 (pacifism), and many hundreds of others. The productivity of 主義 across this vast vocabulary makes the compound arguably the single most consequential wasei-kango suffix in modern East Asian intellectual life — the formal element through which the entire vocabulary of Western philosophical and political doctrines was domesticated into Sino-Japanese characters and transmitted across the modern East Asian political and intellectual sphere. The compound's adoption into Chinese (zhǔyì) through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile period (1898–1912) and the late-Qing reformist press made the Japanese coinage the operating doctrinal-suffix of modern Chinese political and intellectual vocabulary as well, with all the Japanese-coined -ism compounds entering Chinese discourse with their structural and grammatical features intact. The compound is also embedded in a productive grammatical system of its own: 主義者 (the holder of a doctrine), 主義的 (adjectival form, '-istic'), 主義主張 (doctrinal commitment), 主義によって (in accordance with one's doctrine), and so on, supplying a fine-grained vocabulary for articulating the relationship between persons and the doctrines they hold.

false_friends.divergence: 教義 (kyōgi, jiàoyì) names religious or sectarian doctrine — the teaching of a religious tradition, especially in its dogmatic-articulated form. The compound is structured as 教 (teaching) + 義 (doctrine/principle) and names the body of dogma that a religious tradition holds and transmits. 主義 in its modern Meiji-stabilized usage is structurally distinct: it names doctrine not as the teaching of an authoritative tradition but as the principle one takes as master, and is calibrated for the secular-political-philosophical register of Western -isms rather than for the religious-dogmatic register of 教義. Reading 主義 as if it were equivalent to 教義 imports the religious-dogmatic register that the modern Meiji compound is calibrated to distinguish itself from.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound of 社会 (society) + 主義 (-ism), entering Japanese political vocabulary through Meiji translations of Western political-economic literature in the 1870s–1880s; consolidated through the early Japanese socialist movement (Kōtoku Shūsui, Sakai Toshihiko, Katayama Sen) in the 1890s–1900s; popularized in Chinese discourse through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings and the late-Qing reformist and revolutionary press

gathering, meeting, convergence — people coming together in shared occasion; paired with 社 to articulate the modern abstract sense of 'society' as the autonomous sphere of human collective life

conceptual_remainder: 社会主義 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango compound that combines two structural elements — 社会 (society, itself a Meiji coinage) and 主義 (-ism, the productive doctrine-suffix) — to render the Western political-economic doctrine of socialism. The compound is doctrinally interesting because both of its constituent elements are themselves Meiji coinages: the compound 社会 (society) was newly stabilized in the Meiji period to render the Western concept of an autonomous social sphere distinct from the state, the family, and the religious community, and the suffix 主義 was newly productive in the Meiji period as the formal element for rendering Western -isms. 社会主義 thus operates at two layers of Meiji translation simultaneously: it rests on the Meiji rendering of 'society' as 社会, and on the Meiji productivity of 主義 as the -ism suffix. What the Japanese characters carry is the structural transparency that the Western 'socialism' has largely lost: the compound's literal sense of 'the doctrine of the social' (the principle that takes society as its master) is immediately legible in the Sino-Japanese characters, where the European 'socialism' carries its Latin etymological transparency (socialis 'social') only as a specialist's awareness. The Japanese-coined transparency has been doctrinally consequential: East Asian socialist discourse has often foregrounded the compound's literal sense of 'the doctrine of the social' against more individualist or liberal political doctrines, with the structural opposition between 社会主義 and 個人主義 (individualism) doing significant doctrinal work across modern East Asian political vocabulary. What the compound cannot easily carry is the specifically Marxian register of socialism as the historical-materialist program of the proletariat — the technical-theoretical apparatus of Marxian theory (class struggle, surplus value, dialectical materialism) is rendered through other compounds (階級闘争 class struggle, 剰余価値 surplus value, 弁証法的唯物論 dialectical materialism), and 社会主義 in Sino-Japanese tends to be received as the more general doctrine of social reorganization rather than as the specific Marxian theory. The doctrinal cluster 社会主義 / 共産主義 (socialism / communism) reproduces in Sino-Japanese the Marxian distinction between socialism as the transitional phase of social ownership and communism as the higher phase of fully collective production and distribution, and the differential deployment of the two compounds across twentieth-century East Asian political vocabulary tracks the differential commitments of social-democratic and Leninist-communist movements respectively.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the most institutionally consequential wasei-kango compounds of the modern period. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asia is enormous: the Japanese socialist movement (the Social Democratic Party 社会民主党 of 1901, the Japan Socialist Party 日本社会党 of 1906 and 1945, and their post-war successors) deployed 社会主義 as their organizing doctrinal commitment across the twentieth century; the Chinese Communist Party (founded 1921) and the People's Republic of China (founded 1949) constitutionally articulate the PRC as a 社会主義国家 (socialist state) with the operating doctrinal frame of 中国の特色ある社会主義 / 中国特色社会主义 (socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Deng-era articulation that has structured Chinese political vocabulary since 1978); the Korean and Vietnamese socialist movements similarly deploy the Japanese-coined compound as their operating doctrinal vocabulary. The compound also stands at the head of an extensive cluster of related coinages: 社会主義者 (shakaishugisha, socialist), 社会主義革命 (shakaishugi kakumei, socialist revolution), 社会主義国家 (socialist state), 社会民主主義 (social democracy), 国家社会主義 (state socialism / national socialism — itself a compound that requires careful contextual interpretation across Marxian and Nazi German registers), 民主社会主義 (democratic socialism), 科学的社会主義 (scientific socialism, the Marxian register), 空想的社会主義 (utopian socialism, the pre-Marxian register). The compound has been politically dangerous across modern East Asian history: the Meiji and pre-war Japanese state suppressed the early socialist movement violently (the High Treason Incident of 1910, in which Kōtoku Shūsui and twenty-five others were arrested and twelve executed; the subsequent Peace Preservation Law of 1925 explicitly criminalized advocacy of changing the kokutai or the system of private property — i.e., explicitly criminalized 社会主義 as a political position), and the compound's institutional vicissitudes across the post-war period in Japan, China, Korea, and Vietnam have been one of the central axes of modern East Asian political history.

false_friends.divergence: 共産主義 (kyōsanshugi, gòngchǎnzhǔyì, 공산주의) names communism specifically, in distinction from the broader category of 社会主義 (socialism). The Marxian articulation distinguishes socialism as the transitional phase of social ownership and distribution-according-to-labor from communism as the higher phase of fully collective production and distribution-according-to-need, and the Sino-Japanese vocabulary preserves this distinction across the two compounds. The post-1949 Chinese state is constitutionally a 社会主義国家 (socialist state) advancing toward 共産主義 (communism), and the structural ordering of the two compounds tracks the Marxian-Leninist staging of historical development. Reading 社会主義 as if it were equivalent to 共産主義 collapses the Marxian doctrinal distinction that the two compounds preserve, and conflates the broader category of socialism (which includes social democracy and democratic socialism) with the specifically Marxist-Leninist register of communism.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound of 共産 (joint production) + 主義 (-ism), entering Japanese political vocabulary through Meiji translations of Western political-economic literature in the 1870s–1880s; consolidated through Kōtoku Shūsui and Sakai Toshihiko's 1904 Japanese translation of the Communist Manifesto and the early Japanese socialist-and-communist movement; adopted into Chinese (gòngchǎnzhǔyì) through the late-Qing reformist press and the Marxist study circles of Chinese students in Japan, becoming the operating term of the Chinese Communist movement from the founding of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921

components.meaning: together, joint, mutual — two hands lifting a shared object; here paired with 産 to articulate the principle of joint production, the means of production held in common rather than as private property

to produce, to bring forth — the productive act of generating goods, value, or offspring; here the productive register that 共 transforms from individual to joint, articulating the Marxian principle of collectively-owned means of production
lord, master, that which is principal — here the first character of the suffix 主義, contributing the structural register of 'that which one takes as master'

rightness, principle, doctrine — the Confucian moral register of righteousness extended to guiding principle; paired with 主 in the suffix 主義 to articulate the doctrinal commitment that organizes thought and action around joint production

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in political-economic and political-theoretical contexts; covers the full range of communist doctrines from the early-nineteenth-century French and German communist movements through Marxian scientific communism to the twentieth-century Marxist-Leninist and Maoist articulations

literal-decompositional rendering — preserves the structural transparency of the compound 共産 (joint production) + 主義 (-ism) by foregrounding the literal sense of 'the doctrine of holding production in common'; useful for explaining the Sino-Japanese semantic transparency that the European 'communism' has lost through its Latin etymological abstraction

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the German and French political-theoretical lineages from which Meiji translators drew; preserves the connection to the European communist tradition that the Meiji compound was calibrated to render

conceptual_remainder: 共産主義 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango compound that combines two structural elements — 共産 (joint production) and 主義 (-ism, the productive doctrine-suffix) — to render the Western political-economic doctrine of communism. The compound's structural logic is precise: 共 (joint, shared) + 産 (production) names the mode of production held in common, and 主義 names the doctrinal commitment to that mode. What the Japanese characters carry is the structural transparency that the Western 'communism' has largely lost: the compound's literal sense of 'the doctrine of joint production' (the principle that takes joint-production as its master) is immediately legible in the Sino-Japanese characters, where the European 'communism' carries its Latin etymological transparency (communis 'common') only as a specialist's awareness. The Japanese-coined transparency has been doctrinally consequential in two directions. First, it foregrounds the productive-economic register specifically — communism in the Sino-Japanese characters is the doctrine that production is held jointly, and the structural opposition to 私産 (private property) and 資本 (capital) is immediately legible in the compound. Second, it makes the structural relation between 社会主義 (socialism) and 共産主義 (communism) doctrinally precise in a way that the European pair only does for specialists: 社会主義 is the doctrine of the social (the social character of economic life), 共産主義 is the doctrine of joint production specifically (the collective ownership of the means of production), and the Marxian-Leninist staging from socialism to communism is articulated through the structural relation of the two compounds. What the compound cannot easily carry is the specifically utopian or pre-Marxian register of communism — the early-nineteenth-century French communist movement of Cabet and others, and the broader pre-Marxian articulations — which the Japanese compound tends to subsume into the dominant Marxian register. The compound also cannot easily carry the contemporary distinction between 'communist' as the historical-doctrinal register and 'communist' as the institutional designation of post-1917 communist parties and states, with both registers collapsed under the same compound across modern East Asian usage.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the most institutionally consequential and politically dangerous wasei-kango compounds of the modern period. The compound's institutional life across twentieth-century East Asian history has been enormous: every East Asian communist party deploys 共産党 (Communist Party) as its institutional name with 共産主義 as its operating doctrinal commitment — the Chinese Communist Party (中国共産党, founded 1921), the Japanese Communist Party (日本共産党, founded 1922), the Communist Party of Korea (조선공산당) and its post-1945 successors in North and South Korea, the Communist Party of Vietnam (Đảng Cộng sản Việt Nam, founded 1930), and the various Southeast Asian communist movements all operate under the wasei-kango designation. The compound's institutional vicissitudes across modern East Asian political history have been one of the central axes of twentieth-century political life: the Meiji and pre-war Japanese state suppressed the early communist movement violently (the Peace Preservation Law of 1925 explicitly criminalized advocacy of 共産主義, leading to the suppression of the Japanese Communist Party until the post-war American occupation legalized the party in 1945; the 3.15 Incident of 1928 saw mass arrests of suspected communists across Japan); the Chinese Communist movement underwent the long civil war and the establishment of the People's Republic in 1949 with 共産主義 as the constitutional-doctrinal frame; the Korean War of 1950–1953 was fought across the structural division between communist and anti-communist Korea articulated through the same compound 共産主義 on both sides; the Vietnam War of 1955–1975 similarly turned on the 共産主義 / 反共 (anti-communism) axis. The compound stands at the head of an extensive cluster of related coinages: 共産党 (kyōsantō, Communist Party), 共産党員 (kyōsantōin, party member), 共産主義者 (kyōsanshugisha, communist), 共産主義革命 (kyōsanshugi kakumei, communist revolution), 共産国 (kyōsankoku, communist country), 国際共産主義 (kokusai kyōsanshugi, international communism), 反共 (hankyō, anti-communism), 反共主義 (hankyōshugi, anti-communism as doctrinal commitment). The compound is among the most ideologically saturated terms in the East Asian political lexicon and continues to shape political discourse across the post-Cold-War period in ways that the European 'communism' has largely shed.

false_friends.divergence: 社会主義 (shakaishugi, shèhuìzhǔyì, 사회주의) names socialism as the broader political-economic category, in distinction from the specifically Marxist-Leninist register of 共産主義 (communism). The Marxian articulation distinguishes socialism as the transitional phase of social ownership and labor-based distribution from communism as the higher phase of fully collective production and need-based distribution, and the Sino-Japanese vocabulary preserves this distinction across the two compounds. The post-1949 PRC is constitutionally a 社会主義国家 (socialist state) advancing toward 共産主義, and the structural ordering of the two compounds tracks the Marxian-Leninist staging of historical development. Reading 共産主義 as if it were equivalent to 社会主義 collapses the staging-distinction that the two compounds preserve, and conflates the broader category of socialism (which includes social democracy and democratic socialism) with the specifically Marxist-Leninist register of communism.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango stabilization of a classical Chinese compound (国際 in classical usage named the locative-territorial border or contact-zone between states); repurposed in early-Meiji Japan to render the Western political-theoretical category of 'international.' The early-Meiji translation of international law deployed the related 万国 (bankoku, ten thousand nations) as the operating prefix — Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1865 万国公法 (Japanese rendering of Wheaton's Elements of International Law) fixed that vocabulary — and the more compact 国際 was subsequently stabilized through the post-1880s Meiji legal-political translation as the productive prefix of the modern international vocabulary

components.meaning: state, nation, country — the bounded territorial polity; here marking the polity-as-unit register that the relational compound 国際 takes as its bounded particular, naming the relations between such bounded polities

edge, juncture, border, occasion — the contact-line where two domains meet; paired with 国 to articulate the relational space between states, the contact-zone that becomes the abstract domain of international relations

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in political-theoretical, legal, and institutional contexts; serves as a productive prefix for the entire international-affairs vocabulary

literal-decompositional rendering — preserves the structural sense of 際 as 'edge / juncture' between bounded 国 (states), foregrounding the relational register that the compound carries; useful in classical political-theoretical contexts where the specifically inter-state register matters

rendering used in contemporary contexts where 国際 names cross-border phenomena beyond formal state-to-state relations — international civil society, cross-border markets, transnational social movements; the compound's productivity supports both the formal-diplomatic and the broader trans-national registers

conceptual_remainder: 国際 in its Meiji repurposing operates as a wasei-kango stabilization of a classical Chinese compound, with the doctrinal register elevated from concrete locative border to abstract relational category. The classical Chinese 国際 named the contact-zone between two bounded polities — the territorial border, the meeting-edge — and the Meiji repurposing extends this from concrete spatial sense to the abstract political-theoretical category of 'international' as the relational space between sovereign states. What the Japanese characters carry is the structural figure of the meeting-edge: 際 specifically names the juncture, the contact-line, the place where two domains touch, and 国際 articulates the international as the meeting-zone between states rather than as a substantive third domain of its own. This carries doctrinal consequences. 国際 in the Sino-Japanese register tends to be received as the relational space between states (with the states as the substantive units and the international as the relational predicate), where Western international-theoretical vocabulary often reifies the international as a substantive domain in its own right (the international system, international society, the international order). The compound's structural register makes Hedley Bull's concept of 'international society' more semantically transparent in Sino-Japanese than in English — 国際社会 (kokusai shakai) literally compounds the meeting-edge between states with the social, articulating the structural intuition behind the English School's articulation. What the compound cannot easily carry is the cosmopolitan-universal register of the Stoic and Kantian traditions that articulate the international as the universal domain of humanity transcending state borders; the compound's anchor in 国 (state) keeps the international tied to the inter-state register and tends to make cosmopolitan articulations require additional vocabulary (世界市民 sekai shimin, world citizen; 普遍 fuhen, universal) to carry the trans-state register. The early-Meiji preference for 万国 (the ten thousand nations) over 国際 reflected this anchor specifically: 万国 articulates the international as the totality of nations in their plurality (the universal range of state-units), while 国際 articulates it as the relational space between them, and the early-Meiji deployment of 万国 in 万国公法 (Wheaton's translation) and 万国博覧会 (World's Fair) preserves a more universal register that the later 国際 partially displaces.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as the productive prefix of the entire modern East Asian international-affairs vocabulary. The compound's productivity is enormous: 国際法 (kokusaihō, international law), 国際関係 (kokusai kankei, international relations), 国際政治 (kokusai seiji, international politics), 国際機関 (kokusai kikan, international organizations), 国際連盟 (kokusai renmei, League of Nations), 国際連合 (kokusai rengō, United Nations), 国際的 (kokusaiteki, international as adjectival), 国際化 (kokusaika, internationalization), 国際協力 (kokusai kyōryoku, international cooperation), 国際社会 (kokusai shakai, international society), 国際秩序 (kokusai chitsujo, international order), 国際情勢 (kokusai jōsei, international situation), 国際商業 (kokusai shōgyō, international commerce), 国際金融 (kokusai kinyū, international finance), 国際空港 (kokusai kūkō, international airport), and many others. The compound supplies the operating institutional vocabulary across the contemporary East Asian international-affairs apparatus: every East Asian government deploys 国際 across its diplomatic, legal, economic, and educational institutions; the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (外務省) and its Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese counterparts conduct their operations through this vocabulary; the post-WWII Bretton Woods institutions and UN system are all designated through 国際 across East Asian usage. The structural opposition between 国際 and 国内 (kokunai, domestic) organizes a great deal of contemporary East Asian political-economic discourse, with the international/domestic axis structuring everything from trade policy through legal jurisdiction to academic disciplinary organization (国際関係論 international relations as an academic field versus 国内政治 domestic politics).

false_friends.divergence: 万国 (bankoku, wànguó, 만국, 'the ten thousand nations') is the early-Meiji rendering of 'international' that 国際 partially displaced. 万国 articulates the international as the totality of nations in their plurality — the universal range of state-units conceived as a numerical many — while 国際 articulates it as the relational space between them. The two compounds preserve a doctrinally important distinction: 万国 carries the universal-comprehensive register (all the nations of the world) while 国際 carries the relational-meeting register (the contact-edges between states). The early-Meiji 万国公法 (Bankoku Kōhō, Wheaton's translation) deployed 万国 because the universal register was load-bearing for the international-legal claim that public law applies to all nations; the later 国際法 (kokusaihō) deploys 国際 because the relational register was load-bearing for the framework of inter-state legal relations. Most contemporary usage prefers 国際 as the productive prefix, but 万国 survives in particular institutional names (万国博覧会 World's Fair, 万国郵便連合 Universal Postal Union) where the universal-comprehensive register remains doctrinally pivotal.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound of 民 (people) + 族 (kindred/lineage), stabilized in late-Meiji and Taishō Japanese political-anthropological vocabulary through the writings of Ariga Nagao, Kume Kunitake, and the broader Meiji ethnographic and political-theoretical literature; entered Chinese vocabulary as 民族 (mínzú) through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings (1898–1912) and the late-Qing reformist press, becoming the operating term of late-Qing and Republican Chinese political identity through Liang's articulation of 中華民族 (the Chinese ethnic-nation)

components.meaning: the people, the populace — in classical usage the governed; here paired with 族 to articulate the people specifically as ethnic-cultural collectivity rather than as legal-political category, the people-as-Volk distinct from the people-as-citizenry
lineage, kindred, tribe — those who gather under a common banner; the kindred-collectivity register that distinguishes the political-anthropological 民族 from the legal-political 国民 (state-citizen)

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering in anthropological and political-theoretical contexts emphasizing the ethnic-cultural register; covers the full range of ethnic-group articulations from the narrow-ancestry sense to the broader cultural-linguistic-territorial sense

rendering used in political-theoretical contexts foregrounding the nineteenth-century romantic-nationalist articulation of nation as ethnic-cultural collectivity (Herder's Volksgeist, Fichte's Reden an die deutsche Nation, Renan's Qu'est-ce qu'une nation?); the German Volk and the French ethnie name approximately the same category as 民族

broader literary-political rendering — covers the general sense of a people-collectivity, useful when the specifically ethnic register is not load-bearing; risks ambiguity with 民 (the bare people) and 国民 (the state-citizen people)

rendering used in older translation traditions and in some early-twentieth-century texts; risks importing the biological-typological register of nineteenth-century racial-anthropological vocabulary that the contemporary Sino-Japanese 民族 mostly does not carry, with 人種 (jinshu, race in the biological sense) being the more precise Sino-Japanese equivalent for the biological-racial register

conceptual_remainder: 民族 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango compound that articulates the political-anthropological category of nation/Volk specifically, in distinction from the legal-political category of state-citizenship (国民) and from the institutional category of state (国家). The compound's structural logic is precise: 民 (people) + 族 (kindred-collectivity) names the people not as the governed populace and not as the body of state-citizens but as the ethnic-cultural collectivity bound together by common ancestry, language, culture, or territory. What the Japanese characters carry is the structural figure of the kindred-banner: 族 specifically names those who gather under a common rallying-point and act together as a bound collectivity, and the compound 民族 inherits this kindred-bound register from classical Chinese clan vocabulary while extending it to the modern political-anthropological category. The compound is doctrinally productive precisely because it preserves the distinction between 民族 and 国民 that the European vocabulary often collapses: French nation / German Nation / English nation oscillate between the ethnic-cultural and legal-political registers, while Sino-Japanese vocabulary deploys 民族 for the former and 国民 for the latter. This makes Sino-Japanese discourse on national identity often more analytically precise than its European counterpart — the question whether a polity should be organized around 民族 (ethnic-cultural unity) or 国民 (legal-civic citizenship) can be posed directly in the Sino-Japanese vocabulary, where the European vocabulary requires paraphrastic clarification. What the compound cannot easily carry is the entirely-civic-citizenship register of the French republican tradition that defines la nation française as the body of all who hold French citizenship regardless of ethnic-cultural origin; the structural anchor of 民族 in 族 (kindred) tends to import a kindred-collectivity register that the radical-civic articulation explicitly denies. The compound has been politically dangerous across modern East Asian history: the wartime Japanese articulation of 大和民族 (Yamato ethnic-nation) supplied the doctrinal frame of imperial-Japanese ideology and the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, with the structural ambiguity between ethnic-cultural collectivity and biological-racial collectivity collapsed under the compound; the post-war PRC vocabulary distinguishes 中華民族 (the Chinese ethnic-nation as the political-identity frame of the People's Republic) from 少数民族 (ethnic minority groups within the PRC) in ways that have generated sustained political-anthropological controversy.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the most institutionally and ideologically consequential wasei-kango compounds of the modern period. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asian history has been enormous: Liang Qichao's articulation of 中華民族 (the Chinese ethnic-nation) in the Xinmin Shuo and related Tokyo-exile writings became the operating frame within which late-Qing and Republican Chinese political identity was articulated, and the contemporary PRC continues to deploy 中華民族 as the political-identity frame of the People's Republic; the wartime Japanese articulation of 大和民族 (the Yamato ethnic-nation) as the doctrinal frame of imperial-Japanese ideology produced one of the most politically consequential and morally contested deployments of the compound; the post-war Korean articulation of 한민족 / 韓民族 (the Korean ethnic-nation) became the operating frame of post-colonial Korean political identity across both North and South Korea; the contemporary PRC vocabulary of 少数民族 (shaoshu minzu, ethnic minority groups) names the fifty-five officially-recognized non-Han ethnic groups within the PRC and supplies the operating institutional vocabulary of PRC ethnic-policy. The compound stands at the head of an extensive cluster of related coinages: 民族主義 (minzokushugi, nationalism in its ethnic-cultural register, distinct from 国家主義 statism), 民族自決 (minzoku jiketsu, national self-determination — the Wilsonian principle), 民族解放 (minzoku kaihō, national liberation — the post-WWII anti-colonial register), 多民族国家 (taminzoku kokka, multi-ethnic state), 単一民族 (tan'itsu minzoku, mono-ethnic), 民族浄化 (minzoku jōka, ethnic cleansing), 民族学 (minzokugaku, ethnology), and many others. The structural distinction between 民族主義 (ethnic-cultural nationalism) and 国家主義 (statism / state-nationalism) maps onto the German Nationalismus / Staatsnationalismus distinction with notable precision and supplies the analytical vocabulary through which East Asian political-theoretical discourse navigates the relation between ethnic and political articulations of national identity.

false_friends.divergence: 国民 (kokumin, guómín, 국민, 'state-people') names the legal-political category of state-citizenship — those who hold formal nationality of a sovereign state — distinct from the political-anthropological category of ethnic-cultural collectivity that 民族 names. The two compounds preserve a doctrinal distinction that is load-bearing across modern East Asian political-theoretical discourse: 国民 is the body of state-citizens regardless of ethnic-cultural origin (the contemporary Japanese state's 国民 includes naturalized citizens of all ethnic origins; the PRC's 公民 includes all citizens of the PRC regardless of which 民族 they belong to); 民族 is the ethnic-cultural collectivity that may or may not coincide with the state's citizenry. Reading 民族 as if it were equivalent to 国民 collapses the distinction between ethnic-cultural and legal-political articulations of national identity that is one of the central analytical tools of modern East Asian political theory. The structural pairing 国民 / 民族 maps roughly onto the German Staatsnation / Volk distinction or the French nation civique / nation ethnique distinction, and the analytical precision of the Sino-Japanese pair often exceeds that of the European vocabulary.

人種 (jinshu, rénzhǒng, 인종, 'human kind / race') names the biological-typological category of race in the nineteenth-and-twentieth-century racial-anthropological register, distinct from the cultural-political category of ethnic-nation that 民族 names. Contemporary East Asian usage tends to reserve 人種 for explicitly biological-racial articulations and 民族 for cultural-political articulations, with the former increasingly constrained as the biological-racial vocabulary has been progressively delegitimized in scientific discourse. Reading 民族 as if it were equivalent to 人種 imports the biological-typological register that contemporary Sino-Japanese 民族 mostly avoids.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound of 立 (to establish) + 憲 (constitution / fundamental ordinance), stabilized in Meiji political vocabulary through the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動) of the 1870s–1880s; institutionalized through Ōkuma Shigenobu's founding of the Constitutional Progressive Party (立憲改進党 Rikken Kaishintō) in 1882 and Itagaki Taisuke's later Constitutional Liberal Party (立憲自由党 Rikken Jiyūtō) in 1890; doctrinally institutionalized through the Meiji Constitution of 1889 and Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries (憲法義解, 1889); adopted into Chinese (lìxiàn) through the late-Qing constitutional reform movement of the 1900s

components.meaning: to stand, to establish, to set up, to institute — the figure of a person planted firmly upright; here the verbal-institutional register of bringing-into-being, establishing the constitutive instrument that 憲 names

fundamental norm, binding ordinance, constitution — the constitutive rule that orders the polity from above and stands over ordinary law; here paired with 立 to articulate the act and condition of constitutional establishment

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering in political-theoretical and constitutional-law contexts; covers the doctrine that political authority is legitimately exercised only within the structural limits set by a constitution

rendering when 立憲 functions as the adjectival prefix in compounds such as 立憲政体 (constitutional polity), 立憲君主制 (constitutional monarchy), 立憲国 (constitutional state); names a polity organized under the principle of constitutional government

literal-decompositional rendering — preserves the verb-noun structure of 立 (to establish) + 憲 (constitution); useful for explaining the compound's structural logic and its connection to the historical moment of constitutional establishment in Meiji Japan and late-Qing China

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the German and French political-theoretical lineages from which Meiji constitutionalists drew; preserves the connection to the European constitutional tradition that the Meiji compound was calibrated to render

conceptual_remainder: 立憲 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango compound that articulates the political-theoretical doctrine of constitutional government through the structural pairing of 立 (to establish) with 憲 (constitution). The compound's structural logic is verbal-institutional: 立 names the establishing-act and 憲 names the constitutive instrument, and 立憲 articulates the doctrinal commitment to government bound by such a constitutive instrument. What the Japanese characters carry is the structural transparency that the European 'constitutionalism' largely lacks: the literal sense of 'establishing-the-constitution' (or of being-in-the-state-of-having-established-a-constitution) is immediately legible in the Sino-Japanese characters, where the European 'constitutionalism' carries its etymological connection to the Latin constitutio only as a specialist's awareness. The compound is also structurally distinct from 憲法 (kenpō, constitution as instrument) and from 憲政 (kensei, constitutional government as condition) in ways that the modern East Asian constitutional vocabulary systematically deploys: 憲法 names the textual instrument; 憲政 names the institutional condition of operating under a constitution; 立憲 names the doctrinal commitment to constitutional government as a political-theoretical principle and the act of constitutional establishment as a historical moment. The three compounds together articulate constitutional government across textual, institutional, and doctrinal registers in ways that the single English 'constitution / constitutionalism' often must paraphrase. What the compound cannot easily carry is the specifically common-law constitutional tradition that operates without a single codified document — the British constitutional tradition with its statutory and customary articulation lacks a discrete 立憲 moment in the Meiji-and-after sense, and the British constitution is described in Sino-Japanese vocabulary through more paraphrastic constructions (the unwritten constitution, 不文憲法 fubun kenpō). The compound also carries the historical inflection of its specific Meiji-and-after deployment: 立憲 in Japanese tends to evoke the Meiji constitutional settlement and the specific institutional architecture that Itō Hirobumi and the Meiji drafters established, with the 1947 post-war constitutional moment treated as a distinct historical event rather than as a second 立憲 moment in the original sense.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the structurally pivotal compounds of modern East Asian constitutional politics. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asian history has been substantial: Ōkuma Shigenobu's Constitutional Progressive Party (立憲改進党 Rikken Kaishintō, founded 1882) and Itagaki Taisuke's Constitutional Liberal Party (立憲自由党 Rikken Jiyūtō, founded 1890) — the first modern East Asian political parties — explicitly took 立憲 into their names as the organizing doctrinal commitment, and the broader Meiji parliamentary politics of the post-1889 period was articulated through the structural distinction between 立憲 forces (those committed to constitutional government within the Meiji constitutional architecture) and the residual extra-constitutional currents. The compound is productive across the modern Japanese constitutional vocabulary: 立憲政体 (rikken seitai, constitutional polity), 立憲君主制 (rikken kunshusei, constitutional monarchy — the Meiji constitutional self-description), 立憲政治 (rikken seiji, constitutional government), 立憲主義 (rikken shugi, constitutionalism as doctrinal commitment, with the productive 主義 suffix), 立憲国 (rikkenkoku, constitutional state). The compound entered Chinese (lìxiàn) through the late-Qing constitutional reform movement of the 1900s — the post-Boxer constitutional reform proposals of 1906, the 1908 Outline of Constitutional Authority (欽定憲法大綱), the early-Republican constitutional drafts — as the operating term of late-Qing and early-Republican constitutional politics. The compound's institutional reach in the post-war period continues across all the constitutional polities of East Asia: 立憲 is the operating doctrinal frame within which Japanese, Korean, and Taiwanese constitutional politics articulates its self-understanding as constitutional government. The compound also functions as a political-rhetorical anchor in contemporary debates: Japanese constitutional debates about the post-war constitution (the question of constitutional revision and the related question whether the 1947 constitution should be understood as a continuous extension of the 1889 立憲 moment or as a new constitutional founding) deploy 立憲 as the operative term, and the compound's historical depth makes contemporary constitutional debate inseparable from the Meiji constitutional history that 立憲 carries.

false_friends.divergence: 憲法 (kenpō, xiànfǎ, 헌법) names the constitution as the textual instrument — the foundational document standing above ordinary legislation. 立憲 names the doctrine of constitutional government and the act of constitutional establishment, not the instrument itself. The two compounds articulate a structural distinction that modern East Asian constitutional vocabulary preserves: a polity has a 憲法 (a constitutional document) and is organized under 立憲 (the doctrine of constitutional government). Reading 立憲 as if it were equivalent to 憲法 collapses the distinction between the doctrinal commitment and the textual instrument that the two compounds preserve, and obscures the doctrinal-institutional architecture that the modern East Asian constitutional vocabulary systematically deploys.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound extracted from the classical Confucian idiom 経世済民 (jīngshì jìmín, 'ordering the age, relieving the people'), deployed across early-Meiji translations of Western political economy from the 1860s onward and popularized through Fukuzawa Yukichi's Seiyō Jijō (1866–70); displaced Yan Fu's competing translation 計学 (jìxué) across late-Qing and early-Republican Chinese economic discourse

components.meaning: threading, ordering, passing through — the warp threads of a loom extended to the systematic ordering of doctrine, scripture, and statecraft; here the 経 of classical 経世 (ordering the age), naming the structural-systematic register of governance

crossing, completing, relieving — water ferried across, extended to bringing matters to completion and aiding others through hardship; here the 済 of classical 済民 (relieving the people), naming the ethical-soteriological register of provisioning the populace

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering for the empirical-phenomenal sense of economy as the ordered material life of a society — the structural sphere of production, distribution, and exchange

rendering for the disciplinary-academic sense, especially in the compound 経済学 (keizaigaku, economics as a systematic discipline); covers both the classical political-economy register of Adam Smith through John Stuart Mill and the modern marginalist-neoclassical register

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the German political-economic lineage — the German Historical School (Roscher, Schmoller), the Marxian Kritik der politischen Ökonomie, and the broader continental tradition from which much Meiji economic translation derived

translation_range.rendering: ordering the age, relieving the people
translation_range.emphasis: literal-classical rendering — preserves the Confucian-political-ethical register of the source idiom 経世済民 from which the Meiji compound was extracted; useful for explaining the implicit ethical weight that the Sino-Japanese characters carry but the Greek-Latin oikonomia does not

conceptual_remainder: 経済 in its Meiji extraction operates as a wasei-kango compound that performs a structurally interesting translation maneuver: it does not coin a new compound but extracts a two-character subset from an existing classical four-character idiom — 経世済民 (ordering the age, relieving the people) — and deploys the abbreviated form to translate the Western category of 'economy.' The extraction is doctrinally consequential. The full classical idiom names the ruler-statesman's twin responsibility: to thread the world into right order (経世) and to ferry the people through their material hardships (済民) — the ethical-political horizon of Confucian statecraft. The Meiji extraction preserves the 経 (ordering) and 済 (relieving) characters but drops 世 (the world) and 民 (the people), and the dropped characters take with them the explicit ethical-political horizon of the source idiom. What remains in 経済 is the structural-systematic core (ordering, completing) without the explicit ethical-political content, a calibration that allows the compound to translate the structurally-neutral Western 'economy' while retaining a residual ethical-political resonance that the Greek-Latin oikonomia does not carry. The doctrinal residue has been generative across modern East Asian economic discourse: Japanese and Chinese economic vocabulary tends to retain an implicit normative register — economic activity is, by its characters, the ordering of the world for the relief of the people, not the neutral allocation of scarce resources — that the post-marginalist Anglo-American 'economics' has largely abandoned. Modern East Asian economic-policy discourse continues to be inflected by the residual Confucian-ethical horizon that 経済 carries: the ruler-statesman's responsibility for the material welfare of the populace remains a more naturally articulable claim in 経済-vocabulary than in 'economics'-vocabulary. What the compound cannot easily carry is the specifically marginalist-individualist register of post-1870s neoclassical economics, in which economic activity is reframed as the aggregation of individual utility-maximizing choices in markets. The Sino-Japanese characters carry a structurally collective horizon — the ordering of the age, the relieving of the people — that is in slight tension with the methodologically-individualist apparatus of modern microeconomic theory, and the doctrinal-translational tension between 経済 and the marginalist register has been one of the central axes of modern East Asian economic-theoretical discourse. The compound was at one point in serious competition with Yan Fu's translation 計学 (jìxué, 'calculation-study'), which framed economics through its quantitative-calculative aspect and was deployed in Yan Fu's 1902 translation of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations as 原富 (Yuán Fù). The Japanese-coined 経済 prevailed across East Asian economic discourse by the 1910s and 1920s, displacing 計学 as the operating term in Chinese economic vocabulary through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings and the broader late-Qing reformist press, and the displacement was consequential: 経済 imports the Confucian-ethical residue of the source idiom into the modern East Asian economic vocabulary in a way that the calculative-quantitative 計学 would not have done.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the most institutionally consequential wasei-kango compounds of the Meiji-era economic translation project. The compound stands at the head of an enormous productive vocabulary across modern East Asian economic discourse: 経済学 (economics as a discipline), 経済学者 (economist), 経済政策 (economic policy), 経済成長 (economic growth), 経済発展 (economic development), 経済危機 (economic crisis), 経済恐慌 (economic panic / depression), 国民経済 (national economy), 世界経済 (world economy), 政治経済学 (political economy), マクロ経済学 (macroeconomics), ミクロ経済学 (microeconomics), 経済学部 (Faculty of Economics) — the entire vocabulary of modern academic and policy-oriented economic discourse deploys 経済 as the structural anchor. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asia is foundational: the establishment of the Tokyo Imperial University Faculty of Economics (経済学部) in 1919 — the first economics faculty in Japan, splitting off from the older Faculty of Law — institutionalized 経済学 as a distinct academic discipline; the broader Meiji and Taishō academic-disciplinary apparatus stabilized the modern Japanese economic-theoretical vocabulary; and the post-war Japanese economic-policy apparatus (the Economic Planning Agency 経済企画庁 1955–2001, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry 経済産業省 from 2001) deploys 経済 as the operating institutional frame. The compound was adopted into Chinese (jīngjì) and Korean (경제) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of 'economy' / 'economics' and remains the operating term across all East Asian languages. The Japanese-coined economic vocabulary was diffused across the late-Qing and early-Republican Chinese reform movement through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings and the broader Japanese-trained Chinese intelligentsia, and the early Chinese Marxist economic discourse (Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, the early Chinese Communist Party) deployed the Japanese-coined 経済 vocabulary as its operating analytical frame.

false_friends.divergence: 計学 (jìxué, 'calculation-study') was Yan Fu's competing late-Qing rendering of 'economics,' deployed in his 1902 translation of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations as 原富. The compound frames economics through its quantitative-calculative aspect — economics as a calculation-discipline — and was structurally distinct from the Japanese-coined 経済 in its doctrinal emphasis: 計学 foregrounds the quantitative-methodological aspect of the discipline, while 経済 foregrounds the structural-political-ethical aspect. The Japanese coinage prevailed across East Asian economic discourse by the 1910s–1920s, and 計学 is now obsolete in Chinese usage; the displacement is one of the structurally-significant moments in the modern East Asian vocabulary stabilization, with the Confucian-ethical residue of 経済 prevailing over the calculative-quantitative register of 計学.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound deployed across Meiji translations of Western political economy from the 1870s onward; institutionalized through the early Japanese Marxist movement, especially Kawakami Hajime's economic writings (Bimbō Monogatari 1917) and Takabatake Motoyuki's 1920–24 translation of Marx's Das Kapital under the title 資本論

components.meaning: resources, supplied means, capital — the cowry of monetary wealth beneath the phonetic 次; here the supplied-means register, the funds and material with which an enterprise is provisioned

root, foundation, principal — a tree marked at its base; here the root-foundation register paired with 資 to articulate 'the supplied-means at the root of the enterprise,' the foundational fund from which productive activity proceeds

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering across classical, Marxian, and modern economic registers; covers the full conceptual range from the late-medieval Italian commercial sense of capitale (the principal sum of a venture) through the classical political-economy sense of capital as accumulated productive wealth to the Marxian sense of capital as a self-expanding social relation

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the Marxian political-economic lineage; the Japanese title 資本論 (shihonron) of Marx's Das Kapital is the standard East Asian rendering of the work and the operating frame within which the Marxian-economic register of 資本 is most strongly articulated

rendering for the older commercial-financial register, the principal sum of a loan or venture distinct from the interest or profit it generates; preserves the late-medieval Italian capitale register that the Western word descends from

conceptual_remainder: 資本 in its Meiji coinage operates as a wasei-kango compound that translates the Western category of 'capital' through the structural pairing of 資 (supplied-means) and 本 (root-foundation) — a compound that retains the Sino-Japanese semantic transparency of its components in a way that the Latin capitale (descended from caput, 'head') has largely lost in the modern European languages. The literal sense of 'the supplied-means at the root of the enterprise' is immediately legible in the Sino-Japanese characters and supplies an implicit conceptual content — capital as the foundational fund from which productive activity proceeds — that the Western word carries only as a specialist's etymological awareness. The compound is structurally calibrated for the classical political-economy register: capital as accumulated wealth deployed in productive enterprise, distinguished from rent (paid to land), wages (paid to labor), and interest (paid to lenders). The Marxian register of capital as a structural social relation rather than a thing — the wage-form by which surplus value is extracted from labor power, the M-C-M' circuit of self-expanding value — was articulated in Japanese through 資本 with the assistance of the productive Sino-Japanese compound system: 資本主義 (capitalism), 資本家 (the capitalist as a bearer of the social relation), 可変資本 (variable capital, the wage-bill), 不変資本 (constant capital, the means of production), 資本の有機的構成 (organic composition of capital), 剰余価値 (surplus value), 資本の本源的蓄積 (primitive accumulation of capital). What the Sino-Japanese characters carry that the Western word does not is the structural transparency of the resource-foundation register: 資本 is immediately legible as 'supplied means + root,' which makes the conceptual content of the compound available without specialist apparatus. What the compound cannot easily carry is the etymological-historical specificity of the Latin capitale — the descent from caput (head) through the late-medieval Italian commercial vocabulary, with all its accumulated semantic content of the principal-sum-as-the-head-of-the-venture — which the Western word carries as a buried etymological resonance. The doctrinal-translational result is that 資本 in Sino-Japanese operates as a structurally transparent compound that nevertheless carries the full institutional-historical weight of the Western 'capital' through its productive deployment across the modern Japanese economic-theoretical vocabulary.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the most institutionally consequential wasei-kango compounds of the Meiji-Taishō economic translation project. The compound stands at the head of an enormous productive vocabulary in modern East Asian economic and political-economic discourse: 資本主義 (capitalism), 資本家 (capitalist), 資本論 (Capital, Marx's title), 資本金 (paid-in capital, the registered capital of a corporation), 資本市場 (capital market), 資本投資 (capital investment), 資本収益率 (return on capital), 固定資本 (fixed capital), 流動資本 (circulating capital), 可変資本 (variable capital), 不変資本 (constant capital), 株式資本 (share capital), 自己資本 (own capital, equity), 他人資本 (other-people's capital, debt) — the entire conceptual apparatus of modern political economy, both classical-liberal and Marxian, deploys 資本 as the structural anchor. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asia is substantial: the early Japanese socialist and Marxist movements (Kōtoku Shūsui's Heimin Shimbun period 1903–05, Kawakami Hajime's Kyoto-school economic-theoretical writings of the 1910s–1920s, the Takabatake Motoyuki translation of Marx's Capital 資本論 1920–24, the Iwanami Bunko translations and the broader academic-Marxist apparatus of Taishō and Shōwa Japan) deployed 資本 as the operating analytical category, and the post-war Japanese economic-policy apparatus (the post-war reconstruction policies, the high-growth-period industrial policy of the 1950s–1970s, the asset-bubble economy of the 1980s, the post-bubble economic-policy debates) continues to articulate Japanese economic policy through 資本 as the operating term. The Japanese-coined compound was adopted into Chinese (zīběn) through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings and the early Chinese Marxist movement (Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao), into Korean (자본 jabon), and into Vietnamese, making 資本 one of the most widely-distributed Meiji wasei-kango economic compounds across modern East Asian intellectual life.

false_friends.divergence: 首都 (shuto, shǒudū) names the capital city — the seat of government — and is structurally distinct from 資本 (capital, in the political-economic sense). The English word 'capital' covers both registers (capital city, capital fund), but the Sino-Japanese vocabulary preserves a structural distinction: 首都 (head + metropolis) for the urban-political register, 資本 (supplied-means + root) for the economic-financial register. Reading the English 'capital' as if both senses translated through a single Sino-Japanese compound collapses a distinction that the Sino-Japanese vocabulary systematically preserves.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound of 資本 (capital) + 主義 (-ism), entering Japanese political-economic vocabulary through Meiji and Taishō translations of Western political-economic literature from the 1880s onward; consolidated through the early Japanese socialist and Marxist movements (Kōtoku Shūsui, Kawakami Hajime, Takabatake Motoyuki) in the 1900s–1920s; popularized in Chinese discourse through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings and the early Chinese Marxist movement

components.meaning: resources, supplied means, capital — here the first character of 資本, contributing the supplied-means register to the doctrine-name
root, foundation, principal — paired with 資 in 資本 (capital), naming the foundational fund from which productive enterprise proceeds
lord, master, that which is principal — here the first character of the suffix 主義, contributing the structural register of 'that which one takes as master'

rightness, principle, doctrine — paired with 主 in the suffix 主義 to articulate the doctrinal commitment that organizes thought and action around capital as the structuring principle of the political-economic order

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering across political-economic, sociological, and political-theoretical contexts; covers the full range of capitalist political-economic orders from the early-modern mercantile economies through the industrial capitalism of the nineteenth century to the financialized late capitalism of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the German and French political-theoretical lineages from which much of the early-twentieth-century systematic articulation of the concept derives — Werner Sombart's Der moderne Kapitalismus (1902), Max Weber's Die protestantische Ethik (1904–05), the broader Continental social-theoretical tradition

literal-decompositional rendering — preserves the structural transparency of the compound 資本 (capital) + 主義 (-ism) by foregrounding the literal sense of 'the doctrine that takes capital as its master'; useful for explaining the Sino-Japanese semantic transparency that the European 'capitalism' has lost through its compositional opacity

conceptual_remainder: 資本主義 in its Meiji-Taishō coinage operates as a wasei-kango compound that combines two structural elements — 資本 (capital, itself a Meiji coinage) and 主義 (-ism, the productive doctrine-suffix) — to render the Western political-economic concept of capitalism. The compound is doctrinally interesting because both of its constituent elements are themselves Meiji coinages: 資本 was newly stabilized in Meiji translations of Western political economy to render 'capital,' and 主義 was newly productive in the Meiji period as the formal suffix for rendering Western -isms. 資本主義 thus operates at two layers of Meiji translation simultaneously: it rests on the Meiji rendering of 'capital' as 資本 and on the Meiji productivity of 主義 as the -ism suffix. What the Japanese characters carry is the structural transparency that the Western 'capitalism' has largely lost: the compound's literal sense of 'the doctrine of capital' (the principle that takes capital as its master) is immediately legible in the Sino-Japanese characters, where the European 'capitalism' carries its compositional structure (capital + -ism) only as a specialist's awareness of nineteenth-century French and German neologism-formation. The Japanese-coined transparency has been doctrinally consequential. The structural opposition between 資本主義 and 社会主義 (capitalism and socialism) is more sharply legible in the Sino-Japanese characters than in the European words: 資本 (capital) and 社会 (society) name the two competing structuring principles, and the productive 主義 suffix names the doctrinal commitment to either. The Sino-Japanese compound thus articulates the central political-economic dialectic of the twentieth century with a structural clarity that the European words have to work harder to achieve. What the compound cannot easily carry is the historical-specificity of 'capitalism' as a Marxian polemical term. The European word 'capitalism' was popularized through nineteenth-century socialist polemic against the political-economic order it names — the word carries its origin as a critical category, a term-of-attack rather than a self-description — while the Sino-Japanese 資本主義 has tended to be received more neutrally as a structural-analytical category, as a name for one of the two main forms of modern political-economic order. The doctrinal residue is significant: Japanese capitalist self-description has historically been more comfortable deploying 資本主義 as a self-applied term than English-language capitalist self-description has been comfortable deploying 'capitalism' as a self-applied term, with the asymmetry tracking the differential polemical histories of the two compounds. The doctrinal cluster 資本主義 / 社会主義 / 共産主義 (capitalism / socialism / communism) reproduces in Sino-Japanese the Marxian distinction between the capitalist mode of production and its socialist and communist alternatives, and the differential deployment of the three compounds across twentieth-century East Asian political-economic vocabulary tracks the differential commitments of capitalist, social-democratic, and Leninist-communist movements respectively.
doctrinal_weight: Arrives as one of the most politically consequential wasei-kango compounds of the modern East Asian intellectual world. The compound's institutional life across modern East Asia is enormous: Japanese capitalism developed through the Meiji-Taishō industrial revolution, the inter-war zaibatsu system, the post-war high-growth economy, and the post-bubble financialized economy under the operating self-description of 資本主義 as the structuring principle of the Japanese political-economic order; the early Japanese socialist and Marxist movements (Kōtoku Shūsui's Heimin Shimbun 1903, Kawakami Hajime's economic writings 1910s–1930s, the Takabatake Motoyuki translation of Marx's Capital 1920–24, the Iwanami Bunko Marxist translations of the inter-war period) deployed 資本主義 as the operating critical category for analysis of the order they sought to overturn; the post-war Japanese left and the broader Japanese intellectual tradition continued the analytical-critical deployment of 資本主義 across the high-growth period, the 1968 student movement, the post-bubble economic-policy debates, and the contemporary intellectual scene. The compound stands at the head of an extensive cluster of related coinages: 資本主義者 (shihonshugisha, capitalist as a partisan of capitalism), 資本主義国家 (capitalist state), 国家資本主義 (state capitalism — the deployment of state machinery in service of capitalist accumulation, important for analysis of inter-war East Asian economies), 独占資本主義 (monopoly capitalism), 帝国主義的資本主義 (imperialist capitalism), 後期資本主義 (late capitalism, the Habermasian-Fordist register), カジノ資本主義 (casino capitalism, the financialized register), 民主資本主義 (democratic capitalism). The compound was adopted into Chinese (zīběnzhǔyì) through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings and the early Chinese Marxist movement (Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, the early Chinese Communist Party) and is constitutionally embedded in the operating vocabulary of contemporary Chinese political-economic discourse: the 1978 Deng-era articulation of 中国特色社会主义 (socialism with Chinese characteristics) is structurally articulated against the alternative 資本主義 that the Chinese Communist Party rejects as the structuring principle of the Chinese political-economic order, even as the post-1978 Chinese economy has incorporated very substantial 資本主義 elements into its operating institutional architecture.
