The structural distinction between productive investment and mere speculation is one of the central axes of modern financial-economic discourse — articulated systematically by Keynes in the General Theory's Chapter 12 ('the position is serious when enterprise becomes the bubble on a whirlpool of speculation') and by Hyman Minsky in his theory of financial instability — and the Sino-Japanese vocabulary preserves this distinction with structural transparency through the contrasting second characters. Reading 投資 as if it were equivalent to 投機 collapses the analytical axis between productive investment and speculative gain that the modern financial-economic vocabulary systematically maintains. The compound 投機 carries strongly negative valence in modern East Asian financial-economic discourse — naming the speculative-financial activity that destabilizes markets and detaches financial activity from its productive substrate — while 投資 carries the positive valence of productive capital deployment.

消費 (shōhi, consumption) stands in structural opposition to 投資 (tōshi, investment) within the modern macroeconomic-aggregate vocabulary: consumption uses up wealth in present satisfaction, while investment commits wealth to future productive return. The Sino-Japanese vocabulary articulates this opposition through the contrasting second characters: 消費 carries 費 (spending-and-disbursement, with no return-element), while 投資 carries 資 (capital-as-resource, naming the substance committed for productive deployment). The structural distinction is one of the analytical pivots of modern macroeconomic theory: the Keynesian consumption function (C = a + bY) and the investment function (I = f(r, Y)) name the two principal demand-side aggregates of national-income accounting, and the structural distinction between consumption and investment supplies the conceptual frame within which monetary and fiscal policy intervene to manage aggregate demand. Reading 投資 and 消費 as interchangeable collapses the analytical axis of modern macroeconomic theory.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized in the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, attributed in particular to Mitsukuri Rinshō (箕作麟祥) in his translations of the French Civil Code and the broader French legal corpus across the 1870s; circulated alongside the variant orthography 権理 (with 理 'principle' instead of 利) before stabilizing as 権利 by the 1880s constitutional drafting period; institutionalized through the Meiji Constitution of 1889 (in which Articles 18–32 articulate 臣民の権利) and authoritatively glossed in Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries on the Constitution (憲法義解, 1889)

components.meaning: calibrated authority, the steelyard's counterweight — here in its juridical-prerogative register, naming the authoritative structural element of the right; the same character that carries 'sovereignty' in 主権 is here calibrated to the recipient-side claim that subjects possess against authority

sharp gain, advantage, benefit — here the recipient-side register of claim and entitlement; paired with 権 to articulate the right as 'a power-and-benefit one is authorized to assert,' the juridical claim that subjects hold against political authority

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in modern legal and political theory; carries the Western register of a juridically-recognized claim or entitlement that a subject possesses against other subjects or against political authority
plural rendering used to refer collectively to the bundle of legal entitlements a subject possesses; standard usage in human-rights and constitutional-rights discourse

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the continental European civil-law register; 権利 is structurally calibrated against the German Recht and French droit in their subjective-right (as opposed to objective-law) sense

literal-decompositional rendering — preserves the structural sense of 権 (calibrated authority) + 利 (advantage, benefit) by foregrounding the specifically claim-and-entitlement dimension of the compound, useful for explaining the difference between 権利 and the broader 法 (regulated order)

conceptual_remainder: 権利 is one of the load-bearing wasei-kango of modern East Asian legal vocabulary, and its calibration is doctrinally consequential. The Western concept of subjective right — a juridically-recognized claim or entitlement that an individual subject possesses, vis-à-vis other subjects or vis-à-vis political authority — is a structurally novel category in the modern East Asian legal landscape. Classical Chinese legal vocabulary articulated the structure of legitimate claim through different categories: 分 (one's portion or station within a relational order), 名 (name, title, the office one holds), 義 (rightness, what is properly due within the relational order), but none of these carries the specifically modern register of subjective right as the structural property of an autonomous individual subject standing prior to the social relations within which it is exercised. The compound 権利 was calibrated to render this modern register, and the choice of 利 (advantage, benefit) over 理 (principle, structure) was doctrinally consequential. Early-Meiji translators experimented with both forms, and the variant 権理 circulated through the 1870s precisely because 利 carried the classical Confucian opposition between 利 and 義 — the Mencian repudiation of self-interested gain in favor of moral rightness — that risked locating the modern rights-vocabulary on the morally-suspect side of the classical dichotomy. The stabilization of 権利 over 権理 by the 1880s thus calibrates the Japanese rights-vocabulary closer to the Anglophone 'right' (as benefit one may claim) than to the Kantian Recht (as principle of practical reason): 権利 names the claim or entitlement one has within the legal order, while what makes a claim a right (the principle from which it derives) is left to the broader theoretical apparatus rather than carried in the compound itself. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of authoritative-claim-and-benefit. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically natural-law register in which rights are pre-political moral entitlements grounded in the structure of practical reason or in the dignity of the human person — the register of the American Declaration's 'inalienable rights' or of Kantian Recht as the universal principle of freedom. The Meiji Constitution of 1889 calibrated 権利 in a deliberately limited register: the 臣民の権利 (rights of subjects) of Articles 18–32 are protections established by imperial grace within the constitutional order rather than inalienable claims grounded in popular sovereignty, and the constitutional-doctrinal asymmetry between the imperial-grant register and the popular-sovereignty register continues to shape the post-1947 reception of 権利 within Japanese constitutional politics. The post-war Constitution of 1947 substantially relocates the rights-vocabulary toward the popular-sovereignty register (基本的人権 kihonteki jinken, fundamental human rights, derived from natural-law rather than imperial-grant grounds), but the same compound 権利 carries both the 1889 imperial-grant register and the 1947 popular-sovereignty register, and the doctrinal tension between them is one of the load-bearing features of modern Japanese constitutional doctrine.
doctrinal_weight: 権利 arrives as part of the institutional cluster of liberal-democratic legal-political vocabulary alongside 義務 (duty), 法律 (statutory law), 憲法 (constitution), 主権 (sovereignty), 民主 (democracy), and is structurally pivotal within the cluster as the operating category of legal subjecthood: a 権利 is what a legal subject possesses vis-à-vis other subjects and vis-à-vis the state, and the broader institutional vocabulary of modern legal-political life is articulated around the structure of rights-and-duties (権利義務) that 権利 anchors. The compound's institutional life is enormous. The Meiji Constitution's articulation of 臣民の権利 in Articles 18–32 (the freedoms of residence, assembly, religion, speech, etc.) supplied the foundational rights-vocabulary of pre-war Japanese constitutional politics, with the post-war Constitution's articulation of 基本的人権 in Chapter III (Articles 10–40) substantially extending and entrenching the rights-vocabulary on a popular-sovereignty foundation. The compound's adoption into Chinese (quánlì) made it the operating term across late-Qing and Republican Chinese constitutional discourse, the Republican constitutions of 1912 and 1947, and the People's Republic of China's constitutional documents from the 1954 Constitution through the current 1982 Constitution and its amendments. The compound has been productive across the modern East Asian legal vocabulary in countless derivative compounds — 人権 (jinken, human rights), 公民権 (kōminken, civil rights), 著作権 (chosakuken, copyright), 特許権 (tokkyoken, patent), 所有権 (shoyūken, property right), 選挙権 (senkyoken, right to vote), 参政権 (sanseiken, political rights), 基本的人権 (fundamental human rights) — each calibrating the basic 権利 register to a particular juridical or political domain.

false_friends.divergence: 権理 (kenri, with 理 'principle' instead of 利) circulated as a competing orthography for 'right' in early-Meiji legal-translation usage, particularly through the 1870s. The choice of 利 (advantage, benefit) over 理 (principle, structure) by the 1880s constitutional drafting period was doctrinally consequential: 権利 calibrates the rights-vocabulary toward the claim-and-entitlement register of the Anglophone 'right,' while 権理 would have calibrated it toward the principle-of-reason register of the Kantian Recht. Reading the modern compound 権利 as if it were equivalent to 権理 imports a deontological-principled register that the stabilized compound deliberately did not foreground; the question of how rights are grounded in moral or rational principles is left to the broader theoretical apparatus rather than carried in the compound itself.

権力 (kenryoku, quánlì) names political power or authoritative force — the operational coercive capacity of state authority — rather than the juridical claim that subjects possess against authority. The Sino-Japanese vocabulary distinguishes 権利 (the claim subjects hold) from 権力 (the power authority exercises), and the structural distinction is doctrinally pivotal: rights-claims are made against the exercise of power, and the modern legal-constitutional order is structured around the limitation of 権力 by 権利. Reading 権利 as if it were equivalent to 権力 collapses the structural-political distinction between rights and power that the Western legal-constitutional tradition codes as the limitation of state authority by individual right.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized in the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, with Mitsukuri Rinshō (箕作麟祥) in his translations of the French Civil Code and Penal Code across the 1870s as the principal coinage-agent; institutionalized through the Meiji Constitution of 1889 (Articles 20–21 articulate 臣民の義務 — military service and tax-paying as the compulsory duties of imperial subjects) and the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education (教育勅語), which deployed the broader register of 義務 as the structural correlate of subject-status

components.meaning: rightness, what is properly due — the Confucian register of moral fittingness within the relational order; here calibrated toward the deontological register of what one is bound to perform, supplying the rightness-and-fitness dimension of the duty

work that must be done, office-bound task — the binding force of duty pressed upon one by station, role, or legal relation; paired with 義 to articulate the structurally-required task that constitutes a juridical obligation

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in moral and legal theory; carries the deontological register of what one is bound to perform within a normative or legal order
alternative rendering — foregrounds the juridical-bond register of the compound, useful in legal contexts where 義務 names a specifically enforceable juridical duty rather than a broader moral one

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the continental European deontological-juridical register; 義務 is structurally calibrated against the German Pflicht and French devoir in both their Kantian-moral and civil-law registers

conceptual_remainder: 義務 is the structural correlate of 権利 (right) in the modern East Asian legal vocabulary, articulating the deontological-juridical category of the bond by which a legal subject is required to perform or to refrain from a determinate action. The classical Chinese vocabulary articulated structural-deontological binding through different categories: 分 (one's portion or station), 義 (rightness within the relational order), 礼 (ritual propriety), 職 (office, station-bound task), but none of these carries the specifically modern register of obligation as a juridically-enforceable bond between abstract legal subjects standing in determinate legal relations. The Meiji compound 義務 was calibrated to render this modern register through the pairing of 義 (rightness, what is properly due) with 務 (work that must be done, office-bound duty), producing a compound that names not the relational propriety of the classical Confucian register but the structurally-binding task that constitutes a legal subject's juridical position. The choice of 義 over alternative first elements is doctrinally consequential: 義 carries the Confucian register of relational rightness, and the Meiji deployment in 義務 imports a faint deontological resonance that the more strictly juridical 法務 (legal affairs) or 任務 (task, charge) does not carry. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of binding-task-that-is-properly-due. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Kantian register of duty as the practical-rational ground of moral action — the categorical-imperative register in which Pflicht is the structure of practical reason rather than a juridically-enforceable bond. The Meiji deployment of 義務 in the Constitution of 1889 (Articles 20–21, the duty of military service and the duty of paying taxes) and the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education calibrated the term in a particular direction: 義務 was articulated as the compulsory tasks owed by imperial subjects to the state, with the relational structure running from subjects to sovereign authority rather than between equal legal subjects in a private-law relation. The post-war 1947 Constitution preserves the structural pairing of 権利 and 義務 but recalibrates the relational structure: the duties of Article 26 (compulsory education), Article 27 (the obligation to work), and Article 30 (the duty to pay taxes) are articulated within a framework of popular sovereignty rather than imperial subjecthood, and the compound 義務 carries both the imperial-subject register of 1889 and the popular-citizen register of 1947, with the doctrinal tension between the two registers continuing to shape modern Japanese legal-political vocabulary.
doctrinal_weight: 義務 stands as the deontological correlate of 権利 within the modern East Asian legal-political vocabulary, with the paired articulation 権利義務 (rights-and-duties) supplying the operating analytical axis of modern legal subjecthood. The compound is structurally pivotal within the broader institutional cluster: a legal subject is constituted as the bearer of 権利 (rights one may claim) and 義務 (duties one is bound to discharge), with the two categories articulating the active and passive sides of legal subjecthood in modern continental civil-law vocabulary. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji Constitution of 1889 articulated the 臣民の義務 (duties of subjects) in Articles 20–21 (military service and taxation), with the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education deploying 義務 as the broader normative register of imperial-subject obligation. The post-war 1947 Constitution articulates the 国民の三大義務 (three great duties of citizens) — compulsory education (Article 26), labor (Article 27), and taxation (Article 30) — recalibrating the rights-and-duties pairing within a popular-sovereignty framework. The compound is productive across the modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 義務教育 (gimu kyōiku, compulsory education), 義務違反 (gimu ihan, breach of duty), 兵役義務 (heieki gimu, military-service duty), 納税義務 (nōzei gimu, tax-paying duty), 義務者 (gimusha, the duty-bound party), 義務付ける (gimu-zukeru, to impose a duty). The compound has been adopted into Chinese (yìwù), Korean (의무), and Vietnamese (nghĩa vụ) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of legal obligation.

false_friends.divergence: 責務 (sekimu) names duty-as-responsibility — the obligation that arises from one's position or office, with the connotation of accountability for performance — and operates in a register closer to English 'responsibility' than to 'duty' in the strict juridical sense. 義務 (gimu) names the specifically juridical-deontological obligation as the structural correlate of right, while 責務 names the broader register of role-bound responsibility. Reading 義務 as if it were equivalent to 責務 attenuates the specifically juridical register of the compound and conflates it with the broader moral-and-administrative register of role-responsibility.

義理 (giri) names the classical-Japanese register of social-relational obligation grounded in honor, debt, and the obligations of relationship — a load-bearing category of pre-modern and early-modern Japanese moral-social vocabulary, with the compound articulating duties owed to family, lord, friend, or benefactor by virtue of the relational bond itself. 義務 (gimu) is the modern juridical compound that names legally-enforceable obligation between abstract legal subjects, and the two compounds articulate radically different registers: 義理 is honor-relational and informally-binding, while 義務 is law-juridical and formally-enforceable. The Tokugawa-period vocabulary of 義理人情 (giri-and-ninjō, the dialectic of social obligation and human feeling) is largely superseded in modern juridical contexts by the Meiji vocabulary of 権利義務 (rights-and-duties), and reading 義務 as if it carried the relational-honor register of 義理 imports a pre-modern register that the modern legal compound deliberately does not foreground.

coinage_notes: Re-coinage of a classical-Chinese compound (法律 attested in pre-Qin texts in the sense of 'penal codes and statutes'; the compound is structurally present in the imperial-Chinese 律令 vocabulary) stabilized in its modern sense through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, with Mitsukuri Rinshō, Tsuda Mamichi, and the broader Meiji legal-translation circle as principal coinage-agents across the 1870s; institutionalized through the Meiji Constitution of 1889 (in which Articles 5, 8, 9, and 37 deploy 法律 as the operational category of statutory law within the constitutional framework) and authoritatively glossed in Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries on the Constitution (憲法義解, 1889)

components.meaning: regulated order, dharma, law in the broadest sense — here in its operational-regulatory register, naming the body of legal rules as the regulated structure of state action

calibrated rule, statutory ordinance — the calibrated standard against which conduct is measured; paired with 法 to articulate the body of statutory rules issued by competent legislative authority within the constitutional framework

translation_range.emphasis: general universal rendering; carries the broad register of statutory rules issued by legislative authority, as well as the broader register of legal order generally

specifically juridical rendering — foregrounds the structural-positional register of the compound as the operational layer of legislation, distinguished from the foundational layer of constitutional law (憲法)

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the continental European civil-law register; 法律 is structurally calibrated against the German Gesetz and French loi as products of legislative enactment within the constitutional order

qualified rendering — used to disambiguate 法律 (statute) from 法 in its broader senses (regulated order, dharma, principle); useful in contexts where the structural distinction between constitutional and statutory law is foreground

conceptual_remainder: 法律 was a classical-Chinese compound long before the Meiji period, attested in pre-Qin texts in the sense of 'penal codes and statutes' and structurally present in the imperial-Chinese 律令 vocabulary that supplied the operating administrative-legal vocabulary of the Tang and the institutional model that Nara-Heian Japan adopted in the 大宝律令 (Taihō Code, 701) and 養老律令 (Yōrō Code, 718). What the Meiji period did was not coin the compound but recalibrate it: from the classical register of 'penal codes and statutes within the imperial administrative apparatus' to the modern register of 'statutory law as the product of legislative authority within the constitutional framework.' The recalibration was doctrinally consequential, because the modern register imports a structural-positional dimension that the classical register does not carry: 法律 in the modern Meiji deployment is calibrated against 憲法 (constitutional law) as the operational-statutory layer below the constitutional-foundational layer, with the legitimacy of any 法律 depending on its consistency with the 憲法. This structural-hierarchical articulation is the central doctrinal feature of the modern Meiji legal vocabulary, and the compound 法律 carries it through the late-nineteenth and twentieth centuries as one of the operating terms of modern East Asian constitutional law. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of regulated-statutory-rule. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically modern Western register of statutory law as the expression of popular sovereignty through legislative procedure — the Rousseauian-Atlantic register in which a 法律 is legitimate because it expresses the volonté générale of the people. The Meiji Constitution of 1889 calibrated 法律 in a deliberately Bismarckian-Prussian register: statutes were enacted by the Imperial Diet through procedures involving both the bicameral assembly and imperial sanction, with the structural primacy of imperial sanction reflecting the German-monarchical-constitutional rather than the Atlantic-popular-sovereignty tradition. The post-war 1947 Constitution recalibrates 法律 toward the popular-sovereignty register: Article 41 articulates the Diet as 'the highest organ of state power and the sole law-making organ of the State,' relocating the primary source of statutory legitimacy in popular legislative authority. The compound 法律 carries both the 1889 imperial-sanction register and the 1947 popular-sovereignty register, and the doctrinal tension between the two articulations of statutory legitimacy continues to shape modern Japanese legal-constitutional doctrine.
doctrinal_weight: 法律 sits at the operational core of the modern Meiji legal-constitutional vocabulary, with its structural calibration against 憲法 (constitutional law) supplying the foundational hierarchical articulation of the Western Rechtsstaat tradition that the Meiji Constitution adopted from German constitutional theory. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji Constitution articulated 法律 in Article 5 (legislative power), Article 8 (imperial ordinances having the force of law), Article 9 (regulations supplementing law), and Article 37 (the Imperial Diet's role in legislative consent), supplying the operating institutional-legal vocabulary of pre-war Japanese constitutional politics. The post-war 1947 Constitution preserves the operating role of 法律 within the constitutional framework while substantially recalibrating its political-theoretical foundation toward popular sovereignty. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (fǎlǜ), Korean (법률), and Vietnamese (pháp luật) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of statutory law, with the broader vocabulary of modern legal compounds — 法律家 (hōritsuka, lawyer / legal scholar), 法律学 (hōritsugaku, jurisprudence), 法律問題 (hōritsu mondai, legal question), 法律違反 (hōritsu ihan, statutory violation), 国際法 (kokusaihō, international law), 民法 (minpō, civil law), 刑法 (keihō, criminal law) — articulating the operational vocabulary of the modern East Asian legal landscape.

false_friends.divergence: 憲法 (kenpō, xiànfǎ) names constitutional law — the foundational instrument standing above ordinary statutes — while 法律 (hōritsu, fǎlǜ) names the ordinary statutory law enacted by the legislature within the constitutional framework. The structural-hierarchical distinction between the two compounds is the central feature of the modern continental Rechtsstaat tradition that the Meiji Constitution adopted from German constitutional theory, and reading 法律 as if it were equivalent to 憲法 collapses the structural hierarchy that the modern legal vocabulary is calibrated to articulate. In a constitutional dispute, the question is whether a 法律 is consistent with the 憲法 — and the answer is determined by judicial review under the constitutional framework, not by simple application of the statute itself.

法 alone is radically polysemous — it names dharma in the Buddhist register (the Buddha's teaching, the constitutive elements of phenomena, the law of how things are), method in the technical-procedural register (方法, hōhō), and the broader legal order in the juridical register. 法律 (hōritsu) is the specifically juridical-statutory compound that articulates statutory law as the product of legislative authority within the constitutional framework, distinguished both from the broader 法 in its Buddhist and methodological registers and from 憲法 (constitutional law) in its foundational register. Reading the compound 法律 as merely a redundant doubling of 法 misses the structural-calibrational work that 律 performs: it specifies the statutory-legislative register against the broader range of senses that 法 alone carries.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized in the early-Meiji judicial-reform apparatus across the 1870s–1890s, with the founding of the Justice Ministry (司法省, 1871), the codification of judicial procedure through the 治罪法 (1880, drafted under Gustave Boissonade) and the modern 刑事訴訟法 (1890) and 民事訴訟法 (1890) drafted with German jurists' assistance, and the broader institutional articulation of the modern Japanese judicial system on a French-then-German continental civil-law model; institutionalized through the Court Organization Law (裁判所構成法, 1890) and the Meiji Constitution's articulation of the judicial power in Articles 57–61

components.meaning: to cut and shape, to adjudicate — here in its judicial-cutting register, naming the determinate severance by which the court resolves between competing claims

to split and decide, to pronounce — paired with 裁 to articulate the formal pronouncement that completes the judicial act; the two characters together constitute the structure of judicial trial as both adjudicatory cutting and authoritative determination

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in modern legal usage; carries the procedural register of the formal judicial proceeding by which a court hears competing claims and issues an authoritative determination

alternative rendering — foregrounds the substantive-determinative register of the compound, useful in contexts where the focus is on the court's authoritative resolution rather than the procedural-formal aspect
broader rendering used to encompass both the procedural and substantive aspects of the judicial act; in some contexts 裁判 names the proceeding, in others the resulting determination

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the continental European civil-law register; 裁判 is structurally calibrated against the French procès and German Gerichtsverfahren as the operating procedural categories of the continental civil-law tradition that the Meiji judicial system adopted

conceptual_remainder: 裁判 is one of the principal wasei-kango of the modern Meiji judicial-legal vocabulary, articulating the Western category of judicial trial through the pairing of 裁 (the adjudicatory cutting) and 判 (the formal pronouncement). The classical East Asian judicial vocabulary articulated the structure of authoritative determination through different categories: 訴訟 (sùsòng, litigation in the sense of bringing complaint), 審理 (shēnlǐ, careful inquiry), 判決 (pànjué, formal verdict), 鞫問 (jūwèn, examination), but the modern compound 裁判 was developed as the operating term for the systematic Western category of judicial trial as a structured procedure within an independent judicial branch of constitutional government. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 裁 + 判 articulates is the dual structure of a judicial trial: the cutting-side (裁), in which the court severs competing claims through the application of legal-procedural rules, and the pronouncement-side (判), in which the court issues the formal determination that authoritatively resolves the legal question. The Sino-Japanese compound thus preserves the dual structure that the English 'trial' (from try, to test) does not foreground, supplying a more structurally-articulated rendering of the underlying judicial act. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of authoritative cutting-and-determining. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Anglo-American adversarial-jury-trial register, in which a trial is the testing of competing claims through cross-examination before a lay fact-finder, with the judge as procedural manager rather than as principal adjudicatory authority. The Meiji judicial system was developed on a continental civil-law model — French through the 1870s under Boissonade, German from the 1880s through the constitutional drafting period — with the compound 裁判 calibrated for the inquisitorial-magistrate-centered register of continental judicial practice rather than the adversarial-jury register of common-law trial procedure. The post-war 1947 Constitution and the subsequent introduction of the 裁判員制度 (saibanin seido, lay-judge system) in 2009 have introduced selected adversarial and lay-participation elements into the Japanese judicial system, but the operating register of 裁判 remains within the broader continental civil-law tradition that the Meiji judicial reforms established.
doctrinal_weight: 裁判 sits at the operational core of the modern Meiji judicial-institutional vocabulary, anchoring the broader cluster of judicial-procedural terms that articulate the operation of the modern Japanese judicial system. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji judicial reforms of the 1870s–1890s — the founding of the Justice Ministry (1871), the establishment of the modern court system through the Court Organization Law (1890), the codification of criminal procedure through the 治罪法 (1880) and the modern 刑事訴訟法 (1890), the codification of civil procedure through the 民事訴訟法 (1890), and the broader institutional articulation of an independent judiciary modeled on French and German judicial-administrative practice — supplied the operating institutional vocabulary of modern Japanese judicial life. The compound is productive across the modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 裁判所 (saibansho, court of law), 裁判官 (saibankan, judge), 裁判員 (saibanin, lay judge — introduced in 2009), 裁判長 (saibanchō, presiding judge), 民事裁判 (minji saiban, civil trial), 刑事裁判 (keiji saiban, criminal trial), 行政裁判 (gyōsei saiban, administrative trial), 最高裁判所 (saikō saibansho, Supreme Court), 国際裁判 (kokusai saiban, international trial). The compound has been adopted into Chinese (cáipàn), Korean (재판), and Vietnamese (tài phán) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of judicial trial. The compound's institutional centrality to the modern Japanese state is articulated in Article 76 of the post-war Constitution: 'The whole judicial power is vested in a Supreme Court and in such inferior courts as are established by law' — with 裁判 as the operating term of the judicial power thus vested.

false_friends.divergence: 判決 (hanketsu, pànjué) names specifically the verdict or judgment — the formal determination issued by the court at the conclusion of the trial — while 裁判 (saiban) names the broader procedural-substantive structure of the trial itself, encompassing both the procedure (the proceedings before the court) and the determination (the resulting verdict). Reading 裁判 as if it were equivalent to 判決 collapses the procedural-substantive distinction that the broader compound articulates: a 裁判 is a structured judicial proceeding within which a 判決 is issued, with the procedure-and-determination structure preserved in the dual compound.

訴訟 (soshō, sùsòng) names litigation in the sense of bringing a legal claim before the court — the procedural-actional register of initiating and prosecuting a legal action — while 裁判 names the judicial trial in its operational-determinative register. The two compounds are structurally complementary: a 訴訟 (litigation) is what the parties bring, while a 裁判 (trial) is what the court holds in response. The modern Japanese procedural codes — 民事訴訟法 (Civil Procedure Code) and 刑事訴訟法 (Criminal Procedure Code) — code the litigant-side procedure under 訴訟, while the broader institutional vocabulary of the judicial system is articulated under 裁判 (the trial, the court, the judge).

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized through the early-Meiji liberal-political vocabulary of the 1870s, with the broader compound 天賦人権 (tenpu jinken, heaven-endowed human rights) prominent across the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動) of the 1870s–1880s as the principal Japanese articulation of natural-law rights; principal coinage-agents include Ueki Emori (植木枝盛, whose 1879 Minken Jiyū Ron 民権自由論 supplied a foundational liberal articulation of natural-rights doctrine), Nakae Chōmin (中江兆民, who translated Rousseau's Du contrat social as 民約訳解 in 1882–1883), and the broader Meiji-liberal intellectual circle of the 1870s–1880s; substantially recalibrated through the post-war 1947 Constitution's articulation of 基本的人権 (kihonteki jinken, fundamental human rights) in Chapter III (Articles 10–40)

components.meaning: person, human being — here in its universal-anthropological register, naming the human being as such rather than the citizen-of-a-nation or the imperial subject; the structural unit of the natural-law tradition that articulates rights as inhering in human nature prior to and independent of political institution

calibrated authority, right — here in its juridical-claim register, naming the entitlement that the human being possesses by virtue of human nature itself; the same character that carries 'sovereignty' in 主権 and 'right' in 権利 is here calibrated specifically toward the universal-natural-law register

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in modern legal-political theory; carries the natural-law and international-human-rights register of rights inhering in human beings as such, prior to and independent of political institution

alternative rendering used to foreground the natural-law-doctrinal grounding of the category, particularly resonant with the Meiji-period 天賦人権 (tenpu jinken, heaven-endowed human rights) vocabulary of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the European-continental natural-rights tradition; 人権 is structurally calibrated against the German Menschenrechte and French droits de l'homme as the operating term of the modern continental-European human-rights tradition, with the French Declaration of 1789 supplying the foundational document

qualified rendering corresponding to the post-war Japanese constitutional-doctrinal compound 基本的人権 (kihonteki jinken), which articulates 人権 in the specifically constitutionally-entrenched and popular-sovereignty-grounded register of the 1947 Constitution's Chapter III

conceptual_remainder: 人権 is one of the most doctrinally-charged compounds of modern East Asian political-legal vocabulary, calibrating the Western category of human rights through the structural pairing of 人 (the human being as such) with 権 (calibrated authority, right). The choice of 人 over alternative first elements is doctrinally consequential: 国民権 (kokuminken) would have calibrated the rights-vocabulary toward citizen-of-a-nation membership, 公民権 (kōminken) toward civil rights specifically, and 臣民の権利 (shinmin no kenri) toward imperial-subject status; only 人 calibrates the compound toward the universal-anthropological register that the natural-law tradition requires. The Meiji-period vocabulary of 天賦人権 (tenpu jinken, heaven-endowed human rights), prominent in the 1870s–1880s Freedom and People's Rights Movement, deploys 人 specifically to articulate the natural-law register in which rights are pre-political moral entitlements grounded in the structure of human nature itself rather than imperial-grant prerogatives bestowed by political authority. The doctrinal stakes of the 人 / 臣民 distinction were explicit in late-Meiji constitutional debate: the 1881 draft constitutions of the People's Rights Movement (notably Ueki Emori's 東洋大日本国国憲按) articulated rights as 人民 (jinmin, the people) entitlements grounded in natural-law doctrine, while the 1889 Meiji Constitution articulated the same protections as 臣民の権利 (rights of subjects) bestowed through the imperial constitution as a gift of imperial grace, with the doctrinal asymmetry between the natural-law and imperial-grant registers shaping the structural shape of pre-war Japanese constitutional politics. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of human-being-as-rights-bearer. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Christian-natural-law theological grounding that the eighteenth-century Anglo-American natural-rights tradition inherited from the late-medieval scholastic articulation — the Lockean rights as endowments of the Creator, the inalienable-rights vocabulary that presupposes a particular theological-anthropological framework. The post-war Constitution of 1947 substantially relocates the rights-vocabulary toward the popular-sovereignty register through the compound 基本的人権 (kihonteki jinken, fundamental human rights), articulated in Chapter III as inalienable claims grounded in the dignity of the human person and entrenched against legislative override under the constitutional supremacy doctrine. The post-war recalibration is doctrinally consequential — it imports the natural-law-grounded register of inalienable rights that the Meiji compound had articulated in the 天賦人権 vocabulary but that the Meiji Constitution had not constitutionally entrenched — and the doctrinal trajectory from Meiji 天賦人権 through the imperial-subject-rights register of the 1889 Constitution to the popular-sovereignty 基本的人権 of the 1947 Constitution constitutes the central narrative arc of modern Japanese constitutional-rights doctrine.
doctrinal_weight: 人権 sits at the doctrinally-load-bearing center of the modern East Asian liberal-democratic vocabulary, calibrating the universal-anthropological register of natural-law rights against the citizen-membership and imperial-subject registers that competing rights-vocabularies code. The compound's institutional life across the modern East Asian landscape is enormous. The Meiji-period Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動, 1874–1890) deployed 人権 and the broader compound 天賦人権 as the principal vocabulary of liberal-natural-rights doctrine, with the Itagaki Petition for the Establishment of a Popularly Elected Assembly (民撰議院設立建白書, 1874) and Ueki Emori's Minken Jiyū Ron (民権自由論, 1879) supplying the foundational textual articulations. The post-war 1947 Constitution articulates 基本的人権 (fundamental human rights) in Chapter III (Articles 10–40), with Article 11 ('The people shall not be prevented from enjoying any of the fundamental human rights. These fundamental human rights guaranteed to the people by this Constitution shall be conferred upon the people of this and future generations as eternal and inviolate rights') and Article 97 ('The fundamental human rights by this Constitution guaranteed to the people of Japan are fruits of the age-old struggle of man to be free; they have survived the many exacting tests for durability and are conferred upon this and future generations in trust, to be held for all time inviolate') articulating the natural-law-grounded constitutional entrenchment that the modern Japanese constitutional-rights tradition inherits. The compound's adoption into Chinese (rénquán, 人权), Korean (인권), and Vietnamese (nhân quyền) made it the universal modern East Asian rendering of human rights, with the post-WWII international-human-rights apparatus — the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), the International Covenants of 1966, the broader contemporary international-human-rights treaty system — supplying the international-legal framework within which the compound operates as the operating term of contemporary human-rights discourse. The compound is productive across modern East Asian human-rights vocabulary: 基本的人権 (fundamental human rights), 国際人権 (kokusai jinken, international human rights), 人権侵害 (jinken shingai, human rights violation), 人権擁護 (jinken yōgo, human rights advocacy), 人権宣言 (jinken sengen, declaration of human rights — used of the 1789 French Declaration and the 1948 Universal Declaration).

false_friends.divergence: 公民権 (kōminken, gōngmínquán) names civil rights specifically — the rights of citizens within a particular political community, including political-participation rights such as voting and standing for office — while 人権 (jinken) names the broader category of rights inhering in human beings as such, prior to and independent of citizenship status. The structural distinction between the two compounds tracks the Western distinction between human rights (held by all human beings) and civil rights (held by members of a particular political community), with the structural-categorical relation that all human rights are protected for citizens but not all civil rights extend to non-citizens. Reading 人権 as if it were equivalent to 公民権 collapses the universal-anthropological register that 人 contributes to the compound and limits the rights-vocabulary to citizen-membership in a particular polity.

民権 (minken) names the rights of the people as a collective political body, with the broader vocabulary of the Meiji-period Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動) deploying 民権 specifically in the political-collective register of the people's rights vis-à-vis sovereign authority. The compound is structurally distinct from 人権 (jinken): 民権 names the collective-political register of popular rights, while 人権 names the individual-anthropological register of human-being rights. The two compounds were both productive in late-Meiji liberal-political vocabulary and were sometimes deployed together (民権・人権) to articulate the dual structure of popular-political rights and natural-human-rights, but the structural distinction between them is doctrinally consequential.

coinage_notes: Re-coinage of a classical Sino-Japanese compound (契約 attested in pre-modern East Asian legal-relational vocabulary in the broader register of mutual binding agreement) stabilized in its modern continental-civil-law sense through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, with Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French Civil Code (民法) across 1870–1874 as the principal stabilization-vehicle; institutionalized through the Boissonade Old Civil Code (旧民法, drafted by Gustave Boissonade, promulgated 1890 but never enforced) and the modern Civil Code (民法, drafted by Hozumi Nobushige, Tomii Masaakira, and Ume Kenjirō under both French and German civil-law influence, promulgated 1896 with the property and obligations books, fully enforced 1898) — Articles 521–696 of the current Civil Code articulate the systematic doctrinal apparatus of contract within the modern Japanese civil-law tradition

components.meaning: to incise, to bind by mutual incision — here in its evidentiary-articulating register, naming the formal mutual articulation by which parties commit themselves to determinate undertakings; the etymological ground of paired tally-sticks broken in two and rejoined as proof of mutual agreement

to bind with a cord, to tighten into a knot — here in its binding-and-determining register, naming the structural constraint by which parties are tied to the agreed undertaking; paired with 契 to articulate the dual structure of contract as both formal articulation and structural binding

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering in modern legal usage; carries the systematic continental-civil-law and Anglo-American common-law category of the juridically-enforceable agreement between parties
broader rendering used to encompass both formally-binding contracts and looser mutual understandings; useful in contexts where the strictly juridical-enforceable register is not foreground

rendering used in contexts foregrounding the continental European civil-law register; 契約 is structurally calibrated against the German Vertrag and French contrat as the operating doctrinal categories of the continental civil-law contract tradition that the Meiji Civil Code adopted

alternative renderings used in contexts foregrounding the deeper relational or political-philosophical register of the compound — particularly in social-contract-theoretical contexts where 契約 is deployed as the rendering of the social compact (社会契約, shakai keiyaku, the social contract)

conceptual_remainder: 契約 was a classical Sino-Japanese compound long before the Meiji period, attested in pre-modern East Asian vocabulary in the broader register of mutual binding agreement and structurally available across the spectrum from formal legal contracts to relational and personal pledges. What the Meiji period did was not coin the compound but recalibrate it: from the classical register of 'mutual agreement, binding compact' to the modern register of 'juridically-enforceable contract within the systematic continental-civil-law doctrine of obligations.' The recalibration was doctrinally consequential, because the modern register imports a structural-systematic dimension that the classical register did not carry: 契約 in the modern Meiji deployment is calibrated within the doctrinal apparatus of the modern continental-civil-law obligation system, with the typology of contracts (sales, lease, employment, agency, deposit, partnership), the doctrinal apparatus of formation (offer, acceptance, capacity, consideration), the apparatus of performance and breach (debtor's obligations, creditor's claims, default, damages), and the systematic relation to the broader civil-law vocabulary of property, persons, and obligations. The structural-systematic articulation imported through the Meiji recalibration is the central doctrinal feature of modern East Asian contract law, and the compound 契約 carries it through the late-nineteenth and twentieth centuries as one of the operating terms of modern continental-civil-law-influenced legal practice. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of mutual articulation and structural binding. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Anglo-American common-law bargain-theory register of contract as a bargained-for exchange supported by consideration — the doctrinal apparatus of consideration (the requirement that something of value be exchanged to make a promise legally enforceable) that distinguishes the common-law contract tradition from the continental civil-law tradition is foreign to the systematic apparatus of the Japanese Civil Code, which adopted the continental Willensdogma (the doctrine that the parties' free declaration of will is the structural foundation of contractual obligation) rather than the consideration-based common-law apparatus. The classical-relational register of 契 (intimate pledge, tacit accord) and 約 (personal promise, 約束 yakusoku) continues to inflect the modern legal-juridical register subtly: a 契約 carries faint resonance of relational commitment and personal pledge that the bare Anglo-American 'contract' as bargained-for exchange does not fully convey, and this resonance shapes the doctrinal style of modern Japanese contract law in subtle ways — including the relatively strong doctrinal weight given to good faith (信義則, shingisoku) and to relational considerations in modern Japanese contract practice.
doctrinal_weight: 契約 sits at the operational core of the modern continental-civil-law-influenced Japanese private-law tradition, anchoring the broader doctrinal apparatus of voluntary obligation that the modern Civil Code articulates. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji legal-codification process — from Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1870s translations of the French Civil Code through the Boissonade Old Civil Code of 1890 to the current Civil Code of 1896–1898 drafted by Hozumi Nobushige, Tomii Masaakira, and Ume Kenjirō — supplied the operating doctrinal vocabulary, with Articles 521–696 of the current Civil Code articulating the systematic typology and doctrinal apparatus of contract. The compound is productive across modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 契約書 (keiyakusho, contract document), 売買契約 (baibai keiyaku, sales contract), 雇用契約 (koyō keiyaku, employment contract), 賃貸借契約 (chintaishaku keiyaku, lease contract), 婚姻契約 (kon'in keiyaku, marriage contract), 解約 (kaiyaku, cancellation of contract), 違約 (iyaku, breach of contract), 違約金 (iyakukin, liquidated damages), 契約自由の原則 (keiyaku jiyū no gensoku, the principle of freedom of contract). The compound also carries the broader political-philosophical register of the social contract through the compound 社会契約 (shakai keiyaku) — the rendering of Rousseau's Du contrat social (1762) prominent in Nakae Chōmin's 1882–1883 民約訳解 (Min'yaku Yakkai) translation, which deployed 民約 as the alternative-rendering for 'social contract' and made 契約 / 民約 vocabulary central to late-Meiji liberal-democratic political theory. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (qìyuē, 契约 in simplified script), Korean (계약), and Vietnamese (khế ước) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of contract.

false_friends.divergence: 約束 (yakusoku) names a personal-relational promise — a pledge or commitment between persons in their personal-relational capacity — while 契約 (keiyaku) names the juridically-enforceable contract within the systematic civil-law obligation apparatus. The structural distinction is doctrinally consequential: a 約束 may be a moral or relational obligation enforceable through informal social mechanisms (reputation, trust, affective bond), while a 契約 is enforceable through the formal apparatus of civil litigation under the Civil Code's contract provisions. Modern Japanese usage preserves both compounds productively, with 約束 carrying the broader register of personal commitment and 契約 carrying the specifically juridical register of formal contractual obligation.

条約 (jōyaku, tiáoyuē) names a formal treaty between sovereign states under international law, while 契約 (keiyaku) names the contract between private parties under municipal civil law. The two compounds share the second character 約 but deploy different first characters to articulate the structural distinction: 条 (article, structured-clause) supplies the article-by-article structure of treaty texts, while 契 (mutual-incision, evidentiary articulation) supplies the relational-evidentiary structure of private contract. The structural-domain distinction between international-public-law treaty and municipal-private-law contract is one of the load-bearing distinctions of modern East Asian legal vocabulary, and reading 契約 as if it were equivalent to 条約 collapses the public-private-international-municipal distinction that the modern legal vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

conceptual_remainder: 犯罪 is one of the principal wasei-kango of modern East Asian criminal-law vocabulary, articulating the Western category of crime through the structural pairing of 犯 (the active transgression) and 罪 (the structural-juridical category of the punishable wrong). The classical East Asian criminal-law vocabulary articulated the structure of legal wrong-and-punishment through different categories: 罪 alone in classical Chinese and Sino-Japanese could carry the full register of legal wrongdoing, with the broader cluster 罪刑 (zàixíng, crime-and-punishment), 律令 (lǜlìng, statutes-and-ordinances), 刑罰 (xíngfá, criminal sanction) supplying the operating institutional vocabulary of the imperial-Chinese and Nara-Heian Japanese criminal-administrative apparatus. The Meiji compound 犯罪 was developed as the operating term for the specifically modern Western category of crime as the legally-defined wrong subject to determinate-and-proportionate criminal sanction within the rule-of-law framework — the Beccarian-Feuerbachian articulation of nulla poena sine lege (no penalty without prior law, 罪刑法定主義 zaikei hōteishugi) that supplied the principal doctrinal foundation of modern continental criminal law. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 犯 + 罪 articulates is the dual structure of the criminal occurrence: the act-side (犯), in which the agent crosses the legal-normative line through the commission of the prohibited act, and the category-side (罪), in which the legal system classifies the act as falling within the determinate category of punishable wrong defined by statute. The Sino-Japanese compound thus preserves the doctrinal distinction between the agent-act and the system-classification that the modern Western criminal-law tradition articulates through the Tatbestand doctrine (the statutory-definitional element) and the Tatbestandsmäßigkeit principle (the requirement that the act fall within the statutory definition for criminal liability). What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of authoritative-classified-act-of-transgression. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Beccarian-Enlightenment register of crime as a measured-and-proportionate violation of social-contract obligations subject to determinate-and-proportionate punishment, the Enlightenment-doctrinal apparatus of utilitarian penology that grounded the eighteenth-century criminal-law reform tradition. The Meiji Penal Code adopted the continental-Beccarian doctrinal apparatus, but the systematic doctrinal foundations of the modern criminal-law tradition — the nulla poena sine lege principle, the Tatbestand doctrine, the schuld-principle of culpability-based criminal liability, the broader doctrinal apparatus of the modern Strafrecht — were imported through the legal-translation apparatus rather than carried in the compound 犯罪 itself, with the broader cluster of compounds 罪刑法定主義, 構成要件, 責任主義 articulating the systematic doctrinal apparatus.
doctrinal_weight: 犯罪 sits at the operational core of the modern Japanese criminal-law vocabulary, anchoring the broader cluster of criminal-procedural and criminal-doctrinal terms that articulate the operation of the modern Japanese criminal-justice system. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji criminal-law codification process — from Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1870s translations of the French Code Pénal through the Boissonade Penal Code of 1880 to the current Penal Code of 1907 — supplied the operating institutional-doctrinal vocabulary, with the systematic doctrinal apparatus of modern continental criminal law (the Tatbestand-Rechtswidrigkeit-Schuld three-element structure of criminal liability) entering modern Japanese legal vocabulary through the broader cluster of compounds 構成要件 (kōsei yōken, statutory-definitional element), 違法性 (ihōsei, unlawfulness), 責任 (sekinin, culpability). The compound is productive across modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 犯人 (hannin, perpetrator), 犯行 (hankō, criminal act), 共犯 (kyōhan, accomplice), 主犯 (shuhan, principal offender), 再犯 (saihan, repeat offense), 防犯 (bōhan, crime prevention), 凶悪犯罪 (kyōaku hanzai, violent crime), 経済犯罪 (keizai hanzai, economic crime), 組織犯罪 (soshiki hanzai, organized crime), 国際犯罪 (kokusai hanzai, international crime), 戦争犯罪 (sensō hanzai, war crime). The compound has been adopted into Chinese (fànzuì), Korean (범죄), and Vietnamese (phạm tội) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of crime in its juridical-criminal sense. The structural pairing 犯 + 罪 supplied the productive paradigm for related compounds across the modern Japanese criminal-law landscape: 犯罪者 (the perpetrator), 犯罪学 (criminology), 犯罪率 (crime rate), 犯罪心理学 (criminal psychology) — articulating the broader institutional and analytical apparatus of the modern criminal-justice system.

false_friends.divergence: 罪 alone is radically polysemous across the legal-juridical register (the punishable wrong, 罪状 charges, 有罪 guilty), the moral-ethical register (the moral fault, 罪過), the religious-Buddhist register (罪業 zaigō, the negative karmic burden of unskillful action), and the Christian-translation register (罪 as the rendering of 'sin'). 犯罪 (hanzai) is the specifically modern juridical-criminal compound that articulates crime as the legally-defined wrong subject to formal criminal sanction within the rule-of-law framework. Reading 犯罪 as if it were equivalent to bare 罪 collapses the structural-categorical specificity that the modern legal vocabulary is calibrated to articulate, and conflates the modern juridical category with the broader range of moral, religious, and ethical senses that the bare character carries.

罪業 (zaigō) names the Buddhist-karmic register of unskillful action — the negative karmic burden generated by acts that are unwholesome under the Buddhist analysis of action, with the structural register being the karmic-causal effect of action on subsequent rebirth and the practical register being the practitioner's relation to past unwholesome action through repentance (懺悔, sange) and purification practices. 犯罪 (hanzai) names the modern juridical-criminal category, and the two compounds articulate radically different registers: 罪業 is karmic-soteriological and addressed through Buddhist practice, while 犯罪 is juridical-procedural and addressed through criminal prosecution and sanction. The Buddhist-karmic register continues to inflect modern Japanese moral vocabulary subtly, but the strict juridical category is articulated specifically through 犯罪 rather than through the broader 罪業.

conceptual_remainder: 被告 is one of the structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern East Asian procedural-legal vocabulary, calibrating the Western procedural category of the defendant through the structural pairing of 被 (the passive-receiving prefix) and 告 (the formal-charge register). The Meiji recruitment of 被 as the systematic passive-prefix across legal-procedural compounds — 被告, 被害者, 被疑者, 被選挙権, 被保険者 — calibrated the classical-Chinese passive-grammatical register for the modern continental-civil-law procedural vocabulary, with the prefix-formation pattern productive across the broader modern East Asian legal-administrative landscape. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 被 + 告 articulates is the structural-procedural opposition between the active-charging side (原告 genkoku, the plaintiff or 検察官 kensatsukan, the prosecutor) and the passive-receiving side (被告) of the litigation, with 告 functioning as the structural-articulating element on both sides of the relation: the 原告 lodges the 告 (formal charge) and the 被告 receives the 告 (is informed-against). The structural-procedural symmetry of the 原告 / 被告 pair preserves in the Sino-Japanese compounds a doctrinal precision that the asymmetric English plaintiff / defendant pair (derived from different etymological roots — plaintiff from Old French plaintif, complainant; defendant from Latin defendere, to ward off) does not foreground. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of the passive-receiving party-position. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Anglo-American common-law constitutional-rights apparatus of the criminal defendant — the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, the Sixth Amendment rights to counsel, jury trial, confrontation of witnesses, and compulsory process, the broader Anglo-American procedural-rights tradition that supplies a substantial doctrinal apparatus of due-process protections specific to the criminally-accused. The post-war 1948 Code of Criminal Procedure substantially imported the Anglo-American procedural-rights apparatus into Japanese criminal procedure under the influence of the American Occupation, with the constitutional-rights apparatus articulated in Articles 31–40 of the 1947 Constitution (rights against self-incrimination, to counsel, to a speedy trial, against double jeopardy) and codified in the Criminal Procedure Code, and the modern Japanese 被告人 carries this American-influenced procedural-rights apparatus despite the continental-civil-law structural framework that the broader Japanese legal system retained. The structural-typological distinction between 被告 (civil) and 被告人 (criminal) within the modern Japanese procedural codes preserves the continental civil-law typological articulation against the Anglo-American common-law generalized usage of 'defendant' across both contexts.
doctrinal_weight: 被告 sits at the operational core of the modern Japanese procedural-legal vocabulary, anchoring the broader cluster of procedural-party terms that articulate the operation of the modern Japanese civil and criminal litigation systems. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji procedural-code drafting process — from Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1870s translations of the French procedural codes through the Boissonade-influenced procedural codes of 1890 to the current procedural codes (1996 civil; 1948 criminal) — supplied the operating institutional vocabulary, with the procedural-party typology 原告 / 被告 (plaintiff / defendant in civil proceedings) and 検察官 / 被告人 (prosecutor / accused in criminal proceedings) articulating the structural-procedural opposition that anchors modern Japanese litigation. The compound is productive across modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 被告人 (hikokunin, the criminally accused), 被告席 (hikokuseki, the dock), 共同被告 (kyōdō hikoku, joint defendants), 被告適格 (hikoku tekikaku, defendant standing), 被告側 (hikoku-gawa, the defense side). The compound has been adopted into Chinese (bèigào), Korean (피고), and Vietnamese (bị cáo) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of the procedural defendant. The structural-calibration of the 被 + 告 pattern supplied the productive paradigm for related procedural-passive compounds across the modern Japanese legal landscape: 被害者 (higaisha, victim), 被疑者 (higisha, suspect), 被相続人 (hisōzokunin, the deceased / decedent), 被保険者 (hihokensha, the insured) — articulating the broader institutional vocabulary of passive-receiving party-positions across the modern Japanese legal-administrative apparatus.

false_friends.divergence: 被告人 (hikokunin) names specifically the criminally-accused — the party against whom criminal charges have been formally lodged through prosecutorial indictment — while 被告 (hikoku) is the broader procedural compound that names the defendant in civil proceedings under modern Japanese procedural-code usage. The structural-typological distinction between 被告 (civil) and 被告人 (criminal) within the modern Japanese procedural codes is doctrinally consequential: the criminally-accused 被告人 carries a substantial constitutional-rights apparatus articulated in Articles 31–40 of the 1947 Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Code (rights against self-incrimination, to counsel, to silence, to a speedy and public trial, against double jeopardy), while the civilly-sued 被告 operates within the procedural framework of the Civil Procedure Code with a different doctrinal apparatus calibrated to private-law dispute resolution. Reading 被告 as if it were equivalent to 被告人 collapses the typological distinction between civil and criminal passive-receiving party-positions that the modern Japanese procedural vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

被疑者 (higisha) names the criminal suspect — the party under investigation by police or prosecutors prior to the formal lodging of charges — while 被告人 (hikokunin) names the formally-indicted criminal defendant after charges have been filed. The structural-procedural distinction marks the formal-procedural transition from pre-charge investigation to post-indictment litigation: a 被疑者 becomes a 被告人 upon prosecutorial indictment (起訴), with the procedural-rights apparatus shifting accordingly. The 被疑者 carries pre-trial procedural rights articulated under the Criminal Procedure Code and the broader investigation-stage doctrinal apparatus, while the 被告人 carries the trial-stage procedural-rights apparatus. Reading 被告 (the civil-procedure defendant) as if it were equivalent to 被疑者 (the criminal-investigation suspect) collapses both the civil-criminal distinction and the pre-charge / post-charge procedural-stage distinction that the modern Japanese vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

conceptual_remainder: 原告 is one of the structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern East Asian procedural-legal vocabulary, calibrating the Western procedural category of the plaintiff through the structural pairing of 原 (the originating-active prefix) and 告 (the formal-charge register). The Meiji recruitment of the prefix-pair 原 / 被 across the procedural-vocabulary cluster — 原告 / 被告, with the broader 原 used for originating-active-source and 被 for passive-receiving-recipient — articulates a structural-procedural symmetry that the asymmetric English plaintiff / defendant pair (derived from heterogeneous etymological roots — plaintiff from Old French plaintif via Latin plangere, defendant from Latin defendere) does not foreground. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 原 + 告 articulates is the originating-active side of the litigation: the party from whom the formal complaint originates, who bears the structural burden of articulating the grounds and evidence of the claim, and who corresponds in the criminal-procedural context to the prosecutorial function (検察官, kensatsukan — the public prosecutor that displaces the private-prosecution function in modern continental criminal procedure). The structural-procedural symmetry of the 原告 / 被告 pair preserves in the Sino-Japanese compounds a doctrinal precision: each side of the litigation is articulated through 告 (the formal charge) calibrated by the active-passive prefix-pair, with the procedural opposition rendered as a single structural-conceptual relation rather than two etymologically-unrelated terms. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of the originating-charging party-position. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Roman-law actio doctrine — the substantive-procedural articulation by which the plaintiff's claim is grounded in a recognized legal category of action (the actiones of the Roman classical period: actio in rem, actio in personam, actio bonae fidei, etc.) — that the medieval and early-modern continental civil-procedure tradition systematized into the modern doctrine of subjective rights and corresponding causes of action. The Meiji-and-Taishō Japanese civil-procedure tradition imported the modern continental civil-procedure doctrinal apparatus through the Boissonade and German-influenced civil-procedure codes, but the systematic actio-doctrine and the broader Roman-canonical procedural tradition entered modern Japanese legal vocabulary through the legal-translation apparatus rather than carried in the compound 原告 itself, with the broader cluster of procedural-doctrinal compounds 訴訟 (soshō, litigation), 訴因 (soin, cause of action — particularly in criminal procedure), 請求 (seikyū, claim) articulating the systematic doctrinal apparatus.
doctrinal_weight: 原告 sits at the operational core of the modern Japanese civil-procedural vocabulary, anchoring the structural-procedural opposition with 被告 that articulates the operation of the modern Japanese civil litigation system. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji procedural-code drafting process — from Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1870s translations of the French Code de procédure civile through the Boissonade-influenced civil-procedure code of 1890 to the current Civil Procedure Code (民事訴訟法) of 1996 — supplied the operating institutional vocabulary, with the procedural-party typology 原告 / 被告 articulating the structural-procedural opposition that anchors modern Japanese civil litigation. The compound is productive across modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 共同原告 (kyōdō genkoku, joint plaintiffs), 原告適格 (genkoku tekikaku, plaintiff standing — the structural-procedural requirement that the plaintiff have a legally-cognizable interest in the matter), 原告側 (genkoku-gawa, the plaintiff's side), 反訴原告 (hanso genkoku, counter-plaintiff — the original defendant who files a counter-claim against the original plaintiff). The compound has been adopted into Chinese (yuángào), Korean (원고 wŏn'go), and Vietnamese (nguyên cáo) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of the civil plaintiff. The structural-calibration of the 原 + 告 pattern, paired against 被 + 告 in the procedural opposition, supplied the productive paradigm for the modern Japanese procedural-party vocabulary, with the broader cluster 申立人 (mōshitatenin, petitioner — used in non-contentious and certain administrative procedures), 控訴人 (kōsonin, appellant in intermediate appellate courts), 上告人 (jōkokunin, appellant in supreme-court appeals) articulating the broader institutional vocabulary of party-positions across the modern Japanese legal-procedural apparatus.

false_friends.divergence: Modern Chinese deploys 原告人 (yuángàorén) in some procedural contexts as an alternative to bare 原告 (yuángào), but the modern Japanese standard procedural-code usage articulates the civil plaintiff as 原告 without the suffix -人, distinguishing the Japanese usage from the Chinese pattern. The asymmetry between 原告 (no suffix in the Japanese civil-procedural standard) and 被告 / 被告人 (with the modern Japanese distinction between 被告 in civil contexts and 被告人 in criminal contexts) reflects a structural feature of the modern Japanese procedural-code typology: the criminal-procedural defendant is 被告人 (carrying the constitutional-rights apparatus of Articles 31–40 of the 1947 Constitution and the 1948 Criminal Procedure Code) while the civil-procedural defendant is 被告; but the criminal-procedural prosecution function is articulated through 検察官 (kensatsukan, public prosecutor) rather than through any 原告-derived term, since the modern continental-civil-law tradition that the Japanese procedural codes inherit articulates criminal prosecution as a public-state function rather than a private-plaintiff function.

申立人 (mōshitatenin) names the petitioner in non-contentious procedural contexts — applications for administrative orders, petitions in family-court proceedings, applications for injunctions and provisional remedies, and broader non-adversarial procedural forms — distinguished from 原告 (genkoku) which names specifically the plaintiff in contentious civil litigation. The structural-procedural distinction reflects the modern continental-civil-procedure typological distinction between adversarial litigation (the plaintiff-defendant opposition that the 原告 / 被告 pair articulates) and non-contentious procedure (the petition-application form that the 申立人 articulates), with different procedural-rights apparatus calibrated to each. Reading 原告 as if it were equivalent to 申立人 collapses the contentious / non-contentious procedural-typological distinction that the modern Japanese procedural vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.
