conceptual_remainder: 刑法 is one of the structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern East Asian legal vocabulary, calibrating the Western category of criminal law through the structural pairing of 刑 (the penal sanction) and 法 (the systematic statutory framework). The classical East Asian criminal-law vocabulary articulated the structure of criminal-law-and-administration through different categories: the imperial-Chinese 律令 (lǜlìng, statutes-and-ordinances) tradition, with the foundational Tang Code (唐律, c. 624) supplying the systematic articulation that subsequent East Asian codes inherited (the Japanese Yōrō Code 養老律令 of 718, the Korean Goryeoryul, the Vietnamese Hồng Đức Code), articulating the imperial-penal apparatus through the typology 律 (lǜ, penal statute) / 令 (lìng, administrative ordinance) / 格 (gé, supplementary edict) / 式 (shì, regulation), with the broader vocabulary 刑罰 (xíngfá, criminal sanction), 五刑 (wǔxíng, the Five Punishments), 罪刑 (zàixíng, crime-and-punishment) supplying the operating institutional vocabulary. The Tokugawa-period Japanese penal apparatus continued the broader East Asian classical-penal tradition through the bakufu's 公事方御定書 (Kujikata Osadamegaki, 1742) and the broader han-administrative legal apparatus. The Meiji compound 刑法 was developed as the operating term for the specifically modern Western category of criminal law — the rule-of-law-grounded systematic articulation of the offense-and-punishment relation organized around the principle of nulla poena sine lege — which represents a substantial doctrinal recalibration from the classical-imperial penal tradition. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 刑 + 法 articulates is the dual structure of the criminal-law domain: the sanction-side (刑), in which the state administers determinate penal punishment in response to the criminal occurrence, and the systematic-statutory side (法), in which the determinate penal punishment is articulated through and constrained by the prior-legislated statutory framework. The Sino-Japanese compound thus preserves the doctrinal distinction between the punitive-sanction function and the systematic-codified framework that the modern Western criminal-law tradition articulates through the Beccarian-Feuerbachian apparatus of nulla poena sine lege and the broader rule-of-law constraints on criminal-state authority. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of state-penal-sanction-within-systematic-framework. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Beccarian-Enlightenment register of criminal law as a measured-and-proportionate utilitarian apparatus calibrated toward social-protective ends, the Enlightenment-doctrinal apparatus of utilitarian penology that grounded the eighteenth-century criminal-law reform tradition; nor can they easily carry the systematic-doctrinal apparatus of the modern German Strafrechtswissenschaft (criminal-law science) — the Tatbestand-Rechtswidrigkeit-Schuld three-element structure of criminal liability developed by Karl Binding, Ernst von Beling, Franz von Liszt, Edmund Mezger, and Hans Welzel that supplied the principal doctrinal vocabulary of twentieth-century continental criminal law and that the modern Japanese criminal-law tradition substantially inherits. The doctrinal apparatus was imported through the legal-translation apparatus rather than carried in the compound 刑法 itself, with the broader cluster of compounds 構成要件 (kōsei yōken, statutory-definitional element / Tatbestand), 違法性 (ihōsei, unlawfulness / Rechtswidrigkeit), 責任 (sekinin, culpability / Schuld), 罪刑法定主義 (zaikei hōteishugi, nulla poena sine lege) articulating the systematic-doctrinal apparatus.
doctrinal_weight: 刑法 sits at the operational core of the modern Japanese criminal-law vocabulary, anchoring the broader cluster of criminal-substantive and criminal-procedural terms that articulate the operation of the modern Japanese criminal-justice system. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji criminal-law codification process — from Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1870s translations of the French Code Pénal through the Boissonade Penal Code of 1880 (旧刑法, the French-influenced foundational modern Japanese penal code) to the current Penal Code of 1907 (現行刑法, drafted under German and Italian influence) — supplied the operating institutional-doctrinal vocabulary, with the systematic doctrinal apparatus of modern continental criminal law (the Tatbestand-Rechtswidrigkeit-Schuld three-element structure of criminal liability) entering modern Japanese legal vocabulary through the broader cluster of compounds 構成要件, 違法性, 責任. The compound is productive across modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 刑法総論 (keihō sōron, general part of criminal law / Allgemeiner Teil), 刑法各論 (keihō kakuron, special part of criminal law / Besonderer Teil), 刑法学 (keihōgaku, criminal-law science / Strafrechtswissenschaft), 国際刑法 (kokusai keihō, international criminal law), 軍刑法 (gun keihō, military criminal law). The structural pairing 刑 + 法 supplied the productive paradigm for related compounds across the modern Japanese criminal-law landscape: 民法 (minpō, civil law — the structurally-paired private-law counterpart), 商法 (shōhō, commercial law), 行政法 (gyōseihō, administrative law), 憲法 (kenpō, constitutional law) — articulating the systematic-typological framework of modern Japanese legal disciplines through the productive 法-suffix pattern. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (xíngfǎ), Korean (형법 hyŏngpŏp), and Vietnamese (hình pháp) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of criminal law.

false_friends.divergence: 刑事 (keiji) names the broader procedural-and-substantive category of 'criminal matter' or 'criminal affair' — distinguished from 民事 (minji, civil matter) — and is used in modern Japanese as both a substantive adjective (刑事事件, keiji jiken, criminal case; 刑事裁判, keiji saiban, criminal trial; 刑事責任, keiji sekinin, criminal responsibility) and as a colloquial term for a criminal-investigation police officer (the plainclothes detective). 刑法 (keihō) names specifically the systematic substantive criminal law — the codified articulation of offenses and sanctions in the Penal Code — while 刑事 names the broader procedural-and-substantive category of criminal-justice matters. The structural-typological distinction is doctrinally consequential: 刑法 articulates substantive criminal law, while criminal procedure is articulated through 刑事訴訟法 (keiji soshōhō, the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1948), with the substantive / procedural distinction marking the Meiji-inherited continental civil-law typological articulation. Reading 刑法 as if it encompassed both the substantive and procedural articulations collapses the typological distinction that the modern Japanese legal vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

罪刑法定主義 (zaikei hōteishugi) names the foundational doctrinal principle of modern continental criminal law: nulla poena sine lege (no penalty without prior law) — the principle that criminal sanctions may be imposed only on the basis of prior-legislated statutory provision and that retroactive criminalization is forbidden. The compound articulates the principle as a 主義 (-ism / doctrine) and is institutionalized through Article 31 of the post-war 1947 Constitution and the broader doctrinal apparatus of modern Japanese criminal-law science. 刑法 (keihō) names the codified substantive criminal law, while 罪刑法定主義 names the foundational rule-of-law principle that constrains the operation of the criminal law within the modern continental criminal-law tradition. Reading 刑法 as carrying the doctrinal articulation of 罪刑法定主義 confuses the codified substantive law with the foundational doctrinal principle that constrains it: the principle is foundational to the operation of modern criminal law but is articulated through a separate doctrinal compound, with the broader cluster of compounds 法律不遡及 (hōritsu fusokyū, non-retroactivity of law), 類推解釈の禁止 (ruisui kaishaku no kinshi, prohibition of analogical interpretation), 明確性の原則 (meikakusei no gensoku, principle of legal certainty / Bestimmtheitsgebot) articulating the broader doctrinal apparatus.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, with Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French Code civil across 1870–1874 as the principal stabilization-vehicle; institutionalized through the abortive Boissonade Civil Code (旧民法, drafted by Gustave Boissonade with Japanese collaborators, promulgated 1890 but postponed and never enforced as the result of the Civil Code Postponement Controversy 民法典論争 of 1889–1892) as the first projected modern Japanese civil code on the French Code civil model; substantially recalibrated through the current Civil Code (現行民法, 1898), drafted by Hozumi Nobushige (穂積陳重), Tomii Masaaki (富井政章), and Ume Kenjirō (梅謙次郎) under the principal influence of the first draft of the German BGB, with the Pandectist five-book structural articulation (general part, real rights, claims, family, inheritance) supplying the foundational doctrinal framework

conceptual_remainder: 民法 is one of the structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern East Asian legal vocabulary, calibrating the Western category of civil law through the structural pairing of 民 (the people / private parties / civil-as-distinguished-from-public) and 法 (the systematic statutory framework). The classical East Asian legal vocabulary did not articulate a structural distinction between civil law and criminal law parallel to the modern continental civil-law / criminal-law typological distinction: the imperial-Chinese 律令 (lǜlìng) tradition organized statutory provision around the typology 律 (penal statute) / 令 (administrative ordinance) / 格 (supplementary edict) / 式 (regulation) rather than around the substantive private-law / public-law / criminal-law typology. The classical East Asian regulation of private legal relations operated through a heterogeneous cluster of mechanisms: penal-statute provisions for property and family disputes that today would be civil matters, customary local rules administered through village headmen and lineage-elders, ritual-prescriptive provisions in the Confucian classical tradition, and administrative-bureaucratic regulation through the imperial-magistracy apparatus. The Tokugawa-period Japanese regulation of private legal relations operated through similar mechanisms — the bakufu and han administrative-legal apparatus, customary village and town regulations, the 公事方御定書 (Kujikata Osadamegaki, 1742) as the principal bakufu-level criminal-and-administrative compilation — without a structural-typological distinction between civil law and criminal law as systematic doctrinal domains. The Meiji compound 民法 was developed as the operating term for the specifically modern Western category of civil law — the systematically-codified domain of private legal relations organized around the structural-typological distinction from public law — which represents a substantial doctrinal recalibration from the classical-imperial legal tradition. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 民 + 法 articulates is the dual structure of the civil-law domain: the private-civil-side (民), in which the civil law operates between private parties as the systematic articulation of their legal relations, and the systematic-statutory side (法), in which the private-civil legal relations are articulated through the codified statutory framework. The Sino-Japanese compound thus preserves the doctrinal distinction between the private-law domain and the systematic-codified framework that the modern continental civil-law tradition articulates through the Pandectist-doctrinal apparatus of subjective rights (subjektive Rechte), juristic acts (Rechtsgeschäfte), and the systematic-conceptual apparatus of the General Part. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of private-civil-legal-relations-within-systematic-framework. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically Roman-law ius civile background — the foundational distinction between ius civile (the law applicable to Roman citizens) and ius gentium (the law of nations applicable to all peoples) that grounds the medieval Roman-law revival's articulation of the civil-law tradition; nor can they easily carry the systematic-doctrinal apparatus of the modern German Pandectist-civil-law science — the Willenstheorie (will theory) of juristic acts, the doctrine of the declaration of will (Willenserklärung), the systematic-conceptual articulation of subjective rights, the broader doctrinal apparatus of Friedrich Carl von Savigny, Bernhard Windscheid, and the nineteenth-century German civil-law science that supplied the principal doctrinal vocabulary of the modern Japanese Civil Code. The doctrinal apparatus was imported through the legal-translation apparatus rather than carried in the compound 民法 itself, with the broader cluster of compounds 法律行為 (hōritsu kōi, juristic act / Rechtsgeschäft), 意思表示 (ishi hyōji, declaration of will / Willenserklärung), 権利能力 (kenri nōryoku, legal capacity / Rechtsfähigkeit), 行為能力 (kōi nōryoku, capacity to act / Geschäftsfähigkeit) articulating the systematic-doctrinal apparatus.
doctrinal_weight: 民法 sits at the operational core of the modern Japanese civil-law vocabulary, anchoring the broader cluster of civil-law-doctrinal terms that articulate the operation of the modern Japanese civil-law system. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji civil-law codification process — from Mitsukuri Rinshō's 1870s translations of the French Code civil through the abortive Boissonade Civil Code of 1890 (旧民法) to the current Civil Code of 1898 (現行民法) — supplied the operating institutional-doctrinal vocabulary, with the substantial post-war revision of the family-and-inheritance provisions (1947 revision of Books IV and V under the influence of the post-war Constitution's gender-equality provisions) and the 2017 reform of the law of obligations (the most extensive revision of the law of obligations since the original 1898 enactment) restructuring the modern Japanese civil-law apparatus while preserving the foundational Pandectist-doctrinal framework. The Civil Code Postponement Controversy (民法典論争) of 1889–1892 between the advocates of the Boissonade Civil Code (the so-called 断行派, dankōha, 'enforcement faction,' principally led by Ume Kenjirō) and its opponents (the so-called 延期派, enkiha, 'postponement faction,' principally led by Hozumi Yatsuka 穂積八束 with the famous polemic 民法出デテ忠孝亡ブ, 'the Civil Code emerges and filial piety perishes,' arguing that the Boissonade Code's individualistic articulation of family law would destroy the traditional Japanese ie family system) supplied the foundational doctrinal-political controversy that shaped the development of the 1898 Civil Code. The compound is productive across modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 民法総則 (minpō sōsoku, general provisions of the Civil Code / Allgemeiner Teil), 民法学 (minpōgaku, civil-law science / Zivilrechtswissenschaft), 民法典 (minpōten, civil code), 国際私法 (kokusai shihō, private international law / international civil law). The structural pairing 民 + 法 supplied the productive paradigm for related compounds across the modern Japanese legal landscape: 刑法 (keihō, criminal law — the structurally-paired public-law counterpart), 商法 (shōhō, commercial law), 民事訴訟法 (minji soshōhō, code of civil procedure), 民事 (minji, civil matter — the broader procedural-substantive category) — articulating the systematic-typological framework of modern Japanese legal disciplines. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (mínfǎ), Korean (민법 minpŏp), and Vietnamese (dân luật) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of civil law, with the modern People's Republic of China promulgating its own Civil Code (民法典, Mínfǎdiǎn) in 2020 as the most recent major civil-code codification in the East Asian civil-law tradition.

false_friends.divergence: 民事 (minji) names the broader procedural-and-substantive category of 'civil matter' or 'civil affair' — distinguished from 刑事 (keiji, criminal matter) — and is used in modern Japanese as a substantive adjective (民事事件, minji jiken, civil case; 民事裁判, minji saiban, civil trial; 民事訴訟, minji soshō, civil litigation; 民事責任, minji sekinin, civil responsibility / civil liability). 民法 (minpō) names specifically the systematic substantive civil law — the codified articulation of private-civil legal relations in the Civil Code — while 民事 names the broader procedural-and-substantive category of civil-justice matters. The structural-typological distinction is doctrinally consequential: 民法 articulates substantive civil law, while civil procedure is articulated through 民事訴訟法 (minji soshōhō, the Code of Civil Procedure of 1996), with the substantive / procedural distinction marking the Meiji-inherited continental civil-law typological articulation. Reading 民法 as if it encompassed both the substantive and procedural articulations collapses the typological distinction that the modern Japanese legal vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

民主 (minshu / mínzhǔ) names the modern political concept of democracy — the political-constitutional doctrine of popular sovereignty articulated through the inversion of the classical compound's literal sense ('the people's lord') into the Meiji-coined translation of Western democracy. 民法 (minpō) deploys 民 in an entirely different register: as the private-civil prefix that names the civil-law domain as distinguished from the public-law domain. The structural-typological distinction is doctrinally consequential: 民 in 民主 names the political-collective people as the source of sovereign authority, while 民 in 民法 names the private-civil party-position as distinguished from the public-state party-position. The two registers of 民 — political-collective and private-civil — operate in different doctrinal fields without structural confusion in modern Japanese legal-political vocabulary, but reading 民法 as carrying the political-democratic register of 民 (as if 民法 meant 'democratic law' or 'people's law' in a populist sense) collapses the typological distinction between the political-collective register and the private-civil register that the modern Japanese vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

coinage_notes: Wasei-kango compound stabilized through the early-Meiji institutional-administrative apparatus, particularly through Kawaji Toshiyoshi's (川路利良, 1834–1879) 1872–1873 European mission — undertaken at the direction of the Iwakura Embassy and focused principally on the French Préfecture de Police of Paris with secondary attention to the Prussian and Belgian systems — and his subsequent reports establishing the foundational vocabulary; institutionalized through the 1874 establishment of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Bureau (警視庁, Keishichō) under Kawaji's leadership, the 1875 nationwide reorganization of the Japanese police system through the Administrative Police Regulations (行政警察規則), and Kawaji's 警察手眼 (Keisatsu Shugen, 'Essence of Police Work,' 1879) as the foundational doctrinal-pedagogical text

investigation, discernment, inspection — here in its institutional-suffix register, naming the structural function of investigative inquiry into public-order violations and discerning observation of social conditions; the investigation-side of the institutional articulation, structurally paired with 警 to articulate the dual function of the modern state police institution

renderings used in contexts foregrounding the continental European institutional register; 警察 is structurally calibrated principally against the French police of the Préfecture de Police model that Kawaji studied during his 1872–1873 European mission, with the German Polizei tradition supplying secondary doctrinal-conceptual influence and the broader continental Polizeiwissenschaft tradition supplying the foundational administrative-doctrinal background

conceptual_remainder: 警察 is one of the structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern East Asian institutional vocabulary, calibrating the Western institutional category of the modern police force through the structural pairing of 警 (vigilance / warning / preventive watchfulness) and 察 (investigation / discernment / inspection). The classical East Asian institutional vocabulary did not articulate a structural-institutional category parallel to the modern Western police institution: the imperial-Chinese order-maintenance and criminal-investigation apparatus operated through a heterogeneous cluster of institutions — the magistracy (the local-administrative-judicial unit headed by the prefectural magistrate, who combined administrative, judicial, and police functions in a single office), the 衙役 (yáyì, magistracy-runners, the magistrate's enforcement subordinates), the 保甲 (bǎojiǎ, mutual-responsibility neighborhood-association system that conscripted local communities into self-policing), the 巡捕 (xúnbǔ, patrol-and-arrest officers in particular contexts) — without a structural-institutional category corresponding to the modern unified police force. The Tokugawa-period Japanese order-maintenance apparatus operated through similar mechanisms — the bakufu and han administrative-legal apparatus through 町奉行 (machi-bugyō, town magistracy) with subordinate 与力 (yoriki, mounted enforcement officers) and 同心 (dōshin, foot-enforcement officers), the 五人組 (gonin-gumi, five-household mutual-responsibility groups) parallel to the Chinese 保甲, the 目明し (meakashi, informer-investigators) — without a structural-institutional category corresponding to the modern unified professional police force. The Meiji compound 警察 was developed as the operating term for the specifically modern Western institutional category of the police force — the centralized, professional, uniformed civilian institution with structured ranks and operational divisions, charged with criminal-law enforcement and public-order maintenance — which represents a substantial institutional recalibration from the classical East Asian order-maintenance apparatus. The compound's structural calibration is doctrinally consequential. What 警 + 察 articulates is the dual structural function of the modern police institution: the preventive-vigilant function (警), in which the police institution exercises continuous watchfulness over public order through patrol, surveillance, and the broader presence-of-authority register; and the investigative-discerning function (察), in which the police institution conducts criminal investigation, evidence-gathering, and the broader investigative-procedural register that supports the prosecutorial function. The Sino-Japanese compound thus preserves the doctrinal distinction between the preventive-vigilance function and the investigative-discernment function that the modern police institution carries. What the Japanese characters carry is the basic register of vigilant-investigative state-institutional function. What they cannot easily carry is the specifically continental Polizeiwissenschaft (police science) tradition of the seventeenth-and-eighteenth-century German cameralist administrative thought (Justi, Sonnenfels) — the broader continental-administrative function of state-welfare regulation that the early-modern continental Polizei encompassed, well beyond what the modern Anglophone term 'police' connotes; nor can they easily carry the specifically Anglo-American Peelian-tradition articulation of policing-by-consent — Sir Robert Peel's 1829 Metropolitan Police Act and the Peelian Principles articulating the police as 'citizens in uniform' bound to public consent and minimal-force restraint, the Anglophone-democratic articulation of the police-public relation that descends from the Peelian tradition. The Meiji-Japanese police institution was modeled principally on the French Préfecture de Police rather than the British Peelian model, with the centralized-state and administrative-regulatory register of French and continental policing supplying the foundational institutional articulation rather than the consent-based and minimal-force articulation of the Peelian tradition.
doctrinal_weight: 警察 sits at the operational core of the modern Japanese institutional vocabulary, anchoring the broader cluster of policing-and-security terms that articulate the operation of the modern Japanese state-administrative apparatus. The compound's institutional life is foundational across modern East Asia. The Meiji police-institutional formation process — from Kawaji Toshiyoshi's 1872–1873 European mission and 1874 establishment of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Bureau through the 1875 Administrative Police Regulations and the broader Meiji institutional-administrative apparatus to the post-war 1947 Police Act (旧警察法) and the 1954 Police Act (現行警察法) — supplied the operating institutional vocabulary. The post-war 1947 Police Act, drafted under American Occupation influence, articulated a decentralized-municipal-police model on the American pattern, with the 1954 Police Act recalibrating the institutional structure toward a centralized-prefectural model that combines the National Police Agency (警察庁, Keisatsuchō) at the national level with the prefectural police (都道府県警察, todōfuken keisatsu) as the operational units, preserving the centralized-administrative tendency of the original Meiji French-Préfecture-model articulation while incorporating substantial post-war democratic-accountability elements (the Public Safety Commissions, 公安委員会, kōan iinkai, that exercise civilian oversight of the police at both national and prefectural levels). The compound is productive across modern East Asian institutional vocabulary: 警察官 (keisatsukan, police officer), 警察署 (keisatsusho, police station), 警察庁 (Keisatsuchō, National Police Agency), 警視庁 (Keishichō, Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department), 警察学校 (keisatsu gakkō, police academy), 警察犬 (keisatsuken, police dog), 警察手帳 (keisatsu techō, police identification card), 国家警察 (kokka keisatsu, national police), 自治体警察 (jichitai keisatsu, municipal police). The structural-calibration of the 警 + 察 pattern supplied the productive paradigm for related institutional compounds across the modern Japanese administrative landscape: 検察 (kensatsu, prosecution / public prosecutor's office), 監察 (kansatsu, supervision / oversight), 視察 (shisatsu, official inspection), 査察 (sasatsu, inspection / audit) — articulating the broader institutional vocabulary of investigative-administrative state functions. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (jǐngchá), Korean (경찰 kyŏngch'al), and Vietnamese (cảnh sát) as the universal modern East Asian institutional rendering of police, with the distinctive Japanese institutional articulation of 派出所 / 交番 (hashutsujo / kōban, neighborhood police box) — the small local police station that locates police presence within local communities as a structural feature of Japanese policing — having been exported to several Asian jurisdictions (notably Singapore and the modern Brazilian municipal-police reorganization) as a model of community-based policing.

false_friends.divergence: 検察 (kensatsu) names the prosecutorial function — the institution of public prosecutors (検察官, kensatsukan) charged with reviewing police investigations, deciding whether to file criminal charges, prosecuting cases at trial, and supervising the execution of criminal sentences. The structural-institutional distinction between 警察 (the police institution charged with criminal investigation and public-order maintenance) and 検察 (the prosecutorial institution charged with prosecution) is doctrinally consequential: in the modern Japanese criminal-procedural articulation, the police conduct the initial investigation and the prosecutors review the investigation file (送検 sōken, 'transfer to prosecution') and decide whether to indict the suspect. The post-war Code of Criminal Procedure (1948) institutionalized substantial doctrinal-procedural separation between the police and prosecution functions, with the prosecutorial institution exercising substantive oversight of the police-investigative function while the police retain operational autonomy in the investigation-stage. The structural-institutional distinction marks the modern Japanese articulation of the criminal-justice apparatus, distinguished from the American articulation in which prosecutors are typically more closely integrated with police-investigative work. Reading 警察 as encompassing the prosecutorial function collapses the structural-institutional distinction that the modern Japanese vocabulary is calibrated to articulate.

公安 (kōan / gōng'ān) carries divergent institutional registers across the modern East Asian landscape: in modern Japanese, 公安 names public security in the broader register and specifically the Public Security Intelligence Agency (公安調査庁, Kōan Chōsachō) and the public-security police division (警察庁警備局公安課, the Public Security Bureau within the National Police Agency) charged with counter-intelligence, counter-subversion, and the broader political-security register, distinguished from the general 警察 institution charged with ordinary criminal-law enforcement; in modern Chinese, 公安 (gōng'ān) names the entire police institution (公安部, Gōng'ānbù, the Ministry of Public Security; 公安局, Gōng'ānjú, public security bureau at provincial and municipal levels) — the Chinese equivalent of the Japanese 警察 institution — reflecting the People's Republic of China's institutional articulation that locates the entire police function within the broader 'public security' (公安) administrative category. The structural-institutional asymmetry between Japanese 警察 (general police) / 公安 (political security) and Chinese 公安 (general police) reflects the divergent post-war institutional trajectories: Japan's post-war American-influenced reorganization preserved the Meiji 警察 institution as the operating general-police category, while the People's Republic's institutional articulation organized the police function under the 公安 category through the post-1949 Soviet-influenced reorganization. Reading the Japanese 警察 as if it were equivalent to the Chinese 公安 collapses the institutional asymmetry between the two East Asian articulations.

when the transcendental register of Subjekt is foregrounded; modern Japanese distinguishes 主観 (the perspectival-cognitive subject) from 主体 (shutai, the agentive subject), with the two compounds dividing what the German Subjekt holds together

conceptual_remainder: 主観 reads the Kantian Subjekt as a perspective — a 主 (master / host position) from which a 観 (view) is taken. The compound carries the indexed-relational structure of cognition cleanly but flattens the strictly transcendental register: Kant's Subjekt as the unity of apperception that is the formal condition of any objective synthesis tends in 主観 to read as the empirical viewpoint of a private knower. Modern Japanese philosophical writing compensates with the parallel coinage 主体 (shutai, 主 + 体), which carries the agentive-substantival register that 主観 cannot — the subject of action, the ethical subject, the political subject — leaving 主観 restricted to the cognitive-perspectival register.
doctrinal_weight: Half of the foundational 主観 / 客観 pair that supplies the operating East Asian articulation of the Kantian subject-object distinction. Institutionalized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the post-1880s Japanese university philosophy curriculum under Inoue Tetsujirō and his successors; adopted into Chinese (zhǔguān) and Korean (주관) as the universal modern East Asian rendering. Sets the conceptual template within which all subsequent translation of Kantian, post-Kantian, and phenomenological epistemology into East Asian languages has operated.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical coinage paired structurally with 主観; stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881) as the operating Japanese rendering of the German Objekt within the Kantian Subjekt-Objekt structure

components.meaning: guest, visitor, the one who arrives from elsewhere — here in its dialectical register, naming the side of the cognitive relation that stands over against the knower; the guest-position in the host-and-guest pair 主客
view, perspective — here the same perspectival suffix as in 主観, articulating the cognitive relation as a relation of viewing with the side specified by the prefix

translation_range.emphasis: standard Anglophone rendering across both adjectival and substantival uses

when the transcendental register of Objekt is foregrounded; modern Japanese distinguishes 客観 (the perspectival-cognitive object) from 客体 (kyakutai, the substantival object as counterpart to 主体), paralleling the 主観 / 主体 distinction

conceptual_remainder: 客観 articulates the Objekt as the side of the cognitive relation from which the view is not taken — the externality that stands over against the knower. The classical pairing 主 / 客 (host / guest) supplied the dialectical template ready-to-hand: the host-and-guest distinction was already operational across Sino-Japanese vocabulary, most notably in Linji's four host-and-guest dialectics (四主客). What the compound carries cleanly: the relational structure of the subject-object distinction, the indexed externality of the object to the knower. What it cannot easily carry is the specifically Kantian register of the Objekt as constituted-by-categorial-synthesis — the object as that which is given as objective only through the synthesis of the manifold under the unity of apperception. The Sino-Japanese 客 reads naturally as a relational counterpart rather than as a constituted determination, and the Hegelian register in which Subjekt and Objekt are dialectically reconciled in the absolute movement of Spirit requires further philosophical labor to articulate within the 主観 / 客観 frame.
doctrinal_weight: The other half of the foundational 主観 / 客観 pair stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881). The compound's reuse of the classical 主 / 客 host-and-guest dialectic — already operational in Linji Chan's four host-and-guest dialectics — is structurally elegant: the dialectical pairing was already built into Sino-Japanese vocabulary and merely needed to be transferred from its classical relational register to the Kantian transcendental register. Adopted into Chinese (kèguān) and Korean (객관) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of objectivity, with the broader cluster 客観性 (kyakkansei, objectivity), 客観的 (kyakkanteki, objective), 客体 (kyakutai, the substantival object) supplying the productive paradigm across modern East Asian academic vocabulary.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical coinage stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881) as the operating Japanese rendering of the German Begriff and English 'concept'

components.meaning: the leveling stroke that sweeps the top of a heaped measure — here in its abstracting register, naming the act of taking the general view across particulars (大概, 概要, 概略); the abstraction-side of the compound

thought, mental act, attention — here in its cognitive register, naming the act of holding-in-mind; recruited from its Buddhist contemplative register (念仏, 正念) into the modern philosophical register of mental content

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering across Anglophone philosophical contexts

when the dialectical-speculative register of Hegel's Wissenschaft der Logik is foregrounded — the self-determining unity of universal, particular, and individual that constitutes the structure of dialectical movement
in introductory or popular contexts where the technical philosophical register is not at stake

conceptual_remainder: 概念 articulates the concept as the active mental act of generalization-across-particulars — 概 (the leveling sweep) operating on a multiplicity through 念 (the directed mental act). What this carries cleanly: the German Begriff's emphasis on the active grasping (be-greifen, to grasp) that subsumes a multiplicity under a unity. What the compound distinguishes from is sharper than the English 'concept' tends to mark: 概念 is structurally distinguished within Meiji philosophical vocabulary from 観念 (kannen, idea / Vorstellung — representation in the broader register, with the contemplative resonance of 観) and from 理念 (rinen, ideal / Idee — the regulative ideal in the Kantian sense or the Hegelian absolute Idea). The three compounds 概念 / 観念 / 理念 partition the conceptual territory that English 'idea' and 'concept' tend to merge.
doctrinal_weight: One of the structurally load-bearing terms of Meiji philosophical vocabulary, supplying the operating East Asian rendering of the German Begriff across Kantian, Hegelian, and broader philosophical translation. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (gàiniàn) and Korean (개념) as the universal modern East Asian term for concept, with derivative compounds — 概念化 (gainenka, conceptualization), 概念的 (gainenteki, conceptual), 抽象概念 (chūshō gainen, abstract concept), 基本概念 (kihon gainen, basic concept) — operative across modern East Asian academic vocabulary in philosophy, logic, mathematics, the sciences, and the humanities.

coinage_notes: Re-coinage of a classical Sino-Japanese compound (理 + 性, already paired across Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian metaphysics) recruited in Meiji philosophical translation to render the Kantian Vernunft and the broader Western category of reason; stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881)

components.meaning: principle, rational order, the underlying pattern — here in its philosophical register, naming the universal ordering principle that the rational faculty grasps; load-bearing across Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian metaphysics in the doctrine of 理 as the foundational principle paired with 気 (qi)

nature, the constitutive what-it-is-to-be — here naming the human nature considered as the seat of the rational faculty; the same 性 that operates in 仏性 (Buddha-nature), 自性 (self-nature), 法性 (dharma-nature)

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering across Anglophone philosophical contexts

when the strict Kantian distinction Vernunft / Verstand is foregrounded — Vernunft as the higher faculty of ideas that seeks the unconditioned, distinguished from Verstand (悟性 gosei, the faculty of concepts that constitutes objective experience). The 理性 / 悟性 pair was stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii to articulate the Kantian distinction in Japanese
literal decomposition foregrounding the compound's Neo-Confucian inheritance — reason understood as the principle-nature that constitutes the rational dimension of human being

conceptual_remainder: 理性 carries a doctrinal density that the Western 'reason' does not naturally invoke. Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian metaphysics — particularly the Cheng-Zhu school's articulation of 理 (the foundational principle of all things) paired with 気 (qi, the materializing energy through which 理 is realized) and the doctrine of 性即理 (xìng jí lǐ, 'nature is principle,' the Cheng-Zhu identification of human nature with the universal principle) — supplied the classical compound 理性 with a substantive metaphysical-ethical register that the Meiji repurposing carries forward into modern Japanese philosophical vocabulary. What 理性 thus brings into the rendering of Vernunft that 'reason' does not: the connotation of rationality as participation in a cosmic ordering principle, the Confucian-metaphysical resonance of the rational faculty as the seat of the human's relation to universal principle. What it cannot easily carry is the specifically critical-Kantian register of Vernunft as the faculty whose pretensions to grasp the unconditioned generate the transcendental illusions that Kant's first Critique is designed to diagnose. The Cheng-Zhu inheritance reads 理性 as straightforwardly continuous with universal principle, while the Kantian register reads Vernunft as the faculty whose drive toward the unconditioned must be critically restrained.
doctrinal_weight: One of the foundational terms of the Meiji rendering of Kantian and post-Kantian philosophy, supplying the operating East Asian articulation of the Vernunft / Verstand distinction (paired with 悟性, gosei, for Verstand). The compound's Neo-Confucian inheritance has shaped the East Asian reception of Western rationalist philosophy in distinctive ways: the Cheng-Zhu doctrine of 性即理 was already operational across centuries of East Asian intellectual life, and the Meiji repurposing of 理性 to render Vernunft has continuously cross-pollinated the two traditions. Adopted into Chinese (lǐxìng) and Korean (이성 isŏng) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of reason, with the broader cluster 理性的 (riseiteki, rational), 合理性 (gōrisei, rationality), 理性主義 (riseishugi, rationalism) operative across modern East Asian academic vocabulary.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical-translation movement; stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881), paired against 具象 / 具体 (the concrete)

components.meaning: to draw out, pull forth, extract — the hand drawing a single strand clear of the bundle; here the verb of abstraction as a drawing-away
image, form, the appearing — that which is grasped as figure rather than in concrete presence; here the general form that is drawn out

translation_range.emphasis: the mental operation — standard rendering in logic and epistemology contexts
the adjectival form, opposed to 具体的 (concrete): 抽象的概念 (abstract concept), 抽象芸術 (abstract art)
literal decomposition foregrounding the verbal force of 抽 — occasionally in expository treatments of the coinage's logic

conceptual_remainder: The Latin abstractio and the Japanese 抽象 converge with rare exactness on a single underlying figure: abs-trahere is a drawing-away, and 抽象 is the drawing-out (抽) of the form (象). The calque thus carries the etymological metaphor of the Western term almost without remainder — a convergence uncommon in the Meiji vocabulary, where calques more often re-route the source concept through an unrelated classical resonance. What 抽象 does add is the 象 register: abstraction is figured specifically as the drawing-out of an image-form, which subtly aligns the Japanese term with a representationalist picture of the abstract as a retained figure, rather than with the nominalist or operationalist accounts on which there is no abstract 'image' at all but only a rule or a word. The opposition 抽象 / 具象 (drawn-out form / furnished body) that the Meiji apparatus stabilized also imports a clean binary that the Western tradition's long quarrel over the very possibility of abstract ideas — Berkeley's and Hume's denials — does not settle so tidily.
doctrinal_weight: One of the structural terms of the Meiji epistemological vocabulary, operating across the cluster 抽象 / 具体 (abstract / concrete), 抽象的 (abstract, adj.), 抽象化 (abstraction as process), and load-bearing in the rendering of the post-Lockean and Kantian account of concept-formation as abstraction-across-particulars. Adopted into Chinese (chōuxiàng) and Korean (추상 chusang) as the universal modern East Asian rendering, and foundational to the twentieth-century East Asian vocabulary of abstract art, abstract mathematics, and the abstract / concrete distinction across the human and social sciences.

coinage_notes: Coined by Nishi Amane (西周) in the Meiji philosophical-translation movement to render Ethik; the disciplinary form 倫理学 stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881)

components.meaning: the proper ordering of human relations — load-bearing in the Confucian 五倫 (the Five Relationships); the relational structure within which moral life is enacted
principle, rational order, the underlying pattern — here the principle governing right relational order; the same 理 that operates in 理性, 論理, 物理

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering; the discipline as 倫理学 (rinrigaku)
in contexts where 倫理 names the lived domain of moral relation rather than the academic discipline
literal decomposition foregrounding the Confucian 倫 inheritance — used in expository treatments to mark the relational framing the term carries

conceptual_remainder: 倫理 renders Ethik through 倫, the character of the Confucian Five Relationships, and so locates the ethical first in the proper ordering of graded human bonds — ruler and minister, parent and child — rather than in the Greek ēthos of individual settled character or in the Kantian autonomy of a self-legislating will. What the compound brings that 'ethics' does not naturally invoke is this relational substrate: morality as the rectification of relationship, the self always already situated within bonds it did not choose. What it cannot easily carry is the specifically modern Western construction of the moral agent as a deracinated individual confronting universal law — the construction on which both Kantian deontology and utilitarian calculus are built. The East Asian reception of Western moral philosophy has been shaped by this friction: the imported theories arrive in a vocabulary whose root character already answers, relationally, the question they pose individually.
doctrinal_weight: One of the foundational terms of the Meiji philosophical lexicon and the operating East Asian name for both the discipline of ethics (倫理学) and the domain of moral life. Adopted into Chinese (lúnlǐ) and Korean (윤리 yulli) as the universal modern rendering. The compound is a paradigm case of the Meiji translators' practice of recruiting a doctrinally loaded classical character to carry a Western concept, with the consequence that the East Asian vocabulary of ethics retains, beneath the imported theories, a Confucian relational grammar — a tension that twentieth-century East Asian moral philosophy has worked through rather than around.

coinage_notes: Coined by Nishi Amane (西周) to render Western logic; the disciplinary form 論理学 stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881)

components.meaning: ordered, sequenced discourse; argument, the marshalling of speech into consequence — here the reasoning whose order is at issue
principle, rational order, the underlying pattern — here the principle that valid reasoning must observe; the same 理 as in 理性, 倫理, 物理

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering; the discipline as 論理学 (ronrigaku)
adjectival form: 論理的思考 (logical thinking), 論理性 (logical coherence)
literal decomposition (論 ordered discourse + 理 principle) — used in expository treatments of the coinage

conceptual_remainder: 論理 pairs 論 (ordered discourse) with 理 (principle), framing logic as the principle of well-ordered reasoning. This frames the discipline through the order of discourse rather than through the Greek logos as the structure of being itself, or through the modern formal conception of logic as a calculus of truth-preserving form indifferent to content. The compound's most telling feature is comparative: where most Meiji calques displaced their Chinese transliteration competitors entirely, 論理 entered Chinese but was there partly displaced by Yan Fu's phonetic 邏輯 (luóji, from 'logic'), so that modern Chinese carries both a semantic calque and a transliteration in uneasy coexistence. The case exposes the choice every Meiji coinage faced — to render the concept through native morphemes (and thereby pre-interpret it) or to transliterate (and thereby leave it semantically inert) — and is one of the few where both options survived into modern usage.
doctrinal_weight: A foundational term of the Meiji philosophical lexicon and the operating Japanese and Korean (논리 nolli) name for the discipline of logic and the property of logical coherence. Its divergent fate in Chinese — coexisting with Yan Fu's 邏輯 — makes 論理 a standard case study in the historiography of the wasei-kango, illustrating that the Japanese semantic-calque strategy and the Chinese transliteration strategy were genuine rivals rather than a settled progression, and that the modern East Asian philosophical vocabulary is not uniformly of Meiji-Japanese provenance.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical-translation movement (associated with Nishi Amane); stabilized in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881), paired against 本体 (noumenon / thing-in-itself)

components.meaning: to appear, to manifest, the present-actual — that which comes forth into presence; here the appearing as event
image, form, the appearing-as-figure — that which is grasped as image; here the manifest content presented to a subject

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering across philosophy and the sciences
in the strict Kantian register, opposed to 本体 (the thing-in-itself / noumenon)
literal decomposition (現 manifest + 象 image) — used in expository treatments to mark the appearing-to-a-subject the compound encodes

conceptual_remainder: 現象 renders Phänomen through 現 (to come forth, manifest) and 象 (image, form), so that phenomenon is figured as the manifest-image — that which shows itself as figure to a subject. This tracks the Greek phainomenon (that which shows itself) closely, and the Meiji pairing 現象 / 本体 reproduces the Kantian Phänomen / Noumenon distinction with serviceable precision. What the compound subtly adds is the 象 register's representationalist tilt: by naming the appearing specifically as image, 現象 leans toward a picture in which what appears is a presented figure standing for something behind it — congenial to the Kantian appearance / thing-in-itself split, but less neutral than the bare Greek 'that which shows itself,' and in some tension with the later phenomenological program (Husserl's 'to the things themselves') that sought to recover the phenomenon as self-givenness rather than as image-of-a-hidden-substrate.
doctrinal_weight: One of the load-bearing terms of the Meiji epistemological vocabulary, operating across the cluster 現象 / 本体 (phenomenon / noumenon), 現象界 (the phenomenal world), 現象学 (phenomenology), and foundational to the modern East Asian rendering of Kantian and post-Kantian philosophy. Adopted into Chinese (xiànxiàng) and Korean (현상 hyŏnsang) as the universal modern rendering, and extended beyond philosophy into the general scientific and ordinary-language sense of 'a phenomenon' — any observable occurrence — across all three languages.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical-translation movement; stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881) as the rendering of Bewusstsein / consciousness, drawing on the Yogācāra scholastic value of 識 (vijñāna) within the 心意識 triad

components.meaning: directed mind, intent — the appropriative, leaning-toward aspect of awareness (manas in the 心意識 triad); here the mind's being-turned-toward what it is aware of
discriminating cognition — vijñāna, the Buddhist term for consciousness as the telling-apart and recognizing of objects; here the knowing in which something is given as something

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering across philosophy and psychology; the awareness within which objects are given
in ordinary and phenomenological registers — being conscious-of, the lit field of experience

translation_range.rendering: the conscious (vs. 無意識 the unconscious)
translation_range.emphasis: in the post-Freudian psychological vocabulary, where 意識 is opposed to 無意識 / 潜在意識

conceptual_remainder: 意識 renders Bewusstsein by binding 意 (the directed, appropriative mind — manas) to 識 (vijñāna, discriminating cognition). This is an unusually freighted choice: 識 had been, for a millennium of East Asian Buddhist scholasticism, *the* word for consciousness, and the eight-consciousness taxonomy (八識) gave it a depth and articulation no fresh coinage could match. The gain is that the Kantian "I think that accompanies all my representations" lands in a term already meaning the discriminating awareness in which objects are constituted, and the 意 element supplies precisely the directedness — the toward-an-object structure — that Brentano and Husserl would later thematize as intentionality. The remainder is doctrinal interference running the other way: 識 carries the Yogācāra scaffolding (store-consciousness, the ripening of seeds, the constructed self) as a semantic undertow, so that 意識 can sound, against its will, like a term inside an idealist metaphysics of mind rather than the neutral epistemological "consciousness" Kant intends — and in technical Buddhist contexts 意識 keeps its narrower scholastic sense (the sixth, mano-vijñāna, mental consciousness), a homonymy that the modern philosophical use must continually hold at bay.
doctrinal_weight: One of the anchor terms of the Meiji vocabulary of mind, operating across the cluster 意識 / 無意識 (consciousness / the unconscious), 自意識 (self-consciousness), 意識作用 (the act of consciousness), and standing within the 主観 / 客観 frame as the locus where the subject's relation to objects is articulated. It is foundational to the modern East Asian reception of Kant, German idealism, and later phenomenology and psychoanalysis, and was adopted as the universal modern rendering into Chinese (yìshí) and Korean (uisik 의식), where — as in Japanese — it serves simultaneously as the technical philosophical term and the ordinary word for "being conscious."

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical-translation movement (associated with Nishi Amane); a Buddhist contemplative compound (観 vipaśyanā-seeing + 念 smṛti-recollection) re-coined to render the empiricist and Kantian "idea," stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881)

components.meaning: to contemplate, to view inwardly — the Buddhist 観 of meditative seeing (vipaśyanā) and visualization (観想); here the mind's holding of a content before it
to fix in mind, to recollect — 念 as smṛti, mindful retention (as in 念仏); here the mental presence and persistence of the content

translation_range.emphasis: the empiricist sense (Locke, Hume): the immediate content or object of thought
general philosophical use for a mental representation, often near 概念 but more subjective and less articulated
in the Platonic-Kantian register: the regulative concept of reason exceeding possible experience

translation_range.rendering: a fixed notion / to resign oneself (観念する)
translation_range.emphasis: the derived ordinary sense — a settled mental attitude, and the verb "to give up, accept the inevitable"

conceptual_remainder: 観念 re-coins a Buddhist contemplative term — 観 (vipaśyanā-seeing, meditative visualization) plus 念 (smṛti, the mindful fixing of the object) — for the Western "idea." The compound originally named a *practice*: holding an object steadily before the inward eye (観想念仏, visualization of the Buddha). Redirected to render Locke's "idea" and Kant's Idee, it carries that activity as remainder: where the English "idea" can be a passive, atomistic given (a sense-datum, an impression's faint copy), 観念 leans toward the idea as something the mind *holds and dwells on* — closer to a entertained representation than to a received impression. This makes 観念 an excellent fit for the Kantian regulative Idea and for "idea" as the mind's own construction, but a slightly awkward one for the strict empiricist sense, and it explains the term's ordinary-language drift: a 観念 easily becomes a *fixed* idea, a preconception one is gripped by, and 観念する collapses the contemplative origin into "to resign oneself" — to finally hold the unwanted thought steady and accept it. The division of labour with 概念 (gainen, "concept": the articulated, general, defined) leaves 観念 with the more subjective, imagistic, and attitudinal pole of the Western "idea."
doctrinal_weight: A core term of the Meiji epistemological vocabulary, operating across 観念論 (idealism, the doctrine that the real is idea-constituted), 観念連合 (the association of ideas, rendering the British associationist psychology), and the contrast pair 観念 / 概念 (idea / concept) and 観念 / 実在 (idea / reality). It is foundational to the East Asian reception of British empiricism, Kant, and German idealism, and was adopted as the standard rendering into Chinese (guānniàn) and Korean (kwannyŏm 관념), where it likewise carries both the technical philosophical sense and the everyday sense of a fixed or preconceived notion.

coinage_notes: Nishi Amane (proposed the earlier 善美学 / 美妙学); stabilized as 美学 through Nakae Chōmin's 維氏美学 (1883–84, translating Eugène Véron's L'Esthétique) and the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881)

components.meaning: the beautiful, the fine — the broad classical value-term (excellent, admirable, beautiful) here narrowed to the specifically aesthetic
disciplined study, the -ology suffix — the Meiji workhorse that converts a subject-matter into the name of its systematic discipline

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering: the philosophical discipline taking beauty and art as its objects
where the discipline is framed (post-Hegel) primarily as the philosophy of the artwork
literal decomposition (美 the beautiful + 学 science/discipline) — used to mark the Baumgartenian framing the compound encodes

conceptual_remainder: 美学 renders Ästhetik as "the science/discipline of the beautiful" (美 + 学), and in doing so makes a decision the German word does not force. Baumgarten's Aesthetica is built on aisthēsis — sense-perception — so that aesthetics is first the science of *sensible cognition* and only consequently the science of the beautiful; the standard German term keeps the root that ties art-philosophy to the theory of sensibility. 美学 cuts that tie: by lexicalizing the discipline through 美 (beauty) rather than through a term for sensation, it defines the field by its paradigm object (the beautiful) rather than by its faculty (sense), foreclosing the etymological reminder that aesthetics began as an epistemology of the senses. The remainder runs deeper because 美 itself is not the narrow Western "beautiful": classically it fuses the fine, the excellent, and the morally admirable (尽善尽美), so 美学 inherits a faint ethical-perfectionist coloring foreign to a discipline that, since Kant, defines the aesthetic precisely by its independence from the good and the useful. That the term was fixed through Nakae Chōmin's translation of Véron — for whom art is the expression of emotion, not the imitation of ideal beauty — adds a final irony: the discipline named for 美 was stabilized in Japanese by a book arguing that beauty is not art's essence.
doctrinal_weight: The standard name of the discipline of aesthetics across modern East Asia, anchoring the cluster 美術 (fine art), 美的 (the aesthetic, adjectival), 美意識 (aesthetic consciousness/sensibility), and 美学者 (aesthetician). It carries the East Asian reception of Baumgarten, Kant's third Critique, Hegel's philosophy of art, and Véron's expressivism, and was the vehicle through which a self-standing domain of "the aesthetic" — distinct from ethics and from craft — entered modern Japanese, Chinese (měixué), and Korean (mihak 미학) intellectual life.

coinage_notes: Kawamoto Kōmin (川本幸民), c. 1860, replacing the phonetic loan 舎密 (seimi)

components.meaning: transformation, becoming-other — the lawful changing of one substance into another; the operative core of the discipline
learning, study, -ology — the standard Meiji disciplinary suffix

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering across Japanese, Chinese (huàxué), and Korean
adjectival form: 化学反応 (chemical reaction), 化学結合 (chemical bond)

conceptual_remainder: 化学 names chemistry by its central operation — 化, transformation — rather than by its objects or its method. This is a precise and arguably superior framing: where 'chemistry' is an opaque inheritance from alchemy and Arabic, 化学 transparently says 'the study of how things become other things.' What the calque sets aside is the analytic and compositional dimension of the modern science — chemistry as the resolution of matter into elements and the combinatorial logic of those elements — which is foregrounded by the element-vocabulary (元素, 酸素, 水素) but not by the head term itself. The earlier phonetic loan 舎密 (seimi) carried no meaning at all and could not survive against a calque that made the science self-explaining; the displacement of 舎密 by 化学 is a clean case of motivated coinage defeating transliteration.
doctrinal_weight: 化学 is the bakumatsu counterpart to the great Meiji disciplinary coinages: a pre-Restoration calque, made by a rangaku physician, that nonetheless followed the same logic — a characterization of the field's essence plus the 学 suffix — and was likewise exported into Chinese and Korean. It demonstrates that the systematic Sino-Japanese rendering of Western science was already underway before 1868, and that the decisive contest was not Japanese versus Chinese coinage but motivated calque versus phonetic loan, a contest the calque almost always won.

false_friends.divergence: Exact homophone (kagaku / かがく) but a different discipline: 科学 is science-in-general, 化学 is chemistry specifically. Japanese disambiguates in speech by reading 化学 as 'bakegaku' when confusion threatens.

coinage_notes: Standardized through early Meiji science education; the title 物理階梯 (Katayama Junkichi, 1872) fixes it in the school system

components.meaning: thing, matter — the concrete material particulars whose behavior physics studies
principle, the underlying pattern — the lawful order to be read off matter

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering, usually expanded to 物理学 (butsurigaku) for the discipline
in compounds: 物理現象 (physical phenomenon), 物理法則 (physical law)

conceptual_remainder: 物理 reads as 'the principle within things' — the 理 of matter — and so binds Western experimental physics directly to the Neo-Confucian program of 格物窮理, the investigation of things in order to exhaust their principle. This framing is illuminating and tendentious in equal measure: it makes physics legible as the natural completion of an indigenous epistemic project, but it imports the Neo-Confucian assumption that principle is something read off the surface of things rather than something constructed through mathematized hypothesis and controlled experiment. What the compound cannot carry is the specifically modern sense of physical law as mathematical structure that may have no intuitive 'principle' available to inspection at all. The older Edo umbrella term 窮理 (kyūri), broader and more cosmological, was narrowed by 物理 onto the experimental discipline, leaving 窮理 to fade.
doctrinal_weight: 物理 is the case in which a Meiji scientific coinage most visibly inherits a Neo-Confucian conceptual skeleton. Where 化学 and 科学 are relatively neutral characterizations, 物理 literally re-uses the 物 of 格物 and the 理 of 窮理, so that the reception of Western physics in East Asia ran partly through the assumption that it was the fulfillment of the Confucian investigation of things. The standardization of the term through the 1872 school primer 物理階梯 shows the coinage being fixed not in a treatise but in the new mass-education system.

false_friends.divergence: In Chinese wùlǐ is the standard word for physics, identical in meaning; but the literary Chinese phrase 物理 in classical texts means simply 'the principles of things' in a general philosophical sense, the older reading the compound was lifted from.

coinage_notes: Standardized by the Meiji government telegraph-and-telephone administration; fixed as the service name in 1890

components.meaning: electricity (from 'lightning') — the transmitting medium
speech, talk — what is transmitted

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering — the instrument and, by extension, a phone call (電話をかける, to make a call)
in compounds: 電話番号 (phone number), 公衆電話 (public telephone), 携帯電話 (mobile phone)

conceptual_remainder: 電話 is a transparent descriptive calque — 'electric speech' — that beat both the transliteration テレフォン and the rival calque 伝話器 ('speech-transmitting device'). Its economy is its strength: where 伝話器 named the apparatus, 電話 names the act, and so absorbs effortlessly into verbs and compounds (電話する, to telephone). What the two-character calque drops is the Greek tele- ('at a distance'), the etymological heart of 'telephone': 電話 says by what means (electricity) rather than across what gap (distance). The distance that defines the Western word is left for context to supply. The coinage exemplifies the Meiji preference for 電 as a closed productive prefix generating an entire technological paradigm (電信, 電車, 電話) by a single combinatorial rule.
doctrinal_weight: 電話 is a pure instance of Meiji technological wasei-kango: a brand-new compound for a brand-new object, formed by the rule 電 + (what is conveyed), and exported intact into Chinese (diànhuà) and Korean. It shows the coinage system operating not on inherited philosophical concepts but on industrial novelty, and shows the decisive role of the state — here the telegraph-and-telephone administration — in selecting one candidate term and fixing it as an institutional name, after which the alternatives vanished.

false_friends.divergence: Adopted into Chinese as diànhuà with identical meaning, but Chinese also coined the parallel 電報 for telegram on the same 電-prefix rule; the productive pattern, not just the word, transferred.

coinage_notes: Meiji coinage replacing the rangaku phonetic loan エレキテル (from Dutch elektriciteit); popularized through texts such as Fukuzawa's 訓蒙窮理図解 (1868)

components.meaning: lightning, and hence electricity — the phenomenon named through its natural manifestation
qi, vital energy, pervading vapor — the framing of electricity as an animating energy that fills matter

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering — the physical phenomenon and the utility (電気を消す, to turn off the light/power)
in compounds: 電気工学 (electrical engineering), 静電気 (static electricity), 電気回路 (electric circuit)

conceptual_remainder: 電気 fuses two metaphors: 電, electricity grasped as domesticated lightning, and 気, the classical cosmological pneuma. The second is the consequential one. By rendering 'electricity' with 気 (qi), the coinage frames the new force not as an abstract physical quantity but as a kind of vital energy pervading bodies and things — intuitively powerful for a 19th-century readership, and continuous with the qi of medicine and cosmology, but carrying a vitalist resonance entirely absent from the Western concept of electric charge. What the compound cannot carry is the precise quantitative and field-theoretic content of 'electricity' as developed by Faraday and Maxwell; that content arrives later, layered on top of a word that still whispers 'lightning-breath.' The displaced phonetic loan エレキテル, by contrast, carried no metaphor and no cosmological freight at all.
doctrinal_weight: 電気 is the keystone of the entire Meiji electrical lexicon: once 電 is fixed as 'electric-' in this term, the productive paradigm (電話, 電車, 電信, 電力, 電子) follows automatically. It also exemplifies the deepest pattern in reverse-flow translation — the recruitment of a heavily freighted classical term (気/qi) to domesticate a Western scientific concept, so that the imported science arrives already interpreted through indigenous cosmology. The pairing of 電気 with 物理 marks the two poles of Meiji physical science: the new force named through old cosmology, and the discipline named through old epistemology.

false_friends.divergence: The 気 of 電気 is the same graph as the qi of traditional medicine and cosmology (気功, 元気), inviting a false continuity: electricity is not qi, and the shared character masks a categorial difference between a measurable physical quantity and a cosmological vital force.

coinage_notes: Udagawa Yōan (宇田川榕菴) in 舎密開宗 (1837), calquing Lavoisier's oxygène

components.meaning: acid, sourness — the (mistaken) Lavoisierian thesis that this gas is the principle of acidity, preserved in the calque
element, elementary constituent — the bound Meiji-scientific suffix for a named chemical element

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering in Japanese; the chemical element O
in compounds: 酸素濃度 (oxygen concentration), 酸素供給 (oxygen supply), 無酸素 (anaerobic)

conceptual_remainder: 酸素 is a faithful calque of oxygène, and it inherits the calque's defect with perfect fidelity. Lavoisier built oxygène on the claim that this gas is the universal principle of acidity; the claim was refuted within decades (hydrochloric acid contains no oxygen), but the name kept its etymology, and so does 酸素 — it still says 'the acid-making element.' What the Japanese term cannot carry, any more than the French could, is the corrected modern understanding in which oxygen's defining role is in oxidation and respiration, not acid formation. The compound is thus doubly historical: it transmits not the science but a superseded moment in the science, embalmed in two characters. Modern Chinese, coining 氧 afresh with the 气 gas-radical, escaped this fossil; Japanese and Korean keep it.
doctrinal_weight: 酸素 is the keystone of the entire 〜素 element series. Once Udagawa fixes the principle — name the gas by what it makes, suffix it with 素 — 水素 (water-maker) and 窒素 (life-denier) follow by the same rule, and the suffix 素 becomes a closed productive morpheme carrying the Lavoisierian thesis that matter resolves into elementary substances. It also marks the bakumatsu, not Meiji, origin of Japanese scientific vocabulary: the analytic chemical lexicon was already systematic in 1837, and the Sino-Japanese contest that mattered was calque versus phonetic loan, not Japanese versus Chinese coinage — though here, unusually, China later declined the Japanese word.

false_friends.divergence: Modern Chinese rejects 酸素 entirely and writes oxygen as 氧 (yǎng), a 19th-century single-character coinage with the 气 gas-radical. The shared concept hides a complete lexical divergence: a reader of Chinese will not recognize 酸素, and a reader of Japanese will not parse 氧.
In isolation 酸 means 'acid' (酸性, sour); the 酸 of 酸素 does not mean the gas is acidic but preserves Lavoisier's discarded theory that it causes acidity — a false transparency built into the calque.

coinage_notes: Udagawa Yōan (宇田川榕菴) in 舎密開宗 (1837), calquing Lavoisier's hydrogène

components.meaning: water — the product by which the gas is named; hydrogen as 'the thing that makes water on burning'
element, elementary constituent — the bound Meiji-scientific element suffix

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering in Japanese; the chemical element H
in compounds: 水素結合 (hydrogen bond), 水素爆弾 (hydrogen bomb), 水素化 (hydrogenation)

conceptual_remainder: 水素 calques hydrogène precisely: 'the element that generates water,' the gas named by its synthetic product rather than by any intrinsic property. This is one of the rare cases where the calque is not only faithful but conceptually durable — hydrogen genuinely does combine with oxygen to make water, so unlike 酸素 the name carries no superseded theory. What it still cannot carry is everything that makes hydrogen the keystone of modern physics and cosmology: the simplest atom, the proton-electron pair, the most abundant element in the universe, the fuel of stellar fusion. 水素 says only what an 18th-century chemist saw at the bench — a gas that burns to water — and is silent on the atomic and cosmic significance layered on later. Modern Chinese again diverges, coining 氫 with the gas-radical.
doctrinal_weight: 水素 is the second term of the 〜素 paradigm and its cleanest instance: the calque principle (name by product, suffix 素) applied to a case where the product-name happens to remain correct, so the term aged well where 酸素 did not. Together with 酸素 it shows the same coiner, Udagawa Yōan, generating a systematic series from a single rule a generation before Meiji — and it pairs with 酸素 not only lexically but referentially, since the two gases combine to make the very water that names one of them.

false_friends.divergence: Modern Chinese writes hydrogen as 氫 (qīng), a coined single character with the 气 gas-radical, and does not use 水素. As with 酸素/氧, the concept is shared but the words are mutually unrecognizable across the two scripts.
The 水 of 水素 names the gas's combustion product, not its nature: hydrogen is not 'a kind of water,' and 水素 is not a watery substance — the character records a synthesis, not a composition.

coinage_notes: Udagawa Yōan (宇田川榕菴) in 舎密開宗 (1837), calquing Lavoisier's azote

components.meaning: to obstruct, to suffocate — the gas in which flame and breath are extinguished; calquing the privative azote
element, elementary constituent — the bound Meiji-scientific element suffix

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering in Japanese; the chemical element N
in compounds: 窒素固定 (nitrogen fixation), 窒素酸化物 (nitrogen oxides), 液体窒素 (liquid nitrogen)

conceptual_remainder: 窒素 is decisive evidence of which European name reached East Asia. Two rival names competed: Lavoisier's azote, 'without life,' naming the gas by what it kills, and the English nitrogen, 'niter-producer,' naming it by what it forms. 窒素 — 'suffocating element' — is unambiguously a calque of azote, so the Japanese (and via Japanese the Korean) term encodes the French privative logic, not the English compositional one. What the privative name cannot carry is everything positive that nitrogen is: the inert bulk of the atmosphere, the indispensable constituent of proteins and nucleic acids, the element whose industrial fixation feeds much of humanity. 窒素 fixes nitrogen forever as the gas that suffocates — true at the 1780s bench, but a thin and negative grip on an element that is, biochemically, the opposite of lifeless. Modern Chinese diverges with 氮.
doctrinal_weight: 窒素 completes the 〜素 trio (酸素 by product, 水素 by product, 窒素 by privation) and shows that the calque principle could absorb a negative naming-decision as readily as a positive one — the suffix 素 stays constant while the head character swings from 'makes acid' to 'makes water' to 'denies life.' Historically it is the cleanest single datum for tracing transmission: the choice of 窒 over any niter-based rendering proves the channel ran through Lavoisier's French nomenclature in Dutch mediation, the rangaku route Udagawa worked in.

false_friends.divergence: Modern Chinese writes nitrogen as 氮 (dàn), a single coined gas-radical character, not 窒素. The terms do not transfer across the two scripts despite the shared element.

The English name means 'niter-producer' (compositional, positive); 窒素 means 'suffocating element' (privative, negative). They name the same gas by opposite logics, because East Asia received the French azote, not the English nitrogen.

coinage_notes: Udagawa Yōan (宇田川榕菴) in the botanical 植学啓原 (1834), calquing cellula / cel

components.meaning: fine, minute — the microscopic scale at which the unit becomes visible; the scalar descent that constituted cell theory
enwrapping membrane, sac, caul — the bounded organic interior; a flesh-radical word for a living envelope

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering across Japanese, Chinese (xìbāo), Korean (세포), and Vietnamese; the biological unit
in compounds: 細胞分裂 (cell division), 細胞膜 (cell membrane), 幹細胞 (stem cell)

conceptual_remainder: 細胞 quietly improves on its etymon. Hooke's cellula was a dead metaphor of masonry — a 'little room,' the empty box he saw in cork — and the European word still carries that architectural emptiness. Udagawa's calque substitutes 胞, the flesh-radical word for the enwrapping birth-membrane, so 細胞 reads as 'fine sac,' a living enclosure rather than a vacant chamber. What the Japanese term gains is a head-start toward the membrane-centred understanding of the cell; what it sets aside is the spatial, room-like intuition that the history of the European concept actually ran through. The 細 supplies the other half — not a chamber as such but a chamber at the limit of sight — so the compound encodes the very microscopic descent that made cell theory possible. Unlike the chemical 〜素 series, this calque was accepted everywhere, becoming the universal East Asian word.
doctrinal_weight: 細胞 is the botanical counterpart to the 舎密開宗 chemical vocabulary: the same coiner, the same rangaku method, applied to the life sciences a few years earlier in 植学啓原 (1834). It demonstrates that systematic Sino-Japanese scientific calquing spanned chemistry and biology together and predated Meiji by a generation. It is also the clearest case in the scientific lexicon of a calque that bettered its source — choosing a living, membranal metaphor over a dead architectural one — and, unlike 酸素/水素/窒素, of a Japanese coinage that China and Korea adopted wholesale rather than replacing.

false_friends.divergence: English 'cell' descends from cellula, 'little room' — an architectural, spatial metaphor of an empty chamber. 細胞 ('fine sac/membrane') is an organic, enclosural metaphor. Same referent, opposite figures: a room versus an envelope.

Chinese xìbāo is the standard word for the biological cell, identical in sense and graph — a rare case where the Japanese scientific calque was adopted unchanged rather than replaced (contrast 酸素→氧, 水素→氫, 窒素→氮).

coinage_notes: Sugita Genpaku (杉田玄白), in the Kaitai Shinsho (解体新書, 1774); a contraction of 神気 (vital spirit) + 経脈 (channels)

components.meaning: vital spirit, animal-spirits — the 神 of 神気, the animating pneuma the nerve was held to convey
channel, conduit, meridian — the 経 of 経脈/経絡, the East Asian medical vocabulary of bodily channels

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering — the anatomical structure (視神経 optic nerve, 神経細胞 neuron)
extended psychological sense: 神経質 (highly strung), 神経が太い (thick-skinned), 神経をすり減らす (to fray one's nerves)

conceptual_remainder: 神経 is the earliest of the great Sino-Japanese scientific calques and the most theory-laden. Sugita Genpaku, confronting in the Ontleedkundige Tafelen a structure for which no Japanese or Chinese medical word existed, did not transliterate the Dutch zenuw but blended two terms from the qi-and-channel physiology already in the language: 神気, the vital spirit, and 経脈, the conduits along which it was thought to course. The result names the Western nerve as 'the channel of the vital spirit' — a fusion that lets the dissected cord be seen at all, but at the cost of importing a pneumatic, energetic conception the European anatomical term had already shed. What the calque cannot carry is precisely the modern nerve's status as a discrete fibrous tissue rather than a conduit for an animating force; the word makes Western anatomy legible by translating it back into the very framework Western anatomy was leaving behind. The extraordinary afterlife of the term — its psychological extensions (神経質, 神経戦) have no anatomical content at all — shows the 'vital spirit' pole of 神 quietly outliving the physiology that motivated the coinage.
doctrinal_weight: 神経 is the proof-of-concept for the entire reverse-flow lexicon: a generation before the Meiji coinages, an Edo rangaku physician demonstrated that a Western scientific concept with no Sino-Japanese equivalent could be domesticated by motivated compounding rather than phonetic loan, and that such a coinage would travel — 神経 was adopted unchanged into Chinese (shénjīng) and Korean (신경). It also exhibits, in its purest form, the structural cost the atlas tracks throughout this module: the receiving language does not absorb the foreign concept neutrally but re-narrates it in inherited terms, here folding Cartesian-Boerhaavian nerve anatomy into the channel-and-pneuma cosmology of East Asian medicine.
