false_friends.divergence: Chinese shénjīng is the standard word for nerve, graphically and semantically identical — a Japanese rangaku calque re-exported to its source script community, predating the Meiji wave by nearly a century.

Standing alone, 神 means god/spirit (kami) with full religious weight; bound into 神経 the same character is bleached to 'vital force' and then, in 神経質, to a purely psychological register with no numinous sense at all.

coinage_notes: Udagawa Yōan (宇田川榕菴), 舎密開宗 (1837–1847)

components.meaning: origin, primary, that which is first — asserting the elements as the originary floor of analysis
elemental constituent, the basic stuff — the standard Meiji bound suffix for chemical elements

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering — 元素記号 (element symbol), 元素周期表 (periodic table)
broader sense of an irreducible component, occasionally figurative (構成元素, constituent element)

conceptual_remainder: 元素 renders Lavoisier's chemical element by binding two claims into one word: 素, the basic constituent (which also heads the calqued gas-names 酸素, 水素, 窒素), and 元, the originary or first. The 素 alone would have carried Lavoisier's operational definition exactly — a substance not yet resolved into simpler ones. The added 元 does something more: it converts that provisional, analysis-relative status into an ontological one, naming the elements not merely as 'so far undecomposed' but as 'the origin-stuff,' the primal floor of matter. This is a small but real surplus the calque introduces over its source: Lavoisier was careful to define elements operationally precisely so as not to prejudge their ultimate simplicity, whereas 元素 grammatically asserts primacy. The drift is invisible in ordinary use but becomes pointed once subatomic structure shows the 'origin-elements' to be themselves composite — at which point the 元 in the word is quietly contradicted by the science it names.
doctrinal_weight: 元素 is the keystone of the rangaku chemical lexicon: it both names the central concept of Lavoisierian chemistry and licenses the productive 〜素 suffix that makes the whole Japanese element vocabulary systematic rather than ad hoc. Its establishment in Udagawa's 舎密開宗 (1837–47) places the decisive coinage, like 神経 and 化学, in the late Edo period rather than the Meiji, and its clean export into Chinese (yuánsù) and Korean (원소) exemplifies the pattern whereby a motivated Japanese calque, not a phonetic loan, became the shared East Asian scientific standard.

false_friends.divergence: Chinese yuánsù is the standard word for chemical element, identical in graph and sense — the Japanese rangaku calque adopted wholesale, in contrast to the gas-names (酸素→氧, 水素→氫) where Chinese rejected the 〜素 series.

coinage_notes: Standardized through Meiji school chemistry and nomenclature reform as the partner of 分子 (molecule)

components.meaning: origin, primal source, the irreducible ground — the level beyond which division cannot pass
small discrete unit, particle — the bound 'minute particle' suffix (cf. 分子, 電子, 粒子)

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering — 原子核 (atomic nucleus), 原子力 (atomic energy), 原子爆弾 (atomic bomb)
adjectival in compounds: 原子論 (atomic theory / atomism), 原子量 (atomic weight)

conceptual_remainder: 原子 calques 'atom' not by its etymon — Greek atomos, 'uncuttable,' a purely privative definition by what cannot be done to it — but positively, as the 'origin-particle,' the primal small unit. The shift is consequential. atomos says only: indivisible. 原子 says: the first thing, the ground from which the divisible (分子, the 'divided-particle') is built. The calque thus supplies a substantive metaphysics of primacy where the Greek offered a bare negation, and it does so in a matched pair: 原子/分子 reads as origin-particle versus divided-particle, an elegant opposition with no counterpart in the atom/molecule pair, which are etymologically unrelated. What the word cannot carry is exactly the privative humility of atomos — and the irony 元素 also suffers falls here with full force, since the 'uncuttable' that 原 declares originary was, within decades of the term's standardization, cut. The 子 suffix, meanwhile, proved the more durable insight: it generalized cleanly into 電子 (electron), 中性子 (neutron), 素粒子 (elementary particle), making 原子 the head of a productive particle-vocabulary.
doctrinal_weight: 原子 shows the calque system operating not on a single word but on a conceptual structure: it is fixed in Meiji science education jointly with 分子, so that the atom/molecule distinction enters East Asian languages already organized as an origin/division opposition. This is the atlas's recurring lesson in concentrated form — the receiving language does not merely label the foreign concept but rebuilds its internal relations on indigenous morphemic logic, and the rebuilt structure (原-vs-分, both suffixed by 子) is then shared intact across Japanese, Chinese (yuánzǐ), and Korean (원자).

false_friends.divergence: Chinese yuánzǐ is the standard word for atom, identical in graph and sense, carrying the same 原/分 paired structure with 分子 — the Japanese scientific calque and its relational logic transferred together.

coinage_notes: Popularized through the Meiji evolution literature, esp. Ishikawa Chiyomatsu's 動物進化論 (1883), rendering E. S. Morse's 1877 Tokyo lectures

components.meaning: advance, progress forward — the directional vector distinguishing evolution from undirected change
transformation, change of state — the lawful becoming-other of forms over time

translation_range.emphasis: universal standard rendering — usually expanded to 進化論 (shinkaron) for the theory; 進化する, to evolve
popular figurative sense of improvement over time (技術の進化, the evolution of technology) — closer to Spencer than to Darwin

conceptual_remainder: 進化 renders 'evolution' as 進 + 化 — 'advancing change' — and in doing so commits, at the level of the morpheme, the precise interpretive error Darwin spent the Origin guarding against. Darwinian evolution is descent with modification: it has no intrinsic direction, no built-in arrow toward higher or better; the very word 'evolution' Darwin adopted only reluctantly because of its progressivist connotations. 進化 hard-codes that connotation: 化 alone (mere change, as in 変化) would have been the neutral and accurate calque, but the added 進 inserts forward motion and improvement into the name itself. This is no accident of translation but a faithful mirror of the term's East Asian reception, which arrived heavily through Spencer's developmental sociology and Morse's progressivist lectures as much as through Darwin. What the calque cannot carry is the directionlessness that is the conceptual core of natural selection; what it adds is a teleology the science explicitly disowns — and that surplus, fused into the standard word, has shaped a century of popular evolutionism in Japanese, Chinese, and Korean.
doctrinal_weight: 進化 is the atlas's sharpest case of a calque importing not a residue but a counter-thesis: where most reverse-flow terms lose nuance, this one actively asserts something its source denies, embedding Spencerian progress into the standard name for a Darwinian theory of non-progressive descent. It demonstrates that the choice of morpheme is itself a doctrinal act — 進 versus a neutral 変 decides how an entire scientific paradigm will be understood — and that the consequences propagate wherever the word travels, jìnhuà and 진화 carrying the same built-in arrow into Chinese and Korean evolutionism.

false_friends.divergence: Chinese jìnhuà is the standard word for evolution, identical in graph and the same 進-vectored sense; both languages inherited the progressivist framing rather than a neutral 'change' calque.

進歩 (shinpo, 'progress') is the genuinely progressivist term; 進化 is supposed to be the value-neutral scientific one, yet its 進 morpheme keeps collapsing it toward 進歩 in popular use — the false friend lives inside the language itself.

coinage_notes: Meiji translators of Western liberal and political-economic literature, 1870s–1880s; the concept's ground prepared by Fukuzawa Yukichi's emphasis on personal independence (一身の独立) in Gakumon no Susume and by Nakamura Masanao's translation of J. S. Mill's On Liberty (自由之理, 1872); the compound stabilized as the standard rendering of 'individual' and carried into Chinese (gèrén) through Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings

components.meaning: the individuating classifier — 'the single one singled out from the mass'; here it does the decisive conceptual work, abstracting one bounded unit from the collective in which classical relational thought had always kept the person embedded
person, human being; supplies the human referent that 個 individuates — together: the person considered precisely as a discrete, self-standing unit rather than as a node in the web of relationships

translation_range.emphasis: standard universal rendering across political, economic, sociological, and ethical contexts

translation_range.rendering: the individual person / the single human unit
translation_range.emphasis: decompositional rendering that surfaces the literal force of 個 (the singled-out one) + 人 (person), useful for showing what the classical relational ontology had to be made to yield
adjectival/possessive register: 個人的意見 (personal opinion), 個人主義 (individualism), 個人情報 (personal data) — the sphere of the private as against the 公 (public) and the 集団 (collective)

conceptual_remainder: Classical East Asian thought had no standing word for 'the individual' because its social ontology never required the unit: the person was always already a son, a subject, an elder, a friend — a relatum within the five relationships (五倫), not a free-standing atom prior to them. 個人 had to manufacture exactly that atom. The translators' choice not to build the term on 人 (person) alone but on 個 — the grammatical classifier whose native job is to extract one discrete unit from an undifferentiated plurality — is the conceptual event: the compound performs at the level of the character the very abstraction the Western concept demands, lifting the single one out of the mass. What the characters carry well is precisely this individuating operation. What they cannot carry without strain is the normative weight the Western term had accreted — the individual as the seat of conscience, the rights-bearer prior to the state, the metaphysically self-grounding subject of liberal and Protestant lineage. In East Asian reception 個人 has therefore often been read with a faint privative or even pejorative shadow (the individual as the one cut off from the relational whole, 個人主義 sliding toward 'selfishness'), a connotation the European 'individual' does not natively carry. The compound's structural opposition to 社会 (society) and its pairing against 国家 (state) — the triangulation 個人 / 社会 / 国家 — is the frame within which modern East Asian political and ethical argument is conducted, and the relative weighting of the three has been one of the central contested questions of modern East Asian thought.
doctrinal_weight: 個人 is one of the load-bearing coinages of the modern East Asian conceptual order. Together with 社会 (society) and 国家 (state) it forms the basic triangle of modern political thought, and the question of how to weight the individual against the collective — debated from the Meiji enlightenment through the Freedom and People's Rights Movement, the early socialist movement, the Taishō-era discourse on personality (人格主義), the wartime ideology of the individual subsumed in the national body (滅私奉公), and the post-war constitutional enshrinement of individual dignity (個人の尊厳, Article 13 of the 1947 Constitution) — has been one of the organizing axes of modern Japanese, Chinese, and Korean intellectual and political history. The compound stands at the head of a large cluster: 個人主義 (individualism), 個人の自由 (individual liberty), 個人の権利 (individual rights), 個人の尊厳 (individual dignity), 個人情報 (personal information, now the operative term of contemporary data-privacy law). Its Chinese reception (gèrén) through Liang Qichao and the late-Qing reformist press, and its Korean reception (개인), made it the shared pan-East-Asian vocabulary in which the relation of person to collective is argued.

false_friends.divergence: 私 (watakushi / shi / sī) names the private, the personal-as-opposed-to-public (公), and by extension the selfish — it is the ethical-evaluative term for the partial and self-regarding. 個人 is by contrast structurally neutral: it names the unit, not a vice. Reading 個人 through 私 (as East Asian moralizing usage sometimes does, e.g. when 個人主義 is heard as mere 利己主義, egoism) imports an evaluative charge the Western 'individual' does not carry and collapses the descriptive social-ontological category into a moral failing.

個体 (kotai / gètǐ) is the biological/physical 'individual' — a single organism or discrete body, the unit of a species or population. It shares 個 with 個人 but lacks the moral-political subjecthood that is the whole point of 個人. Translating 'individual' into 個体 in a political or ethical context strips out exactly the rights-bearing, conscience-bearing register that 個人 was coined to carry.

coinage_notes: A classical Chinese compound (文化, 'transformation through refinement/letters,' as in 文化武功) re-semanticized by Meiji translators in the 1880s–1900s to render the German Kultur and the English ethnographic 'culture'; stabilized through academic philosophy and the Tetsugaku Jii lineage of translation lexica, and diffused into Chinese (wénhuà) and Korean (문화) as the standard term

components.meaning: the patterned, the lettered, the refined — the Confucian register of civil-aesthetic cultivation as against the raw or martial; supplies the 'cultivated/symbolic' content of the compound
transformation, becoming, the productive -ization morpheme — here 'the process by which the refined is brought about': culture as the transforming of the human into its cultivated form

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering across the anthropological, sociological, and humanistic senses

rendering that foregrounds the German Bildung-and-Herder lineage in which culture is the particular spiritual formation of a people, set against the outward technical advance of civilization — the contrast 文化/文明 inherits
the inherited classical sense of 文化 as moral transformation effected by refinement and letters (文化武功), surfaced to show the semantic substrate the modern coinage re-used
adjectival/institutional register: 文化財 (cultural property), 文化人類学 (cultural anthropology), 文化大革命 (Cultural Revolution)

conceptual_remainder: 文化 is not a fresh fabrication but a re-semanticized classical compound: in literary Chinese 文化 already meant the civilizing transformation worked by letters and refinement (the 文 pole of the 文/武 pair, paired with 化's transformation), as in the locution 文化武功 — to civilize by culture and to subdue by arms. Meiji and post-Meiji translators poured into this vessel the modern Western concept, and in doing so imported a tension the classical term did not contain: the German Kultur of the Bildung tradition is the inward, spiritual, particular-to-a-people register, deliberately opposed to the outward, universal, technical Zivilisation, while the English ethnographic 'culture' (Tylor's 'that complex whole') is a descriptive, value-neutral totality of learned behavior. The single coinage was made to carry both, partly conflating them. What the characters carry well is the cultivation/refinement register — 文 makes 'culture' legibly the domain of the lettered and the formed, which suits the Bildung sense. What the compound carries less easily is the value-neutral anthropological totality: 文's inherited evaluative gradient (the refined as against the barbarous) keeps culture from being fully descriptive, pulling it back toward 'high culture' and the cultivated. And the modern term's defining contrast with 文明 (civilization) — 文化 as the spiritual-particular against 文明 as the material-universal — is a calque of the German Kultur/Zivilisation polemic that East Asian usage inherited and continues to negotiate, often unstably, since the two compounds share neither the sharpness nor the political history of the German pair.
doctrinal_weight: 文化 became one of the central organizing categories of twentieth-century East Asian intellectual and political life. Its German-derived contrast with 文明 structured Taishō and interwar Japanese thought (the 文化主義, culturalism, of the Taishō intelligentsia; the wartime opposition of Japanese 文化 to Western 文明). Carried into Chinese as wénhuà, it became load-bearing across the May Fourth New Culture Movement (新文化運動) and, catastrophically, the Cultural Revolution (文化大革命). The compound heads an enormous productive cluster — 文化財 (cultural property, the operative term of heritage law), 文化人類学 (cultural anthropology), 文化交流 (cultural exchange), 多文化 (multicultural), 文化遺産 (cultural heritage) — and in the form 文化 it is now the shared pan-East-Asian word in which questions of identity, modernity, and the relation of the spiritual to the technical are posed.

false_friends.divergence: 文明 (bunmei / wénmíng / 문명) names civilization — the outward, cumulative, comparatively-graded condition of material and institutional advance, the developmental scale of Fukuzawa's Bunmeiron. 文化 by contrast names the inward, particular, spiritual-symbolic formation of a people. The pair calques the German Kultur/Zivilisation opposition, and conflating them — treating 文化 as merely a synonym for 文明 — erases the polemical distinction (the spiritual-particular against the material-universal) on which much modern East Asian self-understanding, including the wartime contrast of Japanese 文化 with Western 文明, was built.

coinage_notes: A classical Chinese compound (文明, 'the brightness of refinement,' attested in the Yijing and the canonical literature) re-semanticized in Meiji Japan to render the developmental Western concept of civilization; decisively popularized by Fukuzawa Yukichi's Bunmeiron no Gairyaku (文明論之概略, 1875), drawing on Guizot and Buckle, and crystallized in the era-slogan 文明開化; carried into Chinese (wénmíng) and Korean (문명) as the standard term

components.meaning: the patterned, lettered, refined — the human form raised above the raw; supplies the 'cultivated achievement' that civilization measures

brightness, clarity, the enlightened and manifest — supplies the developmental-evaluative light: civilization as the condition in which the human pattern has become bright, the metaphor of illumination doing the work of 'progress'

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering, especially in the developmental-comparative sense of Guizot, Buckle, and Fukuzawa — civilization as a graded condition along which peoples and epochs are ranked
the Meiji era-slogan: the programmatic opening into brightness, the watchword under which Westernizing modernization was pursued in the 1870s–1880s
the inherited Yijing/canonical sense of 文明 as the radiance of cultivated virtue, surfaced to show the classical substrate the Meiji concept re-used and re-charged

conceptual_remainder: 文明 is a re-charged classical term. In the Yijing and the canonical literature 文明 already named the brightness of refined virtue — the radiance that cultivated pattern (文) emits (明) — a static, value-laden description of a flourishing moral-aesthetic order. Meiji translators, above all Fukuzawa Yukichi in the Bunmeiron no Gairyaku (1875), poured into it the Western developmental concept drawn from Guizot's Histoire de la civilisation and Buckle's History of Civilization: civilization not as a static radiance but as a relative, cumulative, comparatively-graded process along which nations are ranked savage, semi-civilized, and civilized. The transformation is profound: an evaluative noun of moral flourishing becomes a developmental scale of national assessment. What the characters carry well is exactly the evaluative-luminous charge — 明 supplies the optimistic, teleological 'light dispelling darkness' imagery that the slogan 文明開化 (civilization-and-enlightenment, literally the opening into brightness) exploits, and that resonates with the era-name 明治 ('enlightened rule') itself. What the compound cannot natively carry is the sharp contrast the German tradition draws between Zivilisation (outward, material, universal) and Kultur (inward, spiritual, particular); East Asian usage had to install that contrast artificially across the 文明/文化 pair, and it sits less stably there than in German because both Sino-Japanese compounds share the honorific 文 and the inherited gradient of refinement-versus-barbarism. Fukuzawa's decisive and lasting contribution was to relativize the term: in his argument 文明 is not an absolute good but a means to the higher end of national independence — a move that gave the Meiji concept its characteristic strategic, comparative, and anxious charge, civilization as something Japan must consciously and competitively acquire.
doctrinal_weight: 文明 is arguably the single most consequential category of Meiji self-understanding. Through Fukuzawa's Bunmeiron no Gairyaku and the era-slogan 文明開化 it organized the entire program of Meiji modernization and Japan's anxious comparative positioning against the West; the developmental hierarchy it encoded (savage / semi-civilized / civilized) shaped Meiji and imperial-era thinking about Japan's place among nations, its civilizing mission in Asia, and the terms of treaty-revision diplomacy. Carried into Chinese as wénmíng, it became central to late-Qing and Republican reform discourse on China's standing in the world. The compound heads a large cluster — 文明開化, 文明国 (civilized nation), 物質文明 (material civilization), 精神文明 (spiritual civilization, a load-bearing term of contemporary PRC ideology, e.g. 精神文明建設), 文明社会 (civilized society) — and in the modern period the contemporary Chinese state's deployment of 文明 (as in 生態文明, ecological civilization) shows the term's continuing ideological productivity across East Asia.

false_friends.divergence: 文化 (bunka / wénhuà / 문화) names culture — the inward, particular, spiritual-symbolic formation of a people, the Kultur pole. 文明 names civilization — the outward, cumulative, comparatively-graded material-institutional advance, the Zivilisation pole. The two were made to calque the German polemical distinction; treating 文明 as a mere synonym of 文化 erases the developmental-comparative and material register (the graded scale of Fukuzawa's Bunmeiron) that is the whole point of 文明 and that 文化, with its inward-particular charge, does not carry.

開化 (kaika) names the act/process of opening-into-enlightenment — the dynamic verbal partner in the slogan 文明開化 — not the condition itself. Reading 文明 as if it were 開化 collapses the achieved state (civilization as a graded condition) into the transitional process of becoming civilized, losing the comparative-evaluative ranking that is 文明's distinctive Meiji function.

coinage_notes: A compound given its modern institutional meaning in Meiji Japan to render Western 'education' (Spencer's Education, widely read in translation; the 1872 Gakusei school-system ordinance), distinguishing it from the inherited Confucian vocabulary of moral transformation (教化) and self-cultivation (修身); bound to a national-moral mission by the Imperial Rescript on Education (1890) and carried into Chinese (jiàoyù) and Korean (교육) as the standard term

components.meaning: directed teaching, doctrine handed down — the rod-and-transmission register; supplies the top-down, content-transmitting, morally-forming pole of the compound (cf. the inherited 教化, transformation through teaching)

rearing, nourishing, the bringing-up of the young — the growth-from-below register; supplies the organic, cultivating, capacity-drawing-out pole, holding the compound in tension between transmission and development

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering for the modern institutional concept — schooling organized as a public, national system

decompositional rendering surfacing the two metaphors held in suspension: 教 (doctrine handed down) + 育 (the child grown), the contest between transmission and cultivation that the term's modern history enacts
institutional/adjectival register: 教育制度 (education system), 義務教育 (compulsory education), 教育勅語 (the Imperial Rescript on Education), 高等教育 (higher education)

conceptual_remainder: 教育 fuses two characters whose pull is opposite: 教 is directed transmission — the rod, the doctrine handed down from above, the register of the inherited 教化 (moral transformation worked by the suasion of superiors) — while 育 is organic nurture, the rearing and drawing-out of growth from below. The Western concept the Meiji period needed to render was specifically the modern institutional one: schooling as a state-organized national system, theorized by Spencer and embodied in the 1872 Gakusei ordinance, a thing the inherited vocabulary of Confucian moral cultivation (教化, 修身) named only in part. What the compound carries well is precisely the doubled metaphor — it can hold 'education' as both the transmission of authorized content and the cultivation of the learner's own capacities. But that very doubleness is also the term's unresolved remainder: the whole modern history of 教育 in East Asia can be read as a contest over which pole dominates. The Spencerian, developmentalist reading foregrounds 育 — education as the unfolding of the person. The Imperial-Rescript reading, which became institutionally decisive in Japan after 1890, foregrounds 教 — education as the state's transmission of a loyalist-Confucian moral content, recited before the imperial portrait. The Western 'education' / Bildung carried a charge of individual self-formation that the 教-dominant institutionalization in modern East Asia tended to subordinate to national-moral ends; conversely, the term's 育 pole keeps available, latently, a developmental and child-centered reading that post-war and progressive pedagogy could and did reactivate.
doctrinal_weight: 教育 is one of the institutionally heaviest Meiji coinages, naming the entire apparatus of the modern national school system that the Meiji state built from the 1872 Gakusei ordinance onward as a central instrument of nation-building and 文明開化. Its binding to state ideology in the Imperial Rescript on Education (1890) — recited in every school before the imperial portrait until 1948 — made 教育 the principal site at which the modern history of East Asian schooling, and the contest between schooling as Western-style human formation and schooling as state-directed moral-loyalist cultivation, was institutionally fought out; the post-war Fundamental Law of Education (教育基本法, 1947, revised 2006) re-adjudicated the same question. The compound heads a vast cluster — 義務教育 (compulsory education), 教育制度 (education system), 教育勅語 (Imperial Rescript on Education), 教育基本法, 高等教育 (higher education), 教育学 (pedagogy), 社会教育 (social/adult education) — and in the form 教育 / jiàoyù / 교육 it is the shared pan-East-Asian term in which the relation of the person, the school, and the state continues to be argued.

false_friends.divergence: 教化 (kyōka / jiàohuà) is the inherited Confucian term for moral transformation worked through teaching — the suasion by which superiors form the character of inferiors, a diffuse moral-civilizing influence, not an institution. 教育 by contrast names the modern organized school system. Reading 教育 through 教化 (as the Imperial-Rescript settlement effectively did) collapses institutional schooling into state moral-ideological formation, suppressing the developmental, capacity-cultivating register that 育 contributes and that distinguishes the modern concept from Confucian moral suasion.

修身 (shūshin / xiūshēn) is the classical Confucian 'cultivation of the self' — the person's own ethical self-rectification, the inward work of the Great Learning. It names self-formation, not the rearing of others through an institution. 教育 is transitive and institutional (one educates others, the state educates the nation); collapsing 教育 into 修身 loses both the institutional-systemic dimension and the other-directed transmission that the modern concept centrally requires.

coinage_notes: Meiji translators of the 1870s (treaty and Meiroku-era usage); standardized by the philosophical lexicons of the 1880s (Inoue Tetsujirō et al., Tetsugaku Jii); introduced to Chinese intellectual discourse via Liang Qichao and other Japan-trained writers

components.meaning: ancestral hall → lineage, sect, school; what one takes as fundamental — frames 'religion' as a transmitted doctrinal sect
teaching, doctrine, instruction — the directed handing-down of a content

translation_range.emphasis: the standard, near-universal rendering across modern East Asian usage
adjectival form: 宗教的経験 (religious experience), 宗教改革 (the Reformation)
residual older sense, surviving in 宗派 — the seam where the coinage shows its Buddhist-sectarian origin

conceptual_remainder: Classical East Asia had specific 教 ('teachings' — 仏教, 儒教) and 宗 ('schools, sects') but no superordinate genus under which Buddhism, Confucianism, Shintō, and Christianity stood as co-equal instances. 宗教 manufactures that genus, and in doing so it imports the post-Reformation European assumption that a religion is a bounded, doctrinally defined, voluntary community of belief — a template that fits Christianity and the Buddhist 宗 but distorts diffuse ancestral and Shintō practice, which the new category could only register as deficient or 'not really religion.' The word thus did not neutrally name an existing thing; it created the conceptual slot into which the Meiji state could then sort, license, and discipline 'religions' — and exempt State Shintō by declaring it non-religious.
doctrinal_weight: One of the most consequential reverse-flow coinages, because the category it created became an instrument of governance. Once 宗教 existed, the state could constitutionally 'guarantee religious freedom' while administratively defining what counted as 宗教, a maneuver central to the construction of State Shintō. Carried into Chinese (zōngjiào) and Korean (종교), it reorganized the entire field of belief and practice across East Asia around a Western, largely Protestant, prototype.

coinage_notes: Classical/Buddhist binome re-coined for the political concept; Fukuzawa Yukichi (Seiyō Jijō, 1866–1870, with an explanatory note distinguishing it from 我儘) and Nakamura Masanao (Jiyū no Kotowari, his 1872 translation of Mill's On Liberty)

components.meaning: self, oneself, from — the originating point of the action
to proceed from, by way of, the ground/cause — the channel through which it issues

translation_range.emphasis: the political-philosophical value, as in 自由主義 (liberalism), 言論の自由 (freedom of speech)
the broader condition of being unconstrained; largely coextensive in modern usage
adjectival and adverbial; here the older colloquial 'as one likes' still faintly resonates

conceptual_remainder: The translators did not coin a new word; they conscripted an existing binome that meant 'doing as one pleases,' frequently with the disreputable colour of willful self-indulgence (close to 我儘, 放埒). Fukuzawa felt obliged to append a note in Seiyō Jijō warning that 自由 here does not mean licentious self-will but acting freely without infringing others — an admission that the chosen word carried exactly the wrong connotation and had to be actively re-trained. What 自由 cannot natively carry is the specifically liberal architecture of liberty as a right held against the state and bounded by law; that scaffolding had to be supplied by the surrounding texts (Mill via Nakamura) rather than by the characters, which say only 'proceeding-from-self.'
doctrinal_weight: The keyword of Meiji liberalism and of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動), and the name of Japan's first political party (自由党, 1881). Its semantic instability — liberty versus license — was not a translator's failure but a live political fault line, exploited by both the movement and its state opponents. Re-exported to Chinese (zìyóu) and Korean (자유), it became the standard East Asian term for both 'freedom' and 'liberty,' carrying its productive ambiguity with it.

coinage_notes: Classical compound for graded rank re-coined for the sociological concept through Meiji translations of European social theory; sharpened into the Marxist sense by early Japanese socialists (Kōtoku Shūsui, Sakai Toshihiko) and economists (Kawakami Hajime)

components.meaning: stepped ascent of a terrace → grade, tier, rank in an ordered series
rung in a graded scale → grade, rank, class

translation_range.emphasis: the general sociological sense: 中産階級 (middle class), 支配階級 (ruling class)
the antagonistic structural sense: 階級闘争 (class struggle), 労働者階級 (the working class)
older inherited sense surviving in 位階 and military 階級 (rank)

conceptual_remainder: The compound's internal image is a ladder — steps (階) and rungs (級) — a graduated scale of station inherited from the bureaucratic rank system. That picture fits a hierarchy of honour but misrepresents the European concept it was made to carry: 'class' in the Marxist sense is not a higher or lower rung but a structural relation to the means of production, and an antagonistic one. Rendering it as 階級 quietly substitutes vertical gradation for structural relation, so the conflictual core of the concept (that classes are constituted by and against each other) has to be carried by the surrounding rhetoric — 闘争, 搾取 — rather than by the word itself. It also had to be insulated from the older 身分 (ascribed status by birth), with which it shares the imagery of fixed station.
doctrinal_weight: Became the central category of Japanese socialist and Marxist discourse and, through the immense influence of Japanese Marxism on Chinese revolutionaries, of Chinese political language as well. Carried into Chinese (jiējí) and Korean (계급), 階級 supplied the lexical backbone of twentieth-century revolutionary analysis across East Asia — 階級闘争 (class struggle), 無産階級 (the proletariat) — its bureaucratic-ladder etymology entirely submerged beneath its Marxist charge.

coinage_notes: Re-coined by Nagayo Sensai (長與專齋, c. 1872–1875) from the Zhuangzi's 衛生之經, to translate the German administrative field of Gesundheitspflege / public health; institutionalized in the name of the Home Ministry's Sanitary Bureau (衛生局, 1875)

components.meaning: to guard, ward, safeguard by circuit — protection as active warding
life, the living — the object now placed under collective guard

translation_range.emphasis: the everyday sense: 衛生的 (hygienic), 衛生管理 (sanitation control)
the administrative-institutional sense Nagayo intended: 公衆衛生, 衛生局 (Sanitary Bureau)
the concrete infrastructural register: drainage, water, epidemic control

conceptual_remainder: In the Zhuangzi, 衛生 names an inward Daoist art — the guarding and nourishing of one's own vitality, a regimen of the self. Nagayo's re-coinage keeps the dignified surface of the classical phrase but inverts its orientation: the guarded object is no longer the practitioner's own life but the aggregate health of a population, and the guarding agent is not the self but the administrative state with its statistics, drains, and quarantine. What the elegant old word cannot carry is exactly this collective, governmental, quantified character; the term's classical resonance even works against it, suggesting personal regimen where a public apparatus is meant.
doctrinal_weight: The lexical foundation of the modern East Asian public-health state. By naming public health with a Zhuangzi phrase, Nagayo gave a Western administrative technology an unimpeachably classical pedigree, easing its institutional adoption. Re-exported to Chinese (wèishēng) and Korean (위생), 衛生 became the universal term for hygiene and public health, and its compounds (公衆衛生, 衛生学) the standard vocabulary of sanitary administration across the region.

coinage_notes: Fukuzawa Yukichi (福澤諭吉), Kaigiben (会議弁, 1874) and Gakumon no Susume vol. 12 (学問のすゝめ 第十二編, 1874); institutionalized at the Mita Speech Society (三田演説会, founded 1874) and Japan's first dedicated speech hall, 三田演説館 (1875)

components.meaning: to draw out at length, develop, extend — water flowing on; the time-extended unfolding of a thought before listeners
to speak, expound, set forth a doctrine — articulated speech that opens a matter to an interlocutor

translation_range.emphasis: the core sense Fukuzawa installed: a deliberate, time-extended address before a gathered audience as the medium of civic deliberation (政治演説, 街頭演説)
the academic and ceremonial register: 記念演説 (commemorative address), 演説会 (a public lecture meeting)
the verbal 演説する, with a faint pejorative possibility when the speech is grandstanding or empty

conceptual_remainder: Pre-modern Japan had many varieties of formal address — the Buddhist sermon (説法), the Confucian lecture (講義), the dharma talk (提唱), the court memorial — but none of these was a secular, deliberative, time-extended speech before a gathered citizenry. Fukuzawa was inventing, not merely naming, the practice; the new compound 演説 had to carry both 'public speech' as a translatable noun and 'public oratory as a civic activity not previously practiced in Japan' as an instituted form. The Sino-Japanese components are neutral and dignified — 演 (extended development) joined to 説 (exposition) — and read naturally as 'extended exposition,' which is exactly the procedural shape Fukuzawa wanted to install. What the characters cannot carry is the specifically deliberative civic context in which Western oratory makes sense: a parliament that votes, a press that reports, a public that deliberates. That context had to be supplied by the surrounding institutions Fukuzawa built around the word — the Mita Speech Society, the speech hall, the parliamentary-procedure manual — without which 演説 might have meant only 'extended exposition' in the manner of 説法 or 講義.
doctrinal_weight: The keyword of Meiji civic and political culture and the lexical foundation of modern Japanese parliamentary procedure. By coining 演説 alongside 討論 (debate), 動議 (motion), and 賛成 (second), Fukuzawa installed in Japan a complete procedural vocabulary for deliberative assembly; when the Imperial Diet opened in 1890, its members already had a Japanese vocabulary for what they would do there. Re-exported to Chinese (yǎnshuō, the standard term across Republican-era political culture) and Korean (연설), 演説 became the universal modern East Asian word for public oratory, and its compounds (演説会, 街頭演説, 政治演説) supplied the standing vocabulary of twentieth-century political speech across the region.

coinage_notes: Classical Chinese compound 廣告 ('to inform widely') re-fitted to the institutional category of paid commercial publicity through the editorial practice of the first generation of Meiji daily newspapers (横浜毎日新聞 1871; 東京日日新聞 1872; 郵便報知新聞 1872; Fukuzawa Yukichi's 時事新報 1882); standardized in Meiji commercial law (Shōhō, 1899) and corporate practice (株式広告)

components.meaning: wide, broad, spreading to many — the breadth of an open hall, extended to mass diffusion
to inform, announce, notify — the act of bringing a matter to another's knowledge

translation_range.emphasis: the standard sense — a paid commercial notice in print, broadcast, or digital media (新聞広告, テレビ広告, インターネット広告)
the activity and industry: 広告主 (the advertiser), 広告代理店 (advertising agency), 広告業 (the advertising business)
the residual older sense, surviving in legal-administrative 公告 ('official public announcement') from which 広告 had to be distinguished as the commercial counterpart

conceptual_remainder: The classical compound 広告 / 廣告 already existed in literary Chinese with the bare sense 'to inform widely' — to issue a notice that reaches many — and the Meiji repurposing keeps that surface intact. What is added is the specifically commercial, paid, mass-mediated institutional content: the paid newspaper column, the broadside posted in the street, the magazine insert, the radio spot, the standardized format of an advertising agency's account. The Sino-Japanese characters carry only the 'inform widely' kernel; the entire apparatus of paid placement, brand competition, audience segmentation, and persuasive design that turns a notice into modern advertising has to be supplied by the surrounding commercial-print economy. The split with 公告 (administrative public announcement) shows the seam: when the same root concept had to do both commercial-paid notice and state-administrative notice, the modern usage allocated 広告 to commerce and reserved 公告 for the state, freeing 広告 to carry the full freight of mass-media commercial publicity.
doctrinal_weight: The lexical foundation of the modern East Asian advertising and mass-media economy. By binding paid commercial publicity to the dignified classical compound 広告 rather than to a vernacular term like ちらし (handbill) or 引札 (Edo merchant's flyer), the Meiji newspapers gave the new institutional category an unimpeachably literate face, easing its integration into commercial law and corporate practice. Re-exported to Chinese (廣告 / 广告 guǎnggào) and Korean (광고), 広告 became the universal modern East Asian word for advertisement, and its derivatives (広告主, 広告代理店, 広告効果) supplied the operating vocabulary of twentieth-century commercial publicity across the region.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical lexicography of the 1880s — the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, Inoue Tetsujirō et al., 1881) lists 理想 as the standard rendering of 'Ideal'; literary-critical adoption by Tsubouchi Shōyō (坪内逍遥) in Shōsetsu Shinzui (小説神髄, 1885–86), where 理想 becomes the keyword of the new Japanese debate between idealism and realism

components.meaning: principle, ordering pattern, the rational ground — the structuring logic of things
thought, conception, the form an object takes in mind — image-thought, the heart taking on the aspect of what it considers

translation_range.emphasis: the philosophical and everyday sense: 理想的 (ideal), 理想像 (ideal image), 理想と現実 (ideal and reality)
the philosophical and literary-critical doctrine of pursuing the ideal — opposed to 写実主義 (realism) in Tsubouchi's terms and to 現実主義 in political vocabulary
the everyday sense of an aspiration held forth as a model: 理想を抱く (to cherish an ideal), 高い理想 (a lofty ideal)

conceptual_remainder: The Western Ideal — especially in its Kantian-and-after technical sense — is the rational projection of perfection in concrete exemplary form, distinct from the bare logical Idee and from the abstract Begriff. Japanese had to carry this distinction across a small family of new compounds: 理想 (Ideal), 観念 (Idee), 概念 (Begriff), 理念 (the German Idee in its later normative sense). 理想 reads literally as 'principle-image,' and the 想 element keeps it productively close to the imaginative-projective register — one envisions an ideal, one does not merely entertain it as a concept. What the characters cannot natively carry is the specifically Kantian architecture in which der Ideal is an idea of reason concretely individuated as an exemplar (the wise person, the perfect republic) and not merely an admired aim; nor can they carry the polemical European charge of Idealismus against materialism. That scaffolding had to be supplied by the surrounding translations (Inoue's Tetsugaku Jii pairs 理想 with the English headword and lets the German vocabulary do the conceptual work behind the scenes) and by the literary-critical context (Tsubouchi's Shōsetsu Shinzui, where 理想 names the moralizing didactic aim of the old novel and 写実 the new mimetic ambition).
doctrinal_weight: The lexical anchor of modern East Asian discussion of ideals, idealism, and the gap between aspiration and reality. Through the Tetsugaku Jii 理想 entered the operating philosophical vocabulary of Meiji and later Japanese academic philosophy as the standard rendering of der Ideal; through Tsubouchi's Shōsetsu Shinzui it became the keyword of the long literary-critical debate between 理想主義 and 写実主義 that runs through twentieth-century Japanese, Chinese, and Korean literary thought. Re-exported to Chinese (lǐxiǎng) and Korean (이상), the compound supplies the universal modern East Asian word for the ideal, and 理想主義 supplies the standard term for idealism across the region's philosophical and political vocabulary.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical and pedagogical writing of the 1870s–1880s: Nishi Amane's lexical work, the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) as the principal lexicographic stabilization, and the educational vocabulary of the 1872 Gakusei (Fukuzawa Yukichi's 学問の目的 — 'the purpose of learning' — is among the most-circulated early uses, in Gakumon no Susume)

components.meaning: the eye — that which sees and fixes on a mark
the bull's-eye, the painted mark on the target — the precise point at which the eye is aimed

translation_range.emphasis: the everyday and the philosophical sense alike: 目的を達する (achieve one's purpose), 研究の目的 (the aim of the research), 目的論 (teleology)
the Aristotelian-Kantian τέλος / Zweck: 目的因 (final cause), 目的と手段 (ends and means)
the concrete spatial sense surviving in 目的地 (destination), where the 'mark on which the eye is set' becomes the place toward which one travels

conceptual_remainder: 目的 is a graphically perfect rendering — the eye (目) fixed upon a target (的) is the very picture of intending — and the compound was so immediately legible that it crossed without seam into colloquial, technical, and philosophical use. What the bull's-eye image cannot do, however, is carry the specifically teleological metaphysics that the European Zweck inherits from Aristotle and Kant: the idea that natural processes and rational agency alike are intelligible only as directed toward ends, that the end is the cause of the process in a strong metaphysical sense (causa finalis). The Japanese compound reads instrumentally — purpose as the agent's chosen mark — and the deeper teleological sense has to be borne by surrounding terminology (目的論 'teleology,' 目的因 'final cause') and by the philosophical contexts in which 目的 is deployed. The same instrumental clarity, however, makes 目的 unusually serviceable across philosophy, education, law, commerce, and everyday speech: the same word can name a Kantian rational end, the goal of a school's curriculum, the object of a contract, and the destination of a trip.
doctrinal_weight: One of the most successful Meiji philosophical coinages by sheer range of adoption. Within decades 目的 was the standard Japanese word for purpose across every register of writing — philosophical (目的論, the Aristotelian-Kantian teleology), pedagogical (教育の目的, the purpose of education), legal (契約の目的, the object of a contract), military and administrative (作戦目的, operational objective), and colloquial. Re-exported to Chinese (mùdì) and Korean (목적), it became the universal modern East Asian word for purpose, and its derivatives (目的論, 目的地, 目的意識) became standard across the region's intellectual and everyday vocabulary alike.

coinage_notes: Meiji government exposition office (博覧会事務局), 1872, in the official Japanese translation of the German exhibition regulations for the 1873 Vienna World Exposition; rendered the German 'bildende Kunst' / 'Kunstwerke' as 美術 in the institutional context that required a single Japanese term to bound the Western category of 'fine art' as a category; the term was then institutionalized through the Naimushō's Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai (Domestic Industrial Exhibitions, from 1877) and through the Tokyo Bijutsu Gakkō (東京美術学校, founded 1887 under Okakura Tenshin and Ernest Fenollosa) as the operating Japanese term for fine art

components.meaning: beauty / the beautiful — the classical broad value-term for the fine, excellent, and beautiful, here narrowed by the disciplinary 術 to specifically aesthetic-visual production

trained procedure / craft / discipline — supplies the 'art-as-trained-practice' that converts the value-noun 美 into a domain of cultivated production: the fine arts as a discipline rather than 'the beautiful' as a value

translation_range.emphasis: standard institutional rendering — the bounded domain of painting, sculpture, architecture, drawing, and printmaking as a single category

the institutional sense — what is shown in the 美術館 (art museum), taught in the 美術学校 (art school), and produced by the 美術家 (visual artist); 美術 is the art of the institutional apparatus rather than the broader aesthetic-philosophical category 芸術

the German source-concept rendering, preserving the specifically visual-plastic register against the redenden Künste (word and tone) — the contrast that originally motivated the Japanese coinage at the Vienna Exposition

conceptual_remainder: 美術 is one of the most precisely datable Meiji coinages: it was minted in 1872 by the Meiji government's exposition office for the specific institutional task of translating the German exhibition categories of the 1873 Vienna World Exposition, where Japan had to organize its pavilion within the European apparatus of fine-art classification. The Western category of 'fine art' as a bounded, autonomous domain — painting, sculpture, architecture, drawing, engraving, set off from craft, design, entertainment, and industry — was an eighteenth-century European institutional achievement (Batteux's 1746 systematization, the academies of beaux-arts, Kant's third Critique, the nineteenth-century museum). Pre-Meiji Japan possessed an extraordinary range of cultivated visual practices (painting in multiple schools, calligraphy, sculpture, lacquer, ceramics, garden art, the tea ceremony's material culture) but no concept that bounded a subset of these as 'fine art' distinct from craft (工芸). The Vienna Exposition's bureaucratic requirement that a single Japanese term render 'bildende Kunst' forced the conceptual sorting that the Western category presupposed, and 美術 was the term that did the sorting. What 美術 carries well is exactly the bounded-institutional register: it is the operating term of the museum, the art school, the gallery, the exhibition, the academy. What the term cannot carry without strain is the broader aesthetic-philosophical category of 'art as such' (Kunst in its Kantian-Hegelian register, the totality of aesthetic production across all media) — for that, the Meiji vocabulary developed the separate compound 芸術, which now stands to 美術 roughly as Kunst stands to bildende Kunst. The 芸術 / 美術 pair lets Japanese carry a German distinction that English collapses into the single ambiguous word 'art.' A further conceptual remainder: the very act of bounding 'fine art' as a separate category from craft (工芸) produced, in late-Meiji and Taishō Japan, a long polemical reaction in which figures like Yanagi Sōetsu (the mingei movement, 1920s–30s) argued that the fine-art / craft division was itself a Western imposition that distorted the indigenous Japanese understanding of aesthetic production — a reaction that lives on in the perennial contemporary East Asian debate about the relation of 美術 to 工芸.
doctrinal_weight: 美術 is one of the load-bearing institutional categories of modern East Asian culture. The term organized the Meiji and modern Japanese fine-arts apparatus from its 1872 coinage onward: the Naimushō Industrial Exhibitions (内国勧業博覧会, from 1877) classified their visual-arts submissions under 美術; the Tokyo Bijutsu Gakkō (1887) became the foundational state academy; the Bunten (文部省美術展覧会, from 1907) and its successors became the state-sanctioned annual fine-arts exhibition; and the modern Japanese museum system (the Tokyo National Museum's 美術部 and the major prefectural and metropolitan 美術館) institutionalized the category. The compound also heads the productive 美術 cluster: 美術館 (art museum), 美術家 (artist), 美術品 (artwork as object), 美術史 (art history as discipline), 美術評論 (art criticism). Re-exported into Chinese (měishù 美术) and Korean (misul 미술), it became the standard pan-East-Asian term for the fine arts, with the parallel institutional apparatus (the National Art Museum of China, the Korean National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art) organized around the imported category. The relation of 美術 to its older partner 工芸 (kōgei, craft) and its newer partner 芸術 (geijutsu, art-in-general) is one of the central conceptual questions of modern East Asian aesthetics.

false_friends.divergence: 芸術 (geijutsu / yìshù / yesul) names art in the broadest aesthetic-philosophical sense — the Kantian-Hegelian Kunst, the totality of aesthetic production across all media (visual, plastic, literary, musical, performative). 美術 is the narrower institutional-visual category — bildende Kunst, the fine arts of the museum and academy. Conflating the two erases a distinction that modern Japanese carries with some precision: a poem is 芸術 but not 美術; a sculpture is both. English 'art' collapses both compounds into a single ambiguous word, and translating either 美術 or 芸術 simply as 'art' loses the institutional-versus-philosophical distinction the Japanese pair carries.

工芸 (kōgei / gōngyì / gongye) names craft — the applied or decorative arts (ceramics, lacquer, textiles, metalwork) that the Western fine-art / craft division opposed to fine art. The Meiji coinage 美術 was constituted by precisely this exclusion: 美術 is what 工芸 is not, the institutional bounding that lets the museum hold one and the design-school hold the other. The Yanagi Sōetsu mingei movement (1920s–30s) and broader Taishō-Showa craft-revival discourse argued that the 美術 / 工芸 division was a Western institutional imposition that mis-described the indigenous Japanese understanding of aesthetic production — a perennial polemical fault-line in modern East Asian aesthetics.

coinage_notes: A classical Chinese compound (文学, one of the four Confucian subjects 孔門四科 meaning 'the cultivation of letters / literary learning') re-semanticized in Meiji Japan to render the modern Western disciplinary category of literature; stabilized through the establishment of the Bungakubu (faculty of letters) at Tokyo Imperial University in 1877 and through critical works of the 1880s, most decisively Tsubouchi Shōyō's Shōsetsu Shinzui (1885–86), which argued for the novel (小説) as a serious aesthetic genre and inaugurated modern Japanese literary criticism; carried into Chinese (wénxué) and Korean (munhak) through late-Qing and colonial-period academic transmission

components.meaning: the patterned, lettered, refined — supplies the 'letters' content of the compound: literature as the domain of the written and the cultivated
learning / study / academic discipline — the workhorse Meiji suffix for the named academic disciplines; supplies the 'discipline' that converts 'letters' into 'literature as a field of study'

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering of literature as the modern Western aesthetic-cultural category — the body of imaginative written art (poetry, drama, the novel, the essay) considered as a single domain
the academic-disciplinary register: 文学部 (faculty of letters), 国文学 (national / Japanese literature as a university discipline), 比較文学 (comparative literature), 文学研究 (literary scholarship)

the inherited classical Confucian sense of 文学 as one of the four Confucian subjects (孔門四科: 徳行 conduct, 言語 speech, 政事 government, 文学 letters) — the cultivation of literary learning in the broad sense of polite written culture, surfaced to show the conceptual substrate the modern coinage re-charged
adjectival register: 文学的価値 (literary value), 文学賞 (literary prize, e.g. 芥川賞, 直木賞, ノーベル文学賞 Nobel Prize in Literature)

conceptual_remainder: 文学 is one of the most consequential Meiji recharges of a classical compound. In Confucian usage 文学 named one of the four 孔門四科 subjects under Confucius — the cultivation of letters in the broad sense of polite written culture, including the classical canon, historical writing, philosophical commentary, and the literary arts undifferentiated. The modern Western category of literature as a bounded aesthetic-imaginative domain — separated from history, philosophy, religious writing, and 'mere' polite letters and organized around the criterion of imaginative-aesthetic value — was a late-eighteenth- and nineteenth-century European achievement, constituted through the Romantic valorization of the imaginative work, the consolidation of national literary canons (Nationalliteratur, English literature, littérature nationale), and the academic institutionalization of literary studies. Meiji translators poured this narrower modern category into the inherited compound, and Tsubouchi Shōyō's Shōsetsu Shinzui (1885–86) was the decisive critical text that bounded the new sense: literature as the imaginative-aesthetic genre whose proper object is the depiction of human emotion (人情) and social conditions (世態) as they actually are, freed from the didactic-moral obligations of the Edo gesaku tradition. What 文学 carries well is the cultivated-letters register — 文 makes literature legibly the domain of the formed and the refined, which aligns with the European Romantic valorization of the literary work as an achievement of cultivated form. What the compound carries less easily is the Western category's specific autonomy from didactic, moral, and religious purposes (the inherited Confucian 文 is never simply autonomous: it always bears moral-civilizational weight), and the long Meiji-Taishō literary-critical project — Tsubouchi's argument against kanzen-chōaku, the Naturalist generation's insistence on 自然主義 (Naturalism) and the I-novel (私小説), Sōseki and Ōgai's negotiations with Western aesthetic categories — can be read as the sustained working-out of this conceptual remainder.
doctrinal_weight: 文学 became one of the load-bearing organizing categories of modern East Asian cultural and academic life. The compound institutionalizes the modern academic discipline of literary studies (文学部 as faculty of letters, the standard university unit across modern East Asia) and the broader cultural category of imaginative writing as an autonomous aesthetic domain. The Meiji critical-literary project that the Shōsetsu Shinzui inaugurated produced the modern Japanese novel (近代小説) and the modern Japanese literary-critical tradition, with the long debate between 写実主義 (realism) and 理想主義 (idealism), Naturalism (自然主義), the I-novel (私小説), Mori Ōgai's and Natsume Sōseki's negotiations with Western aesthetic categories, the Shirakaba school's humanism, the proletarian-literature movement of the 1920s–30s, the postwar generations, and the contemporary international Japanese literary scene all proceeding from the conceptual frame the Meiji 文学 stabilized. Re-exported into Chinese (wénxué) through the May Fourth literary-reform movement and the broader twentieth-century Chinese literary-critical tradition, and into Korean (munhak), the compound became the universal pan-East-Asian word for literature as a modern discipline. The compound heads a substantial cluster: 文学部, 文学者, 文学賞, 文学史 (literary history), 国文学, 比較文学, 文学的, the operating vocabulary of the entire modern East Asian literary apparatus.

false_friends.divergence: 文芸 (bungei / wényì / muneye) names 'literature and the arts' (or 'belles-lettres' in a slightly broader register), preserving more of the older inclusive sense of literary-and-cultivated production across genres. 文学 in its modern sense is narrower and more disciplinary — literature as the bounded aesthetic-imaginative category organized as a university discipline. The distinction is uneven and the two terms overlap considerably in usage, but 文芸 tends to retain the broader literary-cultural sense (文芸誌 'literary magazine,' 文芸春秋 the magazine title, 文芸復興 'literary renaissance') while 文学 tends toward the disciplinary-aesthetic sense.

coinage_notes: Meiji philosophical and aesthetic translation of the 1880s–1890s; the compound combines the classical 芸 (cultivated capacity, as in the Confucian 六藝) with 術 (trained procedure) and was stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Tokyo Imperial University academic philosophy lineage as the operating Japanese term for art in the unified Kantian-Hegelian Kunst sense — the totality of aesthetic production across all media — distinct from the narrower institutional 美術; the term was given decisive aesthetic-critical content through Mori Ōgai's translations and aesthetic writings of the 1890s–1900s and through the broader Meiji-Taishō academic-aesthetic apparatus

components.meaning: cultivated capacity / cultivated art — the inherited Confucian sense of 六藝 (the six arts), the disciplined cultivation of a formed skill; here it supplies the cultivated-capacity ground that 術 turns into a domain of trained production
trained procedure / discipline / craft — the workhorse Meiji suffix for the named arts and techniques; here it specifies 芸 as a domain of formed practice rather than just a generic cultivation

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering of art in the broad aesthetic-philosophical sense — the unified domain of aesthetic production across all media (painting, sculpture, music, literature, theatre, dance)

the German source-concept rendering — art as the autonomous philosophical-aesthetic category of the third Critique, Schiller's aesthetic letters, Hegel's Aesthetics; the conceptual frame within which the Meiji compound was stabilized

translation_range.rendering: the arts (in the curricular / institutional sense)
translation_range.emphasis: the institutional register: 芸術大学 (university of the arts, e.g. 東京芸術大学), 芸術祭 (arts festival), 芸術家 (artist in the broad sense across media), the operating term for the broader arts as an institutional field
adjectival register: 芸術的価値 (artistic value), 芸術運動 (artistic movement), 芸術院 (Japan Art Academy)

conceptual_remainder: 芸術 sits to 美術 roughly as Kunst sits to bildende Kunst, or as 'art' sits to 'fine arts': the broader, more philosophically loaded category that includes the institutional fine arts but extends to all aesthetic production. The compound's etymological resources are precisely calibrated for this work. 芸 (in its full traditional form 藝) carries the inherited Confucian sense of cultivated capacity — the 六藝 of the gentleman's curriculum — which gives the compound a depth of cultivated-tradition that the narrowly institutional 美術 does not have. 術 supplies the trained-discipline register that converts 芸 into a domain of formed practice rather than a generic cultivation. The result is a compound that reads as 'cultivated practice as a unified domain' — a precise rendering of the Kantian-Hegelian Kunst. What 芸術 carries well is the philosophical-aesthetic depth: the long Meiji-Taishō academic aesthetic tradition (Mori Ōgai's translations of Hartmann and the German aesthetic tradition; Ōnishi Yoshinori's mid-twentieth-century aesthetic theory; the postwar Kyoto School aesthetic engagements) uses 芸術 across philosophical-aesthetic argumentation in a way that 美術 cannot bear. What the compound carries less well is the precise institutional bounding that 美術 supplies for the museum-and-academy apparatus — 芸術 is too broad and too philosophically charged for routine institutional classification, so the Meiji apparatus tended to use 美術 for the institutional category and reserve 芸術 for the broader philosophical-aesthetic discourse. The pair 芸術 / 美術 thus reproduces in modern Japanese a distinction the European tradition carries (Kunst / bildende Kunst, art / the fine arts) and that English largely collapses into a single ambiguous term.
doctrinal_weight: 芸術 is the operating term of modern East Asian philosophical aesthetics and broad-arts discourse. The compound organizes the long Meiji-Taishō academic-aesthetic tradition (Mori Ōgai's translation work, Ōnishi Yoshinori's Aesthetics, the Kyoto School's aesthetic writings) and the broader twentieth-century Japanese arts-critical apparatus (the Geijutsuin 芸術院 Japan Art Academy founded 1907, the Tokyo University of the Arts 東京芸術大学 formed 1949, the Geijutsu-sai 芸術祭 Arts Festival series). Re-exported to Chinese (yìshù 艺术) and Korean (yesul 예술), it became the standard pan-East-Asian word for art in the broad aesthetic sense, with the parallel academic-aesthetic and arts-institutional apparatus organized around the imported category. The pair 芸術 / 美術 reproduces in modern East Asian discourse the Kunst / bildende Kunst distinction of the German aesthetic tradition, and the relative weighting of the two terms across the various national-academic and institutional contexts (Japanese discourse tends to maintain the distinction more sharply than Chinese, where 艺术 has largely absorbed the broader semantic range) is a productive site for tracking the differential reception of European aesthetic categories across modern East Asia.

false_friends.divergence: 美術 (bijutsu / měishù / misul) names the fine arts in the bounded institutional sense — bildende Kunst, the visual-plastic arts of the museum and academy. 芸術 is the broader aesthetic-philosophical category — Kunst, the totality of aesthetic production across all media including literature, music, theatre, and dance. Conflating the two erases a distinction modern Japanese carries with some precision; English 'art' collapses both into a single ambiguous word.

芸能 (geinō) names the performing arts and entertainment — traditional performing arts (能楽 noh, 歌舞伎 kabuki, 文楽 bunraku) and modern entertainment (the 芸能界 'entertainment industry,' 芸能人 'celebrity / entertainer'). 芸術 by contrast names art in the philosophical-aesthetic sense — the autonomous aesthetic-cultural category. The 芸 the two compounds share is the same character, but 芸術 binds it to 術 (disciplined practice) for the aesthetic-philosophical sense, while 芸能 binds it to 能 (capacity / performative skill) for the performing-arts-and-entertainment sense. The distinction tracks roughly the European distinction between 'high art' and 'entertainment,' though the boundaries are differently drawn in Japanese cultural classification.

coinage_notes: Meiji historiographical and academic-institutional formation, stabilized through the establishment of the Tokyo Imperial University history department in 1887 (under Ludwig Riess, brought from Germany to introduce Rankean source-critical method), through Naka Michiyo's foundational Shina Tsūshi (支那通史, 1888–1890) and his broader scholarly corpus, and through the Meiji project of writing Japan into world history; the compound — combining 歴 (passing-through, sequential traversal) with 史 (the chronicler's record) — re-charged classical resources to render the modern Western academic discipline of history; carried into Chinese (lìshǐ) through Liang Qichao's Xin Shixue ('New Historiography,' 1902) and into Korean (yeoksa)

components.meaning: passing-through, sequential traversal — the experienced succession, the catalogued sequence of events; supplies the 'that-which-has-been-walked-through' that 史 records

the chronicler / the chronicler's record — the scribal preservation of what has occurred; supplies the disciplinary-textual register that converts mere sequence (歴) into history as recorded and studied

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering across the disciplinary, narrative, and ordinary-language senses
the disciplinary register: 歴史学 (history as a scholarly field), 歴史家 (historian), 史学 (also 'historiography / history as a discipline'), 歴史研究 (historical research)

translation_range.rendering: history (as the past itself / the historical process)
translation_range.emphasis: the ontological-temporal register: 歴史的事実 (historical fact), 歴史の流れ (the flow of history), 歴史の必然 (historical necessity / inevitability, often in Marxist or Hegelian usage)
adjectival register: 歴史的価値 (historical value), 歴史的意義 (historical significance), 歴史的瞬間 (historic moment)

conceptual_remainder: 歴史 is one of the most theoretically loaded Meiji reverse-flow compounds because it renames a domain in which East Asia possessed an enormous indigenous tradition. The classical Chinese and Japanese historiographical achievement — Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (史記), the twenty-four standard dynastic histories (二十四史), Sima Guang's Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance (資治通鑑), the six national histories of early Japan (六国史), the medieval and Edo historical traditions — was conceived under the heading 史 (the scribe's record) and organized around the chronicle (編年体) and standard-history (紀伝体) genres, with a strongly moral-evaluative purpose (the Spring and Autumn Annals' 春秋筆法 of 'praise and blame'). The modern Western academic discipline that the Meiji 歴史 was made to render was a nineteenth-century European achievement — Ranke's source-critical method, the seminar method at German universities, the secularizing rejection of providential history, the bounded periodization (ancient / medieval / modern), the disciplinary distinction from chronicle and antiquarianism. The Meiji compound binds these two heritages with productive tension. What the characters carry well is the experiential-recorded register: 歴 (the walked-through sequence) and 史 (the scribal record) together give 歴史 a phenomenological depth that the bare European 'history' inherits only obliquely from Greek ἱστορία (eyewitness inquiry). What the compound cannot natively carry without sustained methodological argument is the secular-critical-source-evidential register of Rankean historiography — that register had to be imported through the Tokyo University history department, Ludwig Riess's instruction, and Naka Michiyo's foundational works, and remains a continuing methodological project rather than a settled implication of the term itself. The long modern East Asian historiographical tradition — the late-Qing reform debate between 旧史学 and 新史学 (Liang Qichao), the early-twentieth-century Marxist historiography (the 'Asiatic Mode of Production' debate, the periodization of Chinese and Japanese history), the postwar Marxist and Annales-influenced historiographical schools, the postcolonial and global-historical reframings — can be read as the sustained working-out of what 歴史 should mean under the Rankean-and-after methodological demands.
doctrinal_weight: 歴史 organizes the modern East Asian academic-historical apparatus and a substantial portion of the broader modern cultural-political imagination. The Meiji period institutionalized the compound through the Tokyo Imperial University history department (1887), the founding of Shigaku Zasshi (史学雑誌, the foundational Japanese historical journal, 1889), the establishment of the trifold disciplinary division Kokushi 国史 / Tōyōshi 東洋史 / Seiyōshi 西洋史 (Japanese / East Asian / Western history) that structured modern Japanese academic historiography, and the foundational Meiji historical projects (Dai Nihon Shiryō 大日本史料 and Dai Nihon Komonjo 大日本古文書, the massive Tokyo University historiographical compilations begun in the late Meiji period and continued to the present). The compound carried into Chinese (lìshǐ) through Liang Qichao's Xin Shixue ('New Historiography,' 1902) and the May Fourth historical-reform tradition, and into Korean (yeoksa), becoming the universal pan-East-Asian word for history as a modern discipline. The compound heads a substantial productive cluster: 歴史学, 歴史家, 歴史的, 歴史観 (historical view / philosophy of history), 歴史哲学 (philosophy of history), 歴史認識 (historical recognition / consciousness — the operating term of contemporary East Asian political-historical controversy), and across the modern East Asian intellectual and political life questions of 歴史 — what counts as history, how the past should be remembered, whose history shall be told — remain among the most contested questions of regional public discourse.

false_friends.divergence: Classical 史 alone — as in 史記, 二十四史, 国史 — names the scribal-chronicle tradition: the standard dynastic histories, the official chronicles, the work of the 史官 (court historian). 歴史 as the modern academic discipline of source-critical, periodized history is constituted by binding 史 to 歴 (the experienced sequence) and re-charging the whole compound under Rankean methodological demands. Reading 歴史 as simply the modern label for the classical 史 tradition erases the methodological-disciplinary rupture: the modern compound names a different kind of intellectual practice, even when its sources and subject matter overlap with those of the classical 史.

故事 (koji / gùshì) names anecdotes from the past, traditional stories, the cited precedents and tales that classical East Asian rhetoric drew on for illustration. 歴史 is not a synonym: 故事 is fragmentary, anecdotal, and rhetorical, while 歴史 is the systematic, evidentially-grounded reconstruction of the human past. The distinction matters: classical East Asian writing made enormous use of 故事 as illustrative anecdote, but the systematic 歴史 of modern academic historiography is a different epistemological project.

coinage_notes: Nishi Amane (西周), stabilized as the title of his 1875 translation of Joseph Haven's Mental Philosophy (心理学), and entered as the standard rendering of 'psychology' in the Tetsugaku Jii (1881); the Wundtian experimental-scientific register was bound to the compound through Motora Yūjirō's establishment of Japan's first psychological laboratory at Tokyo Imperial University in 1888

components.meaning: heart-mind — the inherited Sino-Japanese cognitive-affective seat, here narrowed from its full classical breadth to the bounded modern psychological sense of 'mind' as the object of a disciplinary inquiry
principle, the systematic ordering pattern — the rational structure to be discerned; here the orderly intelligibility of mind that the discipline takes as its object
disciplined study, the -ology suffix — the Meiji workhorse that converts a subject-matter into the name of its systematic discipline

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering across the disciplinary, scientific, and ordinary-language senses — psychology as the academic discipline of mind
the older Scottish-common-sense register of Joseph Haven's textbook tradition, which Nishi Amane's 1875 translation rendered — psychology before its experimental-scientific narrowing
the Wundtian register imported by Motora Yūjirō in 1888 — psychology as the experimental study of mental phenomena, the discipline of the psychological laboratory
adjectival register: 心理的圧迫 (psychological pressure), 心理学者 (psychologist), 心理状態 (psychological state), 心理分析 (psychoanalysis), 深層心理 (depth psychology)

conceptual_remainder: 心理学 is built on the structural pattern that organizes most Meiji disciplinary names: a Sino-Japanese characterization of the discipline's subject-matter followed by the suffix 学. The pattern is uniform across 哲学 (philosophy, 'study of wisdom'), 化学 (chemistry, 'study of transformation'), 物理学 (physics, 'study of the principles of things'), and 心理学 (psychology, 'study of the principles of the heart-mind'). What 心 brings to the compound is dense: the classical Sino-Japanese 心 is the undivided seat of feeling, thought, and moral faculty, and in Chan/Zen and Neo-Confucian discourse it carries a doctrinal weight far heavier than the bounded modern psychological 'mind.' The Meiji deployment of 心 in 心理学 narrows the character drastically: where classical 心 was a metaphysical-ethical-spiritual category, the psychological 心 is a bounded object of experimental-disciplinary inquiry. 理 supplies the systematic-rational structure that the discipline studies, importing the same Sino-Japanese register that organizes 物理 (physics, the principles of things) and 倫理 (ethics, the principles of human relations). What the compound carries less well is the Western distinction between psychology and philosophy of mind: the Anglo-American tradition draws this distinction sharply, with psychology bounded to the experimental-scientific register and philosophy of mind operating as a separate philosophical discipline, but the Sino-Japanese 心理学 covers both registers without internal distinction, and the disciplinary boundary that Anglo-American thought polices through separate departmental institutions has to be supplied by surrounding modifiers (実験心理学 experimental psychology, 哲学的心理学 philosophical psychology) when needed. The compound also carries the residue of its 1875 Scottish-common-sense origin: Nishi's Haven translation was a faculty-psychology textbook in the antebellum American tradition, and the Wundtian experimental-laboratory register that displaced faculty psychology in the late nineteenth century arrived in Japan a generation after the compound had been stabilized. The history of Japanese psychology as a discipline can be read as the working-out of what 心理学 should mean under the experimental-scientific demands of the late-nineteenth-and-twentieth-century discipline that the term had to come to denote.
doctrinal_weight: 心理学 organizes the modern East Asian academic-psychological apparatus and a substantial portion of the broader twentieth-century vocabulary of mental life. The compound heads a productive cluster: 心理学者 (psychologist), 心理的 (psychological), 心理学的 (psychologistic — in the methodological-philosophical sense), 心理分析 (psychoanalysis), 深層心理学 (depth psychology), 行動心理学 (behavioral psychology), 発達心理学 (developmental psychology), 社会心理学 (social psychology), 臨床心理学 (clinical psychology), and the broader twentieth-century apparatus of Japanese, Chinese, and Korean academic psychology. The compound's transmission carries multiple distinct doctrinal-historical layers: the Scottish common-sense faculty psychology of Nishi Amane's 1875 Haven translation; the Wundtian experimental psychology imported by Motora Yūjirō at Tokyo Imperial University in 1888; the early-twentieth-century reception of Freudian psychoanalysis (the Japan Psychoanalytic Association founded 1929), Wertheimer Gestalt psychology, and the French dissociation-tradition of Janet and Ribot; the postwar reception of American behaviorism, cognitivism, and the broader twentieth-century psychological traditions; the contemporary academic-psychological apparatus organized around the Japanese Psychological Association (日本心理学会, founded 1927) and the broader East Asian academic-psychological institutions. The compound's reception in China through Liang Qichao and the late-Qing reform intellectuals, and in Korea through the colonial-period educational apparatus, made 心理学 / xīnlǐxué / simnihak the universal pan-East-Asian word for psychology as an academic discipline.

false_friends.divergence: Classical and Buddhist 心 (xīn / shin / kokoro) names the undivided heart-mind as the metaphysical-ethical-spiritual seat of consciousness, intention, and moral faculty — the 心 of 心経 (the Heart Sutra), of Chan/Zen 即心是仏 ('this very mind is Buddha'), of Neo-Confucian 心学 (Wang Yangming's School of the Mind). The 心 of 心理学 is a bounded modern object of experimental-disciplinary inquiry, narrowed from its full classical register to the operating sense of 'mind as the object of psychology.' The Meiji narrowing is doctrinally consequential: the compound 心理学 imports the Western disciplinary bounding of the mental and applies it to a Sino-Japanese character whose classical range was vastly broader.

心学 (shingaku) is the established compound for the Edo-period Sekimon Shingaku (石門心学) movement founded by Ishida Baigan (石田梅岩, 1685–1744) — a popular moral-educational movement teaching Confucian self-cultivation, the unity of Shintō-Confucian-Buddhist moral teachings, and the proper conduct of merchant and artisan classes. The classical-Chinese register of 心学 also names the Ming-Confucian Yangming school (Wang Yangming's School of the Mind).
