Neither register is psychology in the modern Western disciplinary sense: 心学 is moral cultivation through inward reflection on the heart-mind, while 心理学 is the academic-scientific discipline of mental phenomena. The Meiji choice of 心理学 over 心学 for psychology preserves the Edo-period 心学 compound for its established moral-cultivation register and bounds the modern psychological discipline to the distinct compound that incorporates 理 (the systematic ordering principle) and the disciplinary suffix 学.

coinage_notes: Meiji aesthetic and dramatic translation of the 1870s–1880s; stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Meiji project of rendering the Western dramatic-genre vocabulary in Sino-Japanese form; further institutionalized through the Shingeki (新劇) theatrical movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and through Tsubouchi Shōyō's translations of Shakespeare (1909–1928); the compound was structurally paired with 喜劇 (kigeki, comedy) to render the Western genre-distinction in compact Sino-Japanese form

components.meaning: sorrow, grief — the affective category that names the genre; here narrowed from its broader classical and Buddhist registers (慈悲 compassion, 悲嘆 grief) to the specifically aesthetic-dramatic register of represented sorrow

drama as represented performance — the head element supplying the genre-category; classical 'intensity / violent activity' narrowed to the modern theatrical sense of staged drama as bounded representation

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering: tragedy in the bounded Western theatrical sense — the staged drama of serious action ending in catastrophic loss
extended register: tragic event, catastrophic occurrence — 人生の悲劇 (life's tragedy), 歴史的悲劇 (historical tragedy); the dramatic genre-term extended to name catastrophic-tragic events in life and history
adjectival register: 悲劇的人物 (tragic figure), 悲劇的結末 (tragic ending), 悲劇性 (tragic quality)

conceptual_remainder: 悲劇 renders tragedy as 'sorrow-drama' (悲 + 劇), and in doing so settles on a compact characterization of the genre that captures one dimension of the Western tragic tradition while leaving substantial conceptual remainder on the table. The Western tragic genre is doctrinally complex: Aristotle's Poetics defines tragedy not by sorrow but by the imitation of serious action whose plot-shape involves a fall through hamartia, with catharsis as the affective effect on the audience; the Greek τραγῳδία etymologically names the 'goat-song' of the Dionysian festival, with no internal reference to sorrow; the Hegelian conception of tragedy as the conflict of ethical claims, the Nietzschean conception as the dialectic of Apollonian and Dionysian, the modern conception as the irreducible suffering of the individual under fate or society — none of these is captured by the bare characterization 'sorrow-drama.' What 悲劇 carries well is the affective dominant of the genre: the dramatic action ends in sorrow, the audience leaves moved by sorrow, the tragic mode is the mode in which sorrow rather than joy is the structural endpoint. What the compound cannot natively carry is the structural-dramaturgical apparatus of the Western tragic genre — the hamartia, the peripeteia, the anagnorisis, the cathartic resolution — which has to be supplied through the imported critical-theoretical vocabulary (悲劇的過誤 tragic error, 認識転換 anagnorisis, カタルシス catharsis as transliterated foreign loan). The genre-pair 悲劇 / 喜劇 also imposes a binary opposition on a tradition that classical East Asian theatrical culture did not have. The no, kabuki, and bunraku traditions had their own genre-vocabularies (the five categories of no plays, the historical / domestic / dance categories of kabuki, the period-piece / domestic categories of jōruri), and these traditional categories were not organized by the sorrow / joy axis that the Meiji compound-pair installs. The reception of Western tragedy in Meiji and post-Meiji Japan — through Tsubouchi Shōyō's Shakespeare translations, the Shingeki theatrical movement, the early-twentieth-century Tsukiji Little Theatre, the Mishima Yukio neoclassical revival of the post-war period — required the binary 悲劇 / 喜劇 to make sense, and the binary now organizes the modern East Asian theatrical-critical vocabulary even where it has not displaced the indigenous genre-vocabularies of the traditional theatrical forms.
doctrinal_weight: 悲劇 is the standard modern East Asian term for tragedy as a Western dramatic genre, organizing the reception of European tragic literature and the indigenous Japanese production of tragic drama in the modern period. The compound heads a small but precise cluster: 悲劇的 (tragic), 悲劇性 (tragic quality), 悲劇作家 (tragic playwright), 悲劇俳優 (tragic actor). Its institutional and critical reception is bound to the Shingeki theatrical movement, with Tsubouchi Shōyō's complete Japanese Shakespeare translations (40 volumes, 1909–1928) as the foundational engagement with European tragic drama, and the modern Japanese tragic theatre of Kishida Kunio, Mishima Yukio, and Abe Kōbō unfolding under the genre-category that the Meiji compound installed. The pair 悲劇 / 喜劇 also organizes the broader twentieth-century Japanese critical-theoretical engagement with European aesthetic theory — the reception of Aristotle's Poetics, the post-Kantian Hegelian and Schellingian theories of tragedy, the Nietzschean Birth of Tragedy, the Lukácsian and Heideggerian accounts — all of which arrive in Japanese under the heading 悲劇. The compound transferred into Chinese (bēijù 悲剧) and Korean (bigeuk 비극) as the standard pan-East-Asian term, and the bēijù / xǐjù pair organizes the modern Chinese and Korean theatrical-critical vocabularies as 悲劇 / 喜劇 organizes the Japanese.

false_friends.divergence: 悲哀 (hiai / bēi'āi) names sorrow and lament in the general affective register — the emotional state of grief or sadness in life. 悲劇 is not a synonym: 悲哀 is an affect, while 悲劇 is a bounded dramatic genre that represents sorrow as the structural endpoint of staged action. The classical East Asian literary tradition had ample vocabulary for sorrow-as-affect (悲哀, 悲嘆, 哀愁, 哀しみ) but did not bound a dramatic genre around the affect, and the Meiji 悲劇 names something the classical vocabulary did not name.

慈悲 (jihi / cíbēi) is the Mahāyāna Buddhist compound for loving-kindness and compassion (maitrī-karuṇā) — the bodhisattva's identification with the suffering of all beings, the standard rendering of Sanskrit karuṇā across the East Asian Buddhist tradition. The 悲 of 慈悲 is the active practice of compassionate suffering-with, not the affective category of sorrow that 悲劇 deploys. The same character does both kinds of work in modern Japanese, and the polysemy is generally legible in context but requires care: the 悲 of 慈悲 is a Buddhist virtue, the 悲 of 悲劇 is an aesthetic category.

coinage_notes: Meiji aesthetic and dramatic translation of the 1870s–1880s; stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Meiji project of rendering the Western dramatic-genre vocabulary in Sino-Japanese form; further institutionalized through the Shingeki (新劇) theatrical movement and through Tsubouchi Shōyō's translations of Shakespeare (1909–1928); the compound was structurally paired with 悲劇 (higeki, tragedy) to render the Western genre-distinction in compact Sino-Japanese form

components.meaning: joy, gladness — the affective category that names the genre; here narrowed from its broader classical register (the joy of celebration, the 喜 of 喜怒哀楽's fourfold emotional taxonomy) to the specifically aesthetic-dramatic register of represented joy and laughter
drama as represented performance — the head element supplying the genre-category; the same dramatic-genre suffix that pairs with 悲 in 悲劇

translation_range.emphasis: standard rendering: comedy in the bounded Western theatrical sense — the staged drama of light or humorous action ending in resolution
extended register: 喜劇映画 (comic film), 喜劇俳優 (comic actor), 軽喜劇 (light comedy); the genre-category extended to the broader humorous-performance register of modern Japanese popular culture
adjectival register: 喜劇的場面 (comic scene), 喜劇的効果 (comic effect), 喜劇性 (comic quality)

conceptual_remainder: 喜劇 renders comedy as 'joy-drama' (喜 + 劇) in structural parallel with 悲劇's 'sorrow-drama,' and the parallel is the compound's principal conceptual achievement. The Western genre-pair tragedy / comedy is doctrinally bound to the structural opposition of catastrophe and resolution, of noble protagonists and ordinary characters, of serious action and laughable action, and the Aristotelian and post-Aristotelian dramatic theory organizes the pair along multiple axes simultaneously. The Meiji compound-pair 悲劇 / 喜劇 captures one axis (the affective dominant: sorrow vs. joy) and binds the other axes to it through the surrounding critical-theoretical vocabulary. What 喜劇 carries well is the affective dominant: the comic drama ends in joy or in laughter, the audience leaves entertained, the action has been resolved rather than catastrophized. What the compound cannot natively carry is the structural-dramaturgical specifics of the Western comic tradition — the New Comedy plot of obstacles overcome to reach marriage, the Shakespearean comic structure of confusion-and-resolution, the Molièrian comedy of manners, the Restoration comedy of wit, the modern absurdist comedy of meaninglessness — each of which has had to be supplied through transliterated foreign loans or compound modifications (シェイクスピア喜劇 Shakespearean comedy, 不条理喜劇 absurdist comedy, 風俗喜劇 comedy of manners). The classical East Asian theatrical traditions had their own humorous-performance categories — the kyōgen 狂言 interludes performed between no plays, the comic registers of kabuki (such as the wagoto 和事 style of Kamigata-region soft-style acting), the comic vernacular performance traditions of rakugo 落語 and manzai 漫才 — but none of these traditional categories was the bounded Western comic dramatic genre, and the Meiji compound 喜劇 names a category that classical East Asian theatre did not have. The doctrinal pairing 喜劇 / 悲劇 thus installs in modern East Asian theatrical-critical vocabulary a Western binary that organizes the reception of European drama and that increasingly organized the indigenous Japanese theatrical production of the twentieth century, even where the classical theatrical traditions continued to operate under their indigenous genre-vocabularies.
doctrinal_weight: 喜劇 is the standard modern East Asian term for comedy as a Western dramatic genre, organizing the reception of European comic literature and the indigenous Japanese production of comic drama in the modern period. The compound heads a productive cluster: 喜劇的 (comic), 喜劇性 (comic quality), 喜劇作家 (comic playwright), 喜劇俳優 (comic actor), 軽喜劇 (light comedy), 風刺喜劇 (satirical comedy). Its institutional reception unfolded alongside that of 悲劇 through the Shingeki theatrical movement, with Tsubouchi Shōyō's Shakespeare translations as the foundational engagement with European comic drama, and the modern Japanese comic theatre of Kikuchi Kan, Inoue Hisashi, and the broader twentieth-century Japanese popular theatre developing under the genre-category that the Meiji compound installed. The compound transferred into Chinese (xǐjù 喜剧) and Korean (huigeuk 희극) as the standard pan-East-Asian term. The pair 悲劇 / 喜劇 also organizes the modern East Asian critical engagement with Western aesthetic theory of the genres — Aristotle's distinction between tragic and comic mimesis, the medieval and Renaissance dramatic theory, the Hegelian dialectic of tragic and comic, the post-Romantic and modernist theoretical apparatus around the comic — all of which arrive in Japanese, Chinese, and Korean academic-critical discourse under the heading 喜劇.

false_friends.divergence: Classical 喜 (xǐ / ki / yorokobi) names joy as one of the four canonical emotions of the Confucian 喜怒哀楽 (joy-anger-sorrow-pleasure) taxonomy — the affective category bound to the broader moral-psychological apparatus of the Doctrine of the Mean and its analysis of the centered equilibrium (中) of the unmoved heart-mind. The 喜 of 喜劇 is the aesthetic-dramatic narrowing of this affective category to the bounded modern theatrical genre of represented joy. The Meiji compound exploits the classical taxonomy to bind the aesthetic genre-category to the deeper Sino-Japanese affective vocabulary, but the genre-bounded sense of 喜劇 is doctrinally distinct from the moral-psychological 喜 of classical Confucian discourse.

狂言 (kyōgen) names the comic-theatrical genre of the traditional Japanese stage — the short comic interludes performed between no plays in the no-and-kyōgen theatrical complex, and by extension the broader register of comic-theatrical performance in classical and modern Japanese theatre. 喜劇 is not a synonym: 狂言 is a specific indigenous Japanese theatrical genre with its own conventions, performance tradition, and historical-institutional articulation, while 喜劇 is the Meiji-coined Western dramatic genre-category. The two terms operate in distinct theatrical-historical registers, and modern Japanese theatrical discourse maintains the distinction with some precision: 狂言 names the no-and-kyōgen tradition, 喜劇 names the modern Western-style comic dramatic genre.
